Mr. Speaker reported, that the House had attended His Majesty in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker laid he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Situation of Afiairs, both at Home and Abroad, has enabled Me to allow you that Reeds, which has been usualjn Hines of public Traoquillity.

which is to be solemnized as soon as their respective Ages will permit.

I observe with Pleasure, that the Events which have happened in the course of the last Year, give us Reason to hope for the Duration of that Peace, which has been lb happily established, and which it is my Resolution strictly, to.maintain. The Courts of France and have given Me firelh Assurances of their good Diipo-fitions. . The future Quiet of the Empire has been confirmed by the unanimous Choice of a Successor to the.Imperial Dignity; and the peaceable Rledion of the King of Poland has prevented those fatal Confc-queqces which, upon similar Occasions, have so frequently. been destrudive to the Repose of Europe, I am happy, therefore, to meet my Parliament, at a Time when no foreign Disturbances interrupt their Confutations for the internal good Order and Prosperity of My Kingdoms.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I Qiall dk of you, for the current Service of the Year, no other Supplies, than such as are necessary for those Establishments which have already met with your Approbation; and I will order the proper Estimates for this Purpose to be laid before you.

I must, however, earnestly recommend to you the Continuance of that Attention, which you hfive hitherto shewn, for the Improvement of the Publig Revenue, and the Diminution of the National Debt. For these desirable and necessary Ends, I am persuaded that, you will purfiie every proper Measure, which else State of My Dominions, and the Circumstances of the Times, may require.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Experience which I have had of your former Conduct makes Me rely on your Wisdom, and Firm-ness, in promoting that Obedience to the Laws, and Reiped to the Legislative Authority of this Kingdom, which is essentially necessary for the Safety of the Whole; and in establishing such Regulations, as may best conned: and strengthen every Part of My Dominions, for their mutual Benefit and Support.

The Affedion which I bear to My People excites My earned Wishes, that every Session of Parliament may, be distinguistied by some Plans for the public Advantage, and for their Relief from those Difficulties, which an expensive War has brought upon them. My Concurrence and Encouragement shall never be wanting

That in this Situation, we diink it our Duty to give our particular Attention to such Regulations, as will most effectually promote the internal good Order and Prosperity of these Kingdoms.

To allure His Majesty, that we will, with Chearfol-ness and Dispatch, raile such Supplies as shall be found necessary for the current Service of the Year: And that, thoroughly sensible of His Majesty’s paternal Concern for the Relief and Welfare of His People, in recommending to us the Improvement of the Public Revenue, and the Diminution of the National Debt, on which the future Safety of Great Britain mud depend, we will apply ourfdves, with the utmod Zeal and Assiduity, to cany into Execution every proper Measure which may contribute to these great and salutary Purposes, and which the State of His Majesty’s Dominions, ami the Circumstances of the Times, shall require.

To acknowledge, with the livdied Gratitude, the gracious Expressions of His Majesty’s tender AfieAion, and of His condant Care, for the mutual Benefit and Support of all His Subjects; and to allure His Majesty, that, animated with these Sentiments, We will endeavour to deserve the Confidence which His Majesty is pleased to repose in us, by pursuing every Plan which shall appear to us to be calculated for the Public Advantage; and that we will proceed therein with that Temper and Firmnefe, which will bed conciliate and insure due Sab-million to die Laws, and Reverence to the Legislative Authority, of Great Britain.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had, on Tuesday the 8th Day of this Instant January, received from Vice Admiral Cornish the following Letter, in Re-16

To the Right honourable Si rjfchnCufl Baronet, Speaker of the honourable House of Commons.

Sir,

The Honour of your Letter inclosing the most valuable Testimony of the honourable House of Commons, in Favour of my Conduit, in assisting the Reduction of Manilla and the Philippine Islands, with His Majesty’s Forces under my Command, was hot received till the ICth of August lad: it did not reach India till after my Departure, and confidently could not come to my Hand but by being sent back to England.

But this Delay has no Power to diminish the Satisfaction which every honed Man must receive from the Approbation of that honourable House, which repre-fents the Commons of Great Britain. I can pretend only to the Merit of intending well; and in that Intention I hope this illustrious Distinction will encourage me to persevere.

To you. Sir, I shall always acknowledge my Obligations for your kind Attention, and hope always to retain the Honour of befog,

Sir,

Parliament Street, Your most obliged,

8th January, 1765. most obedient, and

mod bumble Servant,

A PETITION of the Honourable Edward Bouvtrie, Hardingftou Lord of the Manors of Hardingftone and Cotton, in the County of Northampton, and Impropriator of the Great Tythes, and of the Tythe of Lamb arising from the Lands of the Parish of Hardingftone and Cotton aforesaid; and also a Proprietor of the greatest Part of the said Land; the Reverend Robert Faux, Vicar of the said Parish Church, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That there are within the said Manors and Parish several Open Common and Arable Lands and Fields, Common Meadows, and Common Grounds; and also several Lanes and Waste Grounds, wherein the Properties of the Petitioners and others lie intermixed and dispersed, and, in their present Situation, are incapable of any considerable Improvement, but would be of great Advantage to the several Parties interested, and to the Public, if the same were divided and inclosed, and specific Shares allotted to the several Persons interested therein: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Frederick Montagu and Mr. Kynaston do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned againfr.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity againfr such Person.

Address on The Lord JVarkworth reported from the Committee the King’* appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be pre-peec"' fented to His Majesty, that the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the feme in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the feme was read; and is as follow* ethj viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign.

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty the most humble Thanks of this House for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

Permit us, at the same Time, to offer to Your Majesty our dutiful Congratulations upon the Marriage agreed to be solemnized between the Prince Royal of Denmark and Her Royal Highness the Princess Caroline Matilda, as (oon as their respective Ages will permit; which happy Union cannot but be most pleasing to Your faithful Commons, as it must tend to cement and strengthen the ancient Alliance between the Crowns of Great Britain and Denmark, and thereby add Security to the Protestant Religion.

We beg Leave also to declare our Satisfeftion at those Events of the last Year, which promise the Continuance of the Peace (b happily established and maintained by your Majesty’s wife and steady Conduct; and to express our Hopes that the fresh Assurances, which have been given by the Courts of France and Spain, of their good Dispositions, the unanimous Choice of a Successor to the Imperial Throne, and the undisturbed Election of the King of Poland, will secure and confirm the general Tranquillity of Europe, In this situation, we think it our Duty to give our particular Attention to such Regulations, as will most effectually promote the internal good Order and Prosperity of these Kingdoms.

Your Majesty may be allured that we will, with Cheertulnels and Dispatch, raile such Supplies as shall be found necessary for the current Service of the Year. And, being thoroughly sensible of Your Majesty’s paternal Concern for the Relief and Welfare of Your People, in recommending to us the Improvement of the Public Revenue, and the Diminution of the National Debt, on which the future Safety of Great Britain most depend, we will apply ourselves, with the utmost Zeal and Assiduity, to cany into execution every proper Measure which may contribute to these great and falu-tary Purposes, and which the State of Your Majesty’s Dominions, and the Circumstances of the Times, shall require.

We acknowledge, with the liveliest Gratitude, the gracious Expressions of Your Majesty’s tender Affection, and of your constant Care, for the mutual Benefit and Support of all Your Subjects. And we allure Your

Vol. 30.

Majesty, that, animated with these Sentiments, wc will -endeavour to deserve the Confidence which Your Majesty is pleased to repose in us, by pursuing every Plan which shall appear to us to be calculated for the public Advantage; and will proceed therein with that Temper and Firmness, which will best conciliate and ensure due Submission to the Laws, and Reverence to the Legifla-tive Authority of Great Britain.

The said Address being read a Second Time}

A Petition of the several Merchants, whole Names Bringing are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves and Effects frotn several other Merchants concerned in the Trade to Colonies. Guadeloupe, Martinieo, and the Havannah, was presented to the House, and read: Reciting, That, by an Act, made in the Third Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, reciting, that, by the Definitive Treaty of Peace between His Majesty and the Crowns of France and Spain, ratified the ioth Day of March 1763, the Islands of Guadeloupe, Marie Galante, Degrade, Martinieo, and Goree, were ceded to France-, and

all that His Majesty had conquered in the Island of Cuba, was ceded to Spain; and the Term of Eighteen Months, to be computed from the Day of the Ratification of the said Treaty, was thereby allowed to British Subjects to transport their Effects from those Islands, to the end that His Majesty’s Subjects, having Effects in the Places before mentioned, might have all due Encouragement and Opportunity to bring the same from thence; it is enacted, That it should and might be lawful for any of His Majesty’s Subjects to import into this Kingdom, at any Time before the First Day of November 1764, and no longer, in British Ships, navigated according to Law, directly from the Places before-mentioned, any Goods or Effects, being the Growth or Produce thereof respectively, upon Payment of such and the like Customs and Duties only as would be due and payable for the feme, if such Places had remained, and were in Possession of His Majesty; and that, under the Sanction of the said Act, the Petitioners did, agreeable to the said Treaty of Peace, freight several Ships to Martinieo, Guadeloupe, and the Havannah; and that the Inability of the French Subjects, in the Islands of Guadeloupe and Martinieo, to pay the Debts due to the British Subjects, within the Time stipulated by the said Treaty of Peace, having occasioned a Prolongation of the Terms of Payment of such Debts, the Governors of the said Islands permitted the British Ships to remain there till such Payments should be completed; and the constant Easterly Winds having detained at Sea such Ships as were coming from the Havannah beyond the Time so limited by the said Act, none of the said Ships could, or did arrive in any Part of Great Britain, before the said First Day of November last: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and grant the Petitioners such Relief therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

Colonies. appeared to your Committee, by the Evidence of

Henry Guinand, John H Peter Fear on, William

Crichton, and Charles Ogil Esquires, that several Ships

had been freighted to , Guadeloupe, and the

Havannah, to bring home the Effects of the Briti/k Subjects, arising from Debts contrafted in those Islands.

And by Two Lists of Ships produced to your Committee, it appeared that 34 Passes had been taken from His Majesty’s Secretary of State, for Ships to go

to the Islands ceded to by the Treaty concluded

at Paris the 10th Day of February 1763; and Six Pafles for Ships to go to the Havannah.

Then Captain Andrew Cornish laid, That he tailed from Guadeloupe the 26th of October last; and that he could not get his leading before that Time, the French Subjects not being able to pay their Debts sooner; that the Time limited by the Treaty for the Departure of the British Ships, was the 10th of September -, but by the Permission of the several Governors they were allowed a further Time.

Captain Robert Morrison informed your Committee, That he failed from Guadeloupe the 10th of last, being unable to get in his Loading before; and that he had Leave of the Governor to stay till that Time; and that he left several British Ships there at the Time of his Departure.

James Gordon, Master of the Carolina Merchant, laid, That he failed from the Havannah the 1 ith of September, made Land in England the ad of November, and arrived in the River the 10th of the same Month: And that his Ship was the first that arrived from the Havannah.

That the reason of his late Arrival was the contrary Winds, from N.E. to S.E. by which Means the Passage took up Three Months, which he expected to have performed in Five Weeks: And,

Captain John Cowling, Commander of the Ship George, from Guadeloupe, laid. That he left Guadeloupe the 15th of September, and was Three Months in his Padage to England, occasioned by the Easterly Winds.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners produced a Letter from William Woodbridge, to Messieurs John and Co. dated Guadeloupe, 27 1764, wherein the

following Extract was read; " The very heavy and continual Rains, ever since the Month of May last, have " retarded every’ one, and have been of great Prejudice " to the English in particular, so much, that I am " confident, not One Half of the British Effects will be " gathered in by the 13th of October, the Time limited " for our Evacuation."

Ext raft of a Letter from Mr. Woodbridge to the same Persons, dated 7 November 1764, was also read, as follows: " You will perhaps be surprized to find by this ltLetter, that 1 am (till here, but I have not yet been " able to finish alt the public Business; however, as I " am engaged, I am determined to go through with it;

" but this will not now detain me long, for l am to have " Audience Tomorrow of the General and Intendant,

" to settle finally every thing relating to the English " Affairs, and to secure the large Sum yet remaining " due to the British Subjects r A Sum that exceeds " £. 200,000 Currency."

Extract of a Letter from Robert Malcolm to Messieurs ' Fordice, Grant, and Co. dated BaJJeterre, Guadeloupe,

24 October 1764, was also read, as follows: " All or " most of the English here, were convened this Morning before the General and Intendant, as the Time is " now past that was limited for our and out Ships Departure; after much Conversation, it was concluded,

" by a Desire of these Rulers, that those who desired to " stay any longer should give in their Names and Reasons for it. The Intendant^ who is the Man of " Business, and Manager of Civil Affairs, recommended very gently, that such as had but little to do, and 20

" could have it done ay their Friends, would go; but " nothing like any Order to go was hinted: He gave " strong Assurances, that the Planters should not be " allowed to dispose of their Produce for any other Purpose than the Payment of their English Debts; that " they would put in Prison any one that attempted it.

" In short, it is performed as promised, in the most " solemn Manner. We have all the Justice we could " demand; he declared he would allow no more Ships " Frenchified; so after the Ships that now are here with " Permissions are gone, Effects must go for France in " real French Vessels, unless particular Permissions are " got from the Courts of F. and E. not referring to the Treaty; any, in consequence of the Treaty, will be objected to as past the Time."

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for extending the Time granted, by an Act passed in the Third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for allowing His Majesty’s Subjects to import their Goods and Effects, being the Produce of certain Places ceded to France and Spain by the late Treaty of Peace, upon Payment of the same Duties as they would have been liable to, if the same Places had remained in His Majesty’s Possession: And that Mr. Cujl, Mr. Bolton, Mr.

Mr. Blackstone reported from the Committee, ftp- Poor Law*, pointed to revise and consider the Laws relating to the Poor of that Part of Great Britain called England; and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House, as to the Defers, the Repeal, or Amendment, of the said Laws, and as to making of any new Provisions or Regulations for the better Relief, Employment, and Settlement, of the Poor; That the Committee had considered the Matters to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Laws relating to the Poor arc, in many Re-spe&s, defective.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the present Method of regulating the Poor by annual Parochial Officers, in separate Parishes and Townships, is, in general, ineffectual for their proper Relief and Employment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the present Methods of applying the Sums raised for the Relief of the Poor are, in general, grievous to their respective Parishes, and of pernicious effects to the Public.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Employment of the able Poor, in such Works as may be suited to their Strength and Capacity, will be very beneficial to the Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Appointment of a competent Number of Districts throughout England and Wales, by Authority of Parliament, with proper Powers for uniting and incorporating the several Parishes, Townships, and Places in each, and the establishing a proper H ospital, Workhouse, and House of Correction, in each District, under the Management of Governors, Directors, or Trustees, to be specially chosen for that Purp ife, will be the most easy and effectual Method for relieving the impotent, employing the industrious, and reforming the vicious Poor.

The laid Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Gilbert, Mr. Blackstone,

Sir Roger Newdigate, the Lord Cary fort, Mr. Peter Burrell, Mr. Fuller, Sir George Savile, Mr. Morton, Mr.

John Richmond Webb, and Mr. Gray, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said- Petition, Mr.

Oliver being examined, said. That the several Roads leading from the Town of Wareham, in the County of to and through the several Places described in the Petition, by Reason of the Narrownels in some Parts, and of several steep Hills and stony Rocks, are very inconvenient, and, on Account of the many heavy Carriages passing thereon, are, in many Parts thereof, become ruinous, and dangerous to Passengers and Carriages; and that the said Roads cainnot he effectually widened, amended, and kept in Repair, by the present Methods prescribed by Law.

The above Evidence was confirmed by several Members present at the Committee.

And the said Petition was read; Red ting? That by an High Price Act made in the Thirty-first.Ydar of his late Majesty, for o{ Whctr» the due making of Bread, and to regulate the Price and &c Assize thereof, and to punish Persons who shall adulterate Meal, Flour, or Bread, Returns are required to be made Weekly to lhe said Court of Mayor and Aldermen, by, the MeaL weighers of the said City, upon Oath, of the Prices which Wfieat and the several Kinds of Grain, Meal, and Flour, fit for Bread, fell for in the Markets of the said.

City; and the Assize and Price of Bread is, by the said Act, required to be, from Time to Time, let. by, the said Court of Mayor and Alderman, if fitting, of ty the Mayor of the said City, if the said Court should not fit, to be in Force for the said City of London, and the Liberties thereof, and the Weekly Bills of Mortality, .: : */ except as in the said Act is excepted; that, in pursuance of the said Act, such. Returns have been, from Time to Time, regularly made, upon Oath, by the Meal-weighers of the said City, and the Assize of Bread to take Place, and be in Force as aforesaid, hath been duly set by the said Court of Mayor and Aldermen, or by the Mayor of the said City for the Time being, according to the said Act, and according to the R.ght and Custom of the City of London, and the Practice there ufrd to let the fame, that the Petitioners think it a Duty they owe to the Public, in the Exercise of this great Trust, humbly to represent to this House, that it appears to the said Court of Mayor and Aldermen, by such Returns made upon Oath, that the Price of Wheat hath advanced gradually from the Tjme of the last Harvelt; and that, by the last Return made to the Mayor of the said City,-On Tueftday the 22d-of this instant January, the Price of

Wheat was from Forty-three to Forty-seven Shillings and Six-pence a Quarter; and that the Price of Bread is now higher than it has been at any Time, since the Act, under which the Assize is now set, was made; and that the Petition's have lleafon to fear that, as the Kingdom was much exhausted by the large Export of the last Year to Italy, Spain, and Portugal, and considerable Tracts of Corn Land suffered greatly by the excessive Rains in the last Winter, the Price of Wheat will still advance, to the Distress of the Poor, and to the Prejudice of the Manufacturers of this City and Kingdom in general; and that the Petitioners humbly apprehend, that the prohibiting the Exportation of Wheat and Flour for a Time, may be a Means of preventing this Evil: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration; and to grant such Relief therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

ing next, resolve itself into a Comrhittee of the whole House, ioconsiderof the said Petition.

A Petition of the Bailiffs, Wardens, Assistants, and Silk Commonalty of the Trade, Art, and Mystery of Wea- M*n"f"aure* vers of London. in Behalf of themselves and the Silk Manufacturers of Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Silk Manufacture labours under great Discouragement from the Increase in the Use and Wear of French and other Foreign Wrought Silks imported into this Kingdom; and that by reason of this Discouragement, a great Number of Weavers in the Silk Manufacture have been, and still are out of Employ; and, unless some speedy and effectual Relief be obtained, the Masters will be under a Necessity of discharging many more; and that there is great Reason to apprehend that the Silk Manufacture will fall to Decay and Ruin, which has been brought to great Perfection, and given Employment to many thousands of H is Majesty’s faithful Subjects, who will be reduced to great Distress, or driven to go abroad to seek Employment, to the Detriment of the Public and Loss to the Revenue: And therefore praying the Hrtufe to take the Premises into their Consideration; and to give such Relief therein, as to the House shall appear reasonable.

Supply. Mr. Alderman Dickinson, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had di reded him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read} and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Four hundred and Seven thousand Seven hundred Thirty-four Pounds Eleven Shillings and Three Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for the Ordinary of the Navy, including Half-pay to Sea and Marine Officers, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Five Thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account, to be applied by the Commissioners or Governors of the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich, for the Support and Relief of Seamen worn out and become decrepit in the Service of their Country, who shall not be provided for within the said Hospital.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, u That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred thousand

Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, towards the Building, Re-buildings, and Repairs of His Majesty’s Ships, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-five.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ways The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a and Means. Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson reported from the Committee, Th^t they had come to a Resolution} which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson also acquainted the House, that he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again!

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a and Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to indem-Empioyment*. njjy such persons as have omitted to qualify themselves for Offices and Employments; and to indemnify Justice9 of the Peace, Deputy Lieutenants, Officers of the Mi-, litia, or others, who have omitted to register, or deliver in, their Qualifications, within the Time limited by Law; Rnd lor giving further Time for those Purposes.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Fuller took the Chair of the Committee,

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Fuller reported from the Committee, that they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Mom- Supply, ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act made in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Roads from Mullens Pond, in the County of Southampton, to the Eighteen Mile Stone from the City, of Salisbury near Willoughby Hedge-, and from West Amesbury to Anflow Hill -, and from Amesbury to Fiddleton-, and from the New Inn in Amesbury to the End of the Parish leading to Durington; and from Wily to Cook's House and Land-ford -, and from Beacon Hill to the Nag's Head-, and from thence One Mile of the Road leading to Shrewton, in the County of Wilts; was read.

Mr. Francis Rolfe, Clerk and Treasurer to the said Trustees, produced several Accounts, by which it appears, that the Sum of .2,900 is now owing on the Credit of the said Act; and the net Annual Income of the Tolls, in the last Year, was no more than £. 144. 14. 7f. without making any allowance for the Surveyor’s Sal ary.

And being examined, he laid, That there is now more Money owing than was at the Time of making up that Account; and that it isimpollible to repair the said Roads effectually, unless the Term and Powers granted by the said Act are further enlaged and altered.

Mr. Richard Lever such being examined, confirmed Mr.

Rolfe's Evidence, in regard to the Impofiibility of repairing the said Roads, unless the Term and Powers of the said Act are further enlarged: And said.

That the Part of a Clause in the said Act, which re-llrains the Trustees from erecting any Gate between Mills Close and the House of Thomas Prior Tibbs, has been found very inconvenient.

That he knows the other Roads mentioned in the Petition; that they are, in general in a ruinous Condition; jn many Parts narrow and incommodious; and that they cannot be effectually repaired and widened by the ordinary Course of Law.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, to continue the Term and enlarge the Powers of an Act, passed in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from Mullen’s Pond, in the County of Southampton, to the Eighteen Mile Stone from the City of Salisbury, and several other Roads in the said Act mentioned; and also for repairing and widening the Roads from the said Turnpike Road to Fifty Yards beyond the Blacksmith’s Shop at Littleton-, and from the said Turnpike Road to Mr. Jennen's Well, and to V Lane, at Chalder-ton, and from thence to Mullen's Pond -, and allb a Lane called Applejhaw Lane, leading out of East Chalderton, to the Andover Turnpike Road: and that Sir Robert Long, Mr. Ridley, and Sir Edward Bayntun, do prepare, and bring in, the feme.

That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of this House, that Application has been made by the Bailiffs, Wardens, Assistants, and Commonalty of the Trade, Art, and Mystery of Weavers of London, on behalf of themselves and the Silk Manufacturers of Great Britain; alleging, that the>Silk Manufacture labours under great Discouragement from the Increase in the Use and Wear of French and other Foreign Wrought Silks imported into this Kingdom; and alleging, that, if the Importation into this Kingdom of all Foreign Wrought Silks were to be prohibited, or any higher Duties laid, it would be very injurious, not only to the Petitioners, but the Public in general, and likewise a great Loss to the Revenue: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be heard before the Committee, to whom the said Petition is referred.

A Petition of the several Hosiers, Frame-work-knitters, Manufacturers of, and Dealers in Frame-work-knitted Silk Stockings, Silk Gloves, and Silk Mitts, whole Names are thereunder written, living and redding in the Town of Nottingham, and in several Towns and Places being near to die fame, as well on behalf of themselves as many hundred of poor Manufacturers and their Families employed in the same Trade, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, for many Years past, a very considerable Inland Trade has been carried on in this Kingdom, and particularly in and neat the said Town of Nottingham, in the making and vending Frame work-knitted Silk Stockings, Silk Gloves* and Silk Mitts, for Home Consumption; whereby a* well the Petitioners, as many poor industrious Families; have been employed, and creditably maintained; and that this very valuable Branch of Inland Trade has gone to Decay, and been almost totally ruined, whereby many hundred industrious Families have been, and are now, reduced to very great Hardships, Poverty, and Distress; and that the Petitioners humbly apprehend, that this Decay has arisen from the large Quantities of Foreign Silk Stockings, Silk Gloves, and Silk Mitts, which are clandestinely imported into this Kingdom; and that the Public Revenue is greatly detrimeoted by such Imports, as no Duty is paid for the Silk of which such Foreign Goods are made; and that the Petitioners humbly apprehend, that, if a Law was made entirely to prohibit the Importation of any Foreign Silk Stockings, Silk Gloves, and Silk Mitts, it would not only tend to restore this valuable Branch of Inland Trade, and thereby give Relief to the Petitioners in the Premises, but also greatly increase the Public Revenue: And therefore praying the House to take the Petition into Consideration, and give such Relief to the Petitioners, by restoring this valuable Blanch of Inland Trade, in such Manner as they Hull think fit.

That the Roads from the South End of the Town of Newton Abbot, through the several Places mentioned in the Petition, to King's Ware Passage, are in general very ruinous and narrow, some Parts being not above 8 or 10 Feet wide; and that in mapy Places 'fwo Carriages cannot pass each other.

That the Road from King's Ware to Netbway which is about a Mile and H?lf, is so veiy narrow that a Carriage cannot pass.

That the Witness believes the fltatute Work has been done upon some Part of it, but he does not think the Statute Work can keep the Road in good Repair; that the Road is very hilly.

That the Road from King's Ware to Ledgwqy Cross is very often overflowed by the Tides; that the Water at high Tide flows Feet above the Road at Waterhead; but if Bridges and Causeways were built he believes they would carry off the Water; that the Creek at heady when it is high Water, is not passable without riding Feet deep in Water; that Carriages may go ps for as Waterhead, but nqt to Ware Town.

That the Road from Newton Abbot to King's Ware Passage is about Fifteen M*les in Length; and that if the Road was raised apd made Turnpike, it would Ipe passable at all Times.

Mr. George Morry produced to your Committee, a Computation of the Tolls from the 23d December to the 10th January, during which Time there were not any Fairs; and he likewise informed your Committee, that he made this Computation from his own Observation at Ford Gate, where he was placed, and had an Opportunity of seeing all the Passengers that passed the different Roads.

That the Number of Horses which travelled on the Peep inn Road in the same Time were 1,308, and the Number of Carriages were Five, and the Number of Oxen and Sheep were 239.

To prove the Allegations of the Second-mentioned Petition,

Mr. James Garrett, being examined, said, That the Road from the East End of Newton Abbot to Keyberry Bridge \s,in some Parts, 12 Feet wide, and in other Parts wider, and the Soil is pretty good; that the Statute Work would repair the Road from Woolborough to Keyberry Bridge.

That the Road from Combintinhead to the Passage House in Shaldon is so very narrow, that in many Places Two Horses cannot pass each other without great Difficulty; that there are many Cliffs to ride over, which are vety dangerous; that the Soil is in some Parts gravelly, in some Parts clayey, and in other Parts rocky.

That the Road from Keyberry Bridge to Torkay, which is upwards of Seven Milos, is in many Parts very narrow and founderous, that the narrowefl Part is not above Six Feet wide.

That the Road from Keyberry Bridge to Cockington is rather worse than the rest, and is very founderous, hilly, and narrow.

That Carriages may go to Torkay from Keyberry Bridge, but not without great Danger; that he does not remember any Carriages have passed that Way.

That the Road from Kingskerwell to Keyberry Bridge, and the Road from Kingskerwell ' to the Point of the Lane, coming into the Road from Keyberry Bridge to Newton Abbot, are not above Half a Mile from each -other, and in some Places not so much.

That the Road from Keyberry Bridge to Cockington does not go through the same Village of as

the Road from Newton Abbot to Five Lanes; one Road touches at the End of the Village from Newton Abbot to Five Lanes, and the other goes through the Village.

That the Road from Cockington to Torbay is not more than Half a Mile, and the Road from Paington to bay is about a Quarter of a Mile.

That Cockington is not a Borough Town, but more than a Village, but does not know whether a Market Town, or not.

After Passengers have passed over Keyberry Bridge they come upon a Down; where all the Roads branch upon the Down; that the Road upon the Down is not inclosed, by which Means the Passage cannot be flopped but at Keyberry Bridge.

That the Statute Labour is not sufficient to amend these Three Roads.

That the Road from Coombe's Cellar to Shaldon is impassable till the Tide is half ebbed out, and then Carriages cannot pass, because they cannot turn.

Mr. James Pike, being examined, said. That he was employed from 14th December to 3d January, to take an Account of Tolls, that he was stationed at Ford Gate in such a Situation as to be able to fee all the different Roads, during which Time there were not any Fairs; and he produced to your Committee an Account of the Tolls to be taken (according to the Tolls under the Totness Road Act) upon the Road between Ford Gate and Shaldon, for the First Week, which amounted to £. 1. 6s. 11 d.for the Second Week to 1. 4 od.%, and for the Third Week to £. i.- £S.

That the Tolls from Ford Gate to Torkay for the First Week, amounted to £.1.2 7 for the Second Week,-to i$s. od.$; and for the Third Week, to j8r. 2 d.$.

That the Tolls from Newton Abbot to Cockington, by Keyberry Bridge, for the First Week, amounted to 17

That he was very particular in taking this Account; that he knew most of the Inhabitants of the several Parishes upon all the Roads, and those that he did not know, he asked which Road they were going.

That he does not know any particular Reason for the Conflux of Passengers, but he believes th Road must have the Advantage, as the Season for Cabbage Plants was coming in, which occasions great Traffic on the Road. /

John Blake, Esquire, informed your Committee, That

the Fish Carts from Btixham, Torkay, Cockington, ton, and Dartmouth, travel through these Roads in their way to London, and that if they were repaired he apprehends they might save an Hour in travelling from Brixhamto Newton Abbot; that they are allowed

Three Hours to do it in, but they are in general Three Hours and an Half} that his Carriages have broke down between Brixham and Newton Abbot by the Badness of the Road; and that if thele Roads were' made Turnpike the London Markets would be supplied with Fish about an Hourfooner than at present.

Mr. William Floyd further said, That the Badness of the Road from Brixham to Newton Abbot damages the Fish; that the Carriages are allowed Three Hours to travel from thence, but they seldom perform it in that Time; that he knew a Carriage that was stopt Eleven JHours by the Badness of the Roads; and not having another Carriage ready to carry the Fish in the room of that which broke down, was the occasion of this Delay.

That if a Fishery was established at , he

does not apprehend it would answer so well as that at Brixham.

_ Mr. James Pike further laid, that he travelled the

Road from Newton Abbot to Keyberry Bridge j that it is a very good Road at all Times of the Year; but the Road from Keyberry Bridge to Shaldon is very crooked, deep, and narrow, lies upon the Cliff, and has many dangerous Turns, and is full of Water; the Road to Torkay is the best of the Three Roads, over the Downs might be made good by very little Repair, but grows worse off the Downs, and is very rocky and bad.

That the Cockington Road lies low, and has much Water in it; in forae Parts it is so narrow; that theft is but just Room for a Chaise.

After Passengers get off the Bridge they come upon a large Down, and there is no other way of flopping the Three Roads but by placing a Gate at the Bridge.

That all the Three Roads are in general in very bad Repair, and he does not think the Statute Latxbut will be sufficient to amend them.

That the Road entering into Paington, between Cockington and Smoky House, which the- Witness called the Middle Road, is the ttfcareft Road, because it can be travelled in the least Time. - ’ '

" Resolved, That the Distance between the Twd

Points in the Gold Studs in the Brass Rod, described in this Report, and delivered herewith, ought to be! the Length called a Yard; and the Instrument, also herewith delivered, adjusted to the same Length* ought to be preferred, and uled for f.zing Measures of Length, at the Exchequer; and that One Third Part of the said Length, called the Yard, should be* a Foot, and the Twelfth Part of that Third, or Foot, deemed One Inch."

" Refolded, That all Measures of Length whatsoevef.

should be taken in Parts, Multiples* or Certain Proportions, of the said Standard Yard."

" Resolved, That Measures, called Measures of Capacity, should be ascertained, according to the Number of cubical Inches therein contained."'

" Resolved, That all Measures of the same Denomination, whether of Liquids, or of dry Goods, ought to contain the same Number of cubical Inches; and that the Gallon ought to contain 282 such Inches, and the Quart One Fourth of the Gallon, and the' Pint One Half of ’the Quart."

" Resolved, That the Bushel ought to contain Eight of the said Gallons, and the Quarter Eight such Bu-Ihels; and all other Measures, called Measures of Capacity, ought to be taken in Parts, Multiples,; or proportional Parts, of the said Gallon." ’

" Resolved, That all Goods myafured by any of the said Measures of Capacity, should not be heaped, but* stricken, with a round Strike of the same Didmcte^ from one End to the other."

" Resolved, That the Standard df Weight ought to

be the Pound herewith delivered, described in Ah is Report, and made upon the Examination and Revifcw of the several present Standard-Troy Weights-'therein mentioned j and that the Twelfth" Part of the said Pound should be an Ounce, the Twentieth Part of such Ounce a Pennyweight, and the Twenty-fourth Part of such- Pennyweight a Grain."- Resolved, That' all other Weights should be taken from Parts, Multiples, or certain Proportions of the said Standard Pound."

" Resolved, That all Contrafts, Bargains, Sales, and Dealings, ought to be taken, and adjudged to be,’ according to the Standards aforesaid; and that no Person should recover the Price of Goods fold, or the Goods themselves, or any Damage? on Account' of any Contrafts, Bargains, Sales; or Dealings, but* according to the said!Standards." * 1 ’’

" Resolved, That it ought to be made penal for any* Person to have in his Possession any Measure, or Weight, that is not agreeable to’the aforesaid Standards." ' ‘

" Resolved, That it ought to be made highly penal’ for any Person to make or 'fell arty Measure,' of Weight, that is nt>t agreeable <0 the aforesaid Stand-' ards." -: 1

Ordered, That the said Surplufes do He upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, an Account of all the Public Debts at the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, Handing out at Christmas last; with the Annual Interest or other Charges payable for the fame.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, an Account of all Coals brought into the Port of London, for the Twenty Years preceding the 5th of January 1765; distinguishing each Year, and from what Places.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, an Account of all Coals exported from Great Britain, for the Twenty Years preceding the 5th of January 1764, with the Duties payable thereon; distinguishing each Year, and distinguishing such Part as have been exported to foreign Countries, such as have been exported to Ireland and the ljle of Man, and such as have been exported to the British Colonies and Plantations.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for appointing Commissioners to put in Execution an Act of this Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised " in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year 1765," together with those named in Two former Acts for appointing Commissioners of the Land Tax: And that Mr. Jenkinson and Mr. JVhateley, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Gentlemen, that they do make Provision in the said Bill, for indemnifying Persons who have, acted as Commissioners of the Land Tax, by virtue of Estates of or above a certain Value, though the same were not rated, or assessed, at the Value of One hundred Pounds per Annum.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Gentlemen, that they do make Provision in the said Bill, for limiting a Time within which Suits and Prosecutions shall be commenced, with respect to the Qualifications of Persons who shall »dt as Commissioners of the Land Tax.

Ordered, That the Knights of the Shires, and other Members of this House, do prepare Lifts, fairly written, of Commissioners Names for executing the said Act, for the respective Counties, Cities, and Places, for which there have been used to be Commissioners; and that the Christian and Syrnames of the said Commissioners be written at Length.

Sir Robert Ladbroke, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to prohibit the Exportation of Wheat, Wheaten Meal, Flour, Bread, Biscuit, and Starch, for a Time to be limited, was committed, the Amendments which the Committee had made to tlje Bill; and which they had directed him to report to the House} and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout, and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were, with an Amendment to One of them, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrafted.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty;

Refolded, That this House will, upon Wedesday Morning next, resolved itself into the said Committee.

21

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the several Acts relating to the Rewards for discovering the Longitude at Sea, and making Experiments of Prbpofals for discovering the Longitude;

Ordered, That the Account of what Money has been issued by the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, pursuant to several Acts of Parliament, made with regard to the making Experiments of Proposals for discovering the Longitude, be referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the Aid Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Dyson took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr.> Dyson reported from the Committee, That they had come to a Resolution; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

Mr. Dyson also acquainted the House, that he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House to consider further of the several Acts relating to the*Rewards for discovering the Longitude at Sea, and making Experiments of Proposals for discovering the Longitude.

Ordered, That the Lord Barrington have Leave to make a Motion, it being after Three of the Clock.

And he moved the House accordingly.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, Copies of the Minutes of the Proceedings of the Commissioners of Longitude, at their Two last Meetings, held on the 19th Day of January last, and the 9th of this Instant February.

Ordered, That Mr. Peter Burrell have Leave to make a Motion.

And he having ihoved the House accordingly. That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to oblige Agents for Prize Money to account for such Sums of Money as remain in their Hands unclaimed, the Property of any of His Majesty’s Land Forces, and for the Application thereof;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty gives His Consent, so far as His Interest is concerned, that the House may do as they think fit, with regard to the said Money.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to oblige Agents for Prize Money to account for such Sums of Money as remain in their Hands unclaimed, the Property of any of His Majesty’s Land Forces, and for the Application thereof: And that Mr. Peter Burrell, Colonel Burgoyne, Lord Barrington, Colonel Barre, Mr. Secretary at War, and Colonel Howe, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Ordered, That Mr. Dempster have Leave to make a Motion.

And he moved the House accordingly.

A Petition of the Owners and Mailers of Ships employed in the Coal Trade of the Port of Scarborough, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Method of unloading Ballast from Ships by Keels or Lighters, and landing it upon Quays or Wharfs on the River Tyne, is not only very expensive.to llie.Petitiocers, but very prejudicial to the said River, by the large Quantity of Ballast that is-frequently washing and blowing off the Quays, which has so much filled up the River, that unless some Remedy be applied, it may be of fatal Consequence, the Price of Coals greatly enhanced, and the valuable Nurseiy of Seamen destroyed: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief, as to the House - shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said' Petition be referred to the Consideration of the_ Committee, to whom the Petition of the Owners and Matters of Ships employed in the Coal Trade between London and Shields, is referred-: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and-report the feme, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. Alexander Boote, Clerk to the Trustees for repairing that Part of the Road leading from Wallingford to Wantage, being examined, said. That the Trustees, according to the Direction of the said Act, separated themselves into Three Branches at their First Meeting in 1752: That those who act for this Branch have borrowed £. 1,000 on the Credit of the fame, for repairing

that Part of the said Road, and that a considerable Pro-grels hath been made therein; but that the said Sum is found insufficient, and the Powers by the said Act granted are defective in many Respects; and that the said Road cannot be completely repaired unless the Term and Powers of the said Act be further continued and enlarged.

Mr. John Toovey, Treasurer to the Trustees for re-

pairing that Branch of the Road, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Boote-, and further said. That the Tolls collected on this Branch of the Road amounts to about 300 a Year: That the Road leading from the Bottom of Gangs-down Hill, in the Parish of Nuffield, in the County of Oxford, to the Commencement of the Road leading from Wallingford to Wantage, is the direct and nearest Road from London to I Palling ford and Wantage, is about Three Miles and an Half in Length, and so much out of Repair, that Carriages are obliged to go a Mile and an Half about to avoid it, but that Materials are very near and plentiful, and if the same was once put into good Repair, and the Statute Work duly performed, the same might be maintained at a very small Expence; and the Witness produced to your Committee, an Account of a Subscription which hath been raised, amounting to £. 106. 11 s. 6 d.for repairing the feme, provided the future Repairs of the Road be put under the Management of the Trustees of the Wantage Turnpike, and that no Toll be taken on this Road.

To prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition, t^ie said Mr. Boote said. That the Trustees for re-. V»l. 30.

pairing that Part of the Road leading from Wantage to Farringdon, have not been able to repair any Part of the feme effectually, but have laid out some Money, and have borrowed £. 150, which is unpaid; that the Income of the Tolls on this Branch of the Road amounts to no more than about £.40 a Year; and that the same cannot be repaid, and the Road effectually repaired, unless the Tolls are increased, and the Term and Powers of the said Act be further continued and enlarged.

Seymour Richmond, Esquire, being examined, laid, That he was appointed Clerk and Treasurer to the Trustees, and Abraham Atkins, Esquire, Surveyor of that Branch of the Road leading from Wantage to Idson, about May 1752, for One Year only, who both undertook to act under the said Appointments, gratis; that a Toll-house and Gate were erected, and a Toll Gatherer was appointed about October 1752, at Five Shillings a Week, and that

before the nth June 1753 he left it, the Toll arising from thence not being sufficient to pay him his Allowance: Another was then appointed to collect the Toll occasionally on Market Days, who loon also left it, the Toll not being sufficient to pay him for his Trouble; that the Toll-house and Gate are now entirely destroyed, and that no Clerk or other Officer has been since appointed, or any regular Meeting had since November 1753; that no Money has been borrowed on the Credit of the Tolls arising in this Part of the Road; that the Share of the Expences in Parliament belonging to this Branch, was paid by the Branch leading from Wallingford to Wantage-, that the Toll-house and Gate were erected at the Charge of some neighbouring Gentlemen and others, who ordered and executed the fame; and that Mr. Atkins, who is a Gentleman of great Property, expended in Repairs, £. 53. 4 7 as appears by his Account, which was chiefly near his own House, about the Middle of the said Turnpike Road.

A Member present informed the Committee, That Mr. Atkins, being apprized of this Application, had signified to him his Consent to every Part of it.

Then an Entry in the Journal of the House of the 14th January 1731, was read; whereby it appeared. That the Branch of Road from Wantage to Idson was ingrafted upon the original Plan of the Bill, in consequence of a supplemental Petition after the Bill was read a Second Time, and committed.

And all the said Witnesses said. That if foe Term and Powers of the said Act were discontinued in respect to the said Idson Road, and the Tolls collected on the Road from Wallingford to Wantage, and from Wantage to Farringdon, were made One Fund, and put under the Management of the same Trustees, as was originally designed, when Application was made to Parliament in 1731, it would be very beneficial to the said Roads, and to the Inhabitants of that Part of the Country.

To prove the Allegations of the third-mentioned Petition, Lovelace Bigge, Esquire, being examined, feid, That Part of the Road leading from the Bottom of Gangsdown Hill, in the Parish of Nuffield, to the Commencement of the Turnpike Road leading from Wallingford to Wantage, leads through many private Grounds, and is liable to be obstructed by Gates, and is in other Parts too narrow for Two Carriages to pals each other; and that it would be more beneficial and commodious, if the ancient High Road leading from the North East Corner of Nuffield Common, on the Top of Gangsdown Hill aforesaid, by the Parish Church of Nuffieldto the Commencement

Amount of ^.8,ooe in the whole; and that the Repairs of the said Roads cannot be completed, without taking up the remaining Two thousand Pounds; and that the Tolls at present taken at the several Gates erected by virtue of the said Acts, which are very numerous on Account of the Openness of the Country in many Places, by Means whereof the said Tolls are much evaded, will be but barely, if sufficient to answer and make good the Interest of the Monies borrowed, and to be borrowed, on the Credit thereof, and to keep the said Roads in Repair; and that the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill or Bills for renewing, amending, or enlarging, the Powers of One or more Act or Acts, for the repairing another or other Turnpike or Turnpikes, in the Neighbourhood of the said Roads, is or are now depending before the House; and that some Clause or Clauses is or are inserted, or intended to be inserted therein, for removing some Gate or Gates on the Petitioners Roads, and adding some Part or Parts of the said Roads to such other Turnpike or Turnpikes, or otherwise to abridge the Power of the Petitioners the Trustees, whereby the Petitioners, who have lent such Sums of Money on the Credit of the said Tolls, will be prejudiced in their Security, their Cud Security become precarious, and them-lelves rendered uneasy in respect thereof; and the Petitioners the Trustees may not be able to borrow the said remaining Sum of £. 2,000, or any Part thereof, for completing the Repairs of the said Roads; the Petitioners therefore relying on their present Parliamentary Security, humbly pray, that no Clause or Clauses may be received or pals into a Law; and for such further and other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Dyers, Calico Printers, and others using Madder in their several Trades, in behalf of themselves and many others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That Madder being a principal Ingredient in Dying and Calico Voi. 30.

Printing, great Quantities thereof are annually used irt this Kingdom; and that an Act was passed in the 31st Year of his kte Majesty’s Reign, for encouraging the Growth and Cultivation of Madder in this Kingdom, by ascertaining the Tythe thereof; which was to continue in Force for Fourteen Years only; and that the said Act, from the Shortness of the said Term, hath not answered the End of the Petitioners,- the Price of Madder having, since its Commencement, been greatly advanced, whereby the Petitioners have been obliged to raise their Prices to their Employers; in consequence whereof great Part of the Trade is removed, and now carrying on in France, and other foreign Parts; and that the manufacturing of Madder from the Setting of it, to its being fit for Use, requires so long Time, and great Expence in building Mills, and other Requisites, that it is apprehended many Persons may be deterred from beginning the Cultivation of it, unless the Term of the said former Act be further continued: And therefore praying, That the Term of the said Act may be extended; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the feme, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That the Gaol of Newgate is the Common Gaol for the City of Lon Jan and the County of Middlesex; and that, for several Years last past, there have been,

Amis, near a Thousand Persons committed to the said Gaol, Two Thirds of which have been Pri-

fotiers; and that the said Gaol is a very ancient, ill-conftxufted, ciofc, and incommodious Building, and, in its present State, unfit for the Reception of Piiloners committed there; and that the Petitioners are well satisfied, that the present State and Condition of the said Gaol merits the Attention of the Legislature; and that. On a careful Examination and Survey, it appears, that the same cannot be rendered healthy and commodious, without being taken down, and rebuilt on a more extended Plan; and that the Petitioners are ready and willing to do every thing towards the promoting a Work of such public Utility, that, on their Part, can equitably be expected or required; but that the same cannot, as the Petitioners are advised, be carried into execution, without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to grant such Relief therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Kymflon, according to Order, reported from the Weigla* Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred and to consider of the Refutations, which, upon the 26th Measure*. Day of May 1758, were reported from the Committee appointed to inquire into the original Standards of

Weights and Measures in this Kingdom, and to consider the Laws relating thereto, and to report their Observations thereupon, together with their Opinion of the most effectual Means for ascertaining and enforcing uniform and certain Standards of Weights and Measures to be used for the future; and which, upon the 2d Day of June following, were, with Amendments to several

of them, agreed to by the House; and also the Rcfolu-tions, which, upon the nth Day of April 1759, were reported from the Committee appointed to inquire into the original Standards of Weights and Measures in this Kingdom, and to consider the Laws relating thereto, and to report their Observations thereupon, together with their Opinion of the most effectual Means for ascertaining and enforcing uniform and certain Standards of Weights and Measures to be used for the future; and which were the next Day agreed to by the House; the Resolutions which the Committee bad directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Cle.L’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Person making or felling Measures of Capacity, shall be obliged to take out an Annual Licence, within the Space of Forty Days after a Day to be limited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Stamp Duty be charged upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, on which every such Licence shall be ingrossed, written, or printed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be paid for every Aflizing, Sealing, or Marking every Gallon, or greater Measure of Capacity, the Sum of Three Pence; for every Quart, or other greater Measure less than One Gallon, the Sum of Two Pence; and for every Measure less than a Quart, One Penny.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Person making and felling of Weights, shall be obliged to take out an Annual Licence, within the Space of Forty Days after a Day to be limited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Stamp Duty be charged upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, on which every such Licence shall be ingrossed, written, or printed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be paid for the First Aflizing, Sealing, or Marking of every Weight, not being less than Sixty-eight Pounds One Ounce and Twelve Penny Weight, the Sum of Three Pence; and for every Re-aflizing, Re-sealing, or Correcting any such Weight, the Sum of One Penny Half-penny; for the First Aflizing, Sealing, or Marking of every Weight, being more than One Pound Two Ounces and Twelve Penny Weight, and less than Sixty-eight Pounds One Ounce and Twelve Penny Weight, the Sum of Two Pence; and for every Re-aflizing, Re-sealing, or Correcting every such Weight, One Penny; and for every Aflizing, Sealing, or Marking of every'Weight, being more than Half of One Ounce, and less than One Pound Two Ounces and Twelve Penny Weight, the Sum of One Half-penny; and for, every Half Ounce, and other inferior Weight, One Farthing.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be paid for every Aflizing, Sealing, or Marking every Measure of Length, the Sum of One Penny.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Monies which shall arise by the said Stamp Duties, and by the Aflizing, Sealing, and Marking of Weights and Measures, as aforesaid, ought to be applied in discharging the Expence of carrying into execution the Regulations, proposed to be established by the Resolutions relating to Weights and Measures, which were

agreed to by the House on the Second Day of June 1758; and the Twelfth Day of April 1759.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon^ agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of Richard Liddell was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That jtlie Petitioner observes by the Votes of the House, that a Petition has been presented, representing that the Harbour of Shields is in Danger of being entirely blocked up by the present Method of discharging Ballast from Ships; and alleging, that the Petitioner apprehends the most effectual Method of preventing the Danger complained of in the said Petition, will be, by making use of the Machines invented by the Petitioner, for the Removal of the Earth, Ballast, Sand, or any other kind of Matter from any Port, River, Harbour, Creek, or Inlet; and that the Petitioner formerly applied to the House for a Bill, to enlarge the Term granted to him by His Majesty’s Letters Patent, for the sole Use and Exercise of the said Invention; and that since the Petitioner’s Application to the House, an Act passed, which enforces the Use of the Petitioner’s Machines in the Harbour of Whitehaven; and that, since the passing of the said Act, the said Machines have been constantly used in carrying out Ballast from the said- Harbour of Whitehaven, and have been found of the greatest

Utility *' And therefore praying. That in case the said Machines should be thought most proper for conveying Ballast from the Ships, and cleaning the said Harbour, that in Consideration of his great Expence, and his not being able to make use of his Machines during the existing Term of his Patent, the House will take his same into Consideration, and grant him such Encouragement as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Owners and Masters of Ships employed in the Coal Trade between London and Shields, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of Charles Schaw, Lord Cat heart, Proprietor of the Estate and Coal Mines of Sauchie, adjoining to the River Devon, in the County of Clackmannan, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the said River has, from Vicarjbridge to the Mouth or Entry of the said River into the River Forth, at all Sca-fons of the Year, a constant Run of Water, sufficient for the Purposes of an Inland Navigation; but, the Course of the said River being through a flat, level, and, in some Places, marlhy Country, is, in the present State of the River, extremely winding, and interrupted by Shallows, so as to make any Navigation impracticable; and that the Navigation of the Forth, betwixt Devon and Alloa, is liable to several Inconveniences of a similar Nature; and that rendering the Devon navigable, from Vicarjbridge, to its Entry into the Forth, and improving the Navigation of the last mentioned River, will be Works of great public as well as private Utility; and, from the Plenty of Water, and the Nature of the Ground through which these Rivers run, can be accotnplished at a moderate Expence, as well as with a Certainty of effectually answering the intended Purposes: And therefore praying. That a Bill may be brought in for rendering the River Devon navigable, from Vicarjbridge, to its Mouth or Entry into the Forth, and for improving the Navigation of the Forth.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, redding in and near the City of and Town of tonbury, in the County of Som was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by virtue of an Act, passed in the 26th Year of his late Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from Piper’s Inn, in the Panlh of Ashcott, to and through and

Wells, to the Direction Post in the great Western Road to the City of Bath; and also from Wells to Rush Hill, leading to the City of Bristol-, the Trustees therein appointed, in order to make and repair the said Roads, borrowed, from time to time, the Sum of £.3,500, or thereabouts, which said Sum now remains due, the said Roads having been, for several Years past, well and effectually made and repaired; and that, in the 4th Year of His present Majesty, a Renewal of the said Act was obtained, with Power to extend the Road from to Shepton Mallett, Camtards Grave, and Stean Bow Bridge, in the Parish of Pilton; and also from to join the

Turnpike Road leading to Froome, where the Froome Turnpike Road ends; and for the Purpose of making and repairing thereof, the further Sum of £. 1,200 is already taken up at Interest, and to complete the same, the further Sum of £. 1,300 at least will be necessary; and that the Petitioners have observed, in the Votes of the House, that, in a Bill now depending, for renewing the Shepton Mallett Turnpike Act, an Application is made for extending the Road from the End of their present Turnpike Road, in the Parish of Pilton, to Glastonbury, and also the Road from, to, and through Shepton Mallett aforesaid, to the Parish of Leighton, leading towards Froome; and also the Road from Shepton Mallett aforesaid, to Long Cross Bottom, which joins the Froome Turnpike Road; which, if the same should pass into a Law, particularly from Pilton, near to the said Town of Glastonbury, the Course of travelling the great and ancient Roads, from the Westetn Parts of England, to the Northern, to and through Glastonbury and Wells, and from Bath to London, will be much lessened; and the Petitioners have the greatest reason to apprehend, that the Tolls, in consequence thereof, will be so much diminished, as to render it impossible to pay the Debt already due, or to complete and finish the aforesaid new Roads, and to keep in good Repair the Roads already made; and that, by means thereof, the Course of Travelling will be so much divided, that the Tolls will be insufficient to keep either of the said Roads in due and proper Repair; and that the Road leading from Pilton to the further End of Glastonbury, where the new Shepton Road is intended to be made, is a private Road, unknown to Travellers, and of no general Benefit, and will be a great Injury to the said ancient public Roads, and to the City of Wells and Town of Glastonbury aforesaid: And therefore praying, That the Extension of the said Road, particularly from Pilton to Glastonbury, may not pals into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be

heard, by their Counsel, or be relieved in such Manner as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees appointed to put in execution an Act of the 26th Year of his late Majesty, for repairing and widening the Roads therein mentioned, leading to and through the Towns of Shepton Mallett and Ivelchester, in the County of Somerset, and also of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, living in and near the said Town of Shepton Mallett, is referred.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the better Supply of the Export Trade of this Kingdom to Africa, with such coarse Printed Calicoes, and other Goods, being the Product or Manufacture of the East Indies, or of other Places beyond the Cape of Good Hope, as are prohibited to £e worn and used in Great Britain, the United Company of Merchants trading to the East Indies be permitted to import the same from any Part of Europe not within His Majesty’s Dominions, under proper Limitations and R'strictions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon Failure of the said Company’s keeping the said Export Trade supplied with a sufficient Quantity of such Calicoes, and other Goods, other Persons be permitted to import the same into this Kingdom, from any such Part of Europe, under proper Limitations and Restrictions.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are RibKird thereunto subscribed, Makers and Manufacturers of Manufactory, Ribbands, in Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Law lately obtained for preventing the clandestine Importation of Ribbands into this Kingdom is {till ineffectual, arising, as the Petitioners humbly conceive, partly from the Smallness of the Penalties, by the Act passed in the Third Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, inflicted on the Importers of foreign wrought Ribbands into this Kingdom, their Aiders, Abettors, and Assistants, and upon the Venders and Retailers of the fame; and partly from the Clause in the said Act, directing and requiring such Ribbands, when seized and condemned, to be publicly burnt; whereby the inferior Officers employed in His Majesty’s Customs, for want of due Encouragement to seize such prohibited Goods, are become remiss in their Duty:'

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to' bring in a Bill for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual the said Act of the Third Year of His present Majesty, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Makers and Manufacturers of mixt Woollen Cloth, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the several Laws in being for the Regulating the Manufacture of Cloth in the said West Riding, have been, by Experience, found not only to be ineffectual for the preventing Frauds and Abuses in making of Woollen Cloths, and the undue and unreasonable Stretching and Straining thereof, but have actually produced the contrary Effect; so that the Frauds in making, and the Abuses in ft.etching of Cloth, never were greater than at present; whereby the fair Trader is injured, and the Manufactory at Home and Abroad is discredited; and representing many Hardships, which, the Petitioners allege, they labour under, by the Laws in being, with re Ip eft to th.e breadths which they are obliged to make their Cloths: And therefore praying the Hpufe to take the Premises into Coiitideration, and, by such Ways and Means as to the House shall seem meet, relieve the Petitioners from the Hardships they now lie under, and, by effectually preventing the Frauds and Abuses above mentioned, restore the Manufacture of mixt Woollen Cloth, within -the West Hiding of the County of York, to its ancient Reputation and Credit, bpth at How and Abroad.

York,. was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the several Laws now in being, for the regulating the Manufacture of Cloth in the said West Riding, have been, by Experience, found not only to be ineffectual for the preventing Frauds in making of Woollen Cloth, and the undue Stretching of it when made, but have actually produced the contrary Effect, whereby the fair Trader is injured, and the Manufactory at Home and Abroad is very much debased and dicredited, to the great Loss and Detriment of the Petitioners in particular, and of the Kingdom in general; and representing to the House many Grievances, which, the Petitioners allege, they labour under by the Laws in being, with respect to the Breadths they are obliged to make their Cloths: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and, by such Ways and Means as to the House shall seem meet, relieve the Petitioners from the Hardships they now lie under, and, by effectually preventing the Frauds and Abul’es above mentioned, restore the Manufacture of White Woollen Cloth, within the West Riding of the said County of York, to its ancient Reputation and Credit, both at Home and Abroad.

A Petition of the Owners and Matters of Ships em- Tyne River* ployed in the Coal Trade of the Port of Whitby, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the River Tyne, is of late Vears greatly injured, occasioned chiefly by the large Quantities of Ball aft that the Colliers are obliged to bring into the Port of Shields; which Ballast, after being landed at a great Expence on the Quays or Wharfs, is frequently washed away by Floods and heavy Rains, and blown off the Heaps in high Winds; and alleging, that the only Place where Ships of Burthen can load, is at Shields; and there it is so apparently filling up, that without some speedy Remedy to prevent the growing Evil, the Price of Coals must greatly advance, and that valuable Nursery for Seamen be destroyed: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petion of the Owners and Masters of Ships employed in the Coal Trade between London and Shields, is referred.
