Mr. Burrell reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trullees, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, assembled at a General Meeting, and others, for putting in execution several Acts of Parliament for repairing the Roads from the Stones End, in Kent Street, and Bermondsey Street, in Southw, to the Lime Kilns, near Blackheath, and to the Town of Dartford, and to the Extent of the Parish of Lewifham, next Bromley and Beckenham, in the County of Kent; and alto the Petition of the Trullees, assembled at a General Meeting, for putting in execution an Act made in the aid of his late Majesty, intituled, An Act for opening and making a new Road from the East End of New Street, in the Parish of Saint John, Southwark, to and through the several Places therein mentioned, and for keeping the said Road in Repair for the future; were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the feme, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first mentioned Petition, an Act passed in the 4th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Highways leading from the Stones End, in Kent Street aforesaid, to the Lime Kilns in East Greenwich, near Black-heath, and to Lewifham Church, in the County of which was to continue, from the 15th Day of 1718, for the Term of 11 Years: And also.

An Act passed in the 6th Year of King George the ill, whereby the Term granted by the first mentioned A ft was enlarged for the further Term of Ten Years, and the Repair of the said Roads was thereby extended from Lewifham Church to the First Mill Pond at South End, within the Parish of Lewifham, and other Tolls and Duties were set on Carriages, Horses, and Cattle, passing on the said Roads: And also,

Another Act passed in the Eleventh Year of his late Majesty King George the 2d, whereby the last mentioned Term was enlarged, and the Tolls and Duties, Clauses and Powers, contained in the former Acts, were continued from the 25th of March 1739, for the further Terra of Thirty-eight Years; and the Repair of the Roads was . thereby further enlarged, from the Lime Kilns aforesaid, to the Town of Dartford, in the County of Kent; and from a Place called St. Thomas a Waterings, in, the Parish of St. George, Southwark, in the County of Surrey, to the Stones End, in Bermondsey Street, in the same County: And also,

A Petition of His Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the County of Middlesex, in Session assembled, on be-

half of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Reciting the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, which hath been lately presented to the House, relating to the Gaol of Newgate; and representing to the House, that the said Gaol is supposed to have been originally built in the Reign of King Henry I. or of King Stephen; that is to lay, between the Years 1100 and 1154; and that the same hath been under the foie Government of, and hath from Time to Time, sometimes by express Mandate from the King,

Vql. 30,

Februarii. 165

been rebuilt, repaired, altered, and enlarged, by the City of London-, and that, supposing the Number of Prisoners yearly committed to the said Gaol to be as great as is alleged, and that Two Thirds of such Prisoners are Middlesex Prisoners (the latter of which Positions these Petitioners do by no means admit) the Number is rather less now than it hath been for a long Series of Years past; and that the County of Middlesex have several Prisons of their own, winch they maintain at a great Expence, wherein no malignant Disease hath ever yet appeared, to which Prisons, Persons for all but the most atrocious Offences are committed; and that the foie Reason why any Middlesex Prisoners at all are in Newgate is, that the Citizens of London do, by their several Charters, among divers other valuable Privileges and Immunities, hold the Shrievalty of Middlesex, together with that of London, in Farm; and that, as they unite those Two several Offices and the Jurisdictions attendant thereon in the same Persons, so do they make the Prison of Newgate, which is situated in and is properly the Prison of London, a Prison for the County of Middlesex-, that therefore the Custody of the Middlesex Prisoners is not to be considered as a Burthen on the Citizens, but as a necessary Consequence of their Nomination of the same Persons as are Sheriffs of London, to be Sheriff of Middlesex, the Right to which Nomination could never have been forced on them; they must necessarily be supposed originally to have solicited it, and the rather, as they constantly exercise it, and, under colour thereof, have, for many Years past, raised immense Sums; in Proof whereof, the Petitioners allege, that, since the Year 1672, the Amount of Sheriffs Fines hath been upwards of £.148,750 a sufficient Part whereof the Petitioners apprehend might very properly have been applied by the Citizens for the rebuilding of their Gaol of Newgate, as it is, in Judgment of Law, the Prison of the Sheriff; and that, although it is now upwards of 600 Years since the first building of the said Gaol, no Attempt hath ever been made to charge the County of Middlesex with any Expence attending the fame; but, on the contrary, immediately after the dreadful Conflagration in 1666, when the real Distresses of the Citizens might oblige them to implore the Aid of Parliament, they, without any previous Application to the County of Middlesex, obtained, for the Purpose of building Prisons for felons and other Malefactors, (among other Tilings) a Grant of a very considerable Revenue by a Dufy on Coals, which hath produced to the City no less a Sum than £. 736,804; and that, how much soever the Petitioners may be disposed to lament that the said Gaol is still ill constructed, close, incommodious, and unhealthy, they humbly hope, that the County of Middlesex is not answerable for any of the bad Consequences of its Construction or Situation, in as much as the City, and not the County, have made it what it is; and that the Citizens have been possessed of at least two Funds, amounting together to near £. 900,000 Sterling, out of which, for aught that has ever yet appeared to the Public, they might have rebuilt their Gaol of Newgate, without any Aid of the County, which already is taxed at near 1000l. a Year for the Maintenance of its own Gaols, and other Purposes, by County Rate, of which Rate, the Petitioners, as Justices of the Peace, are Trustees; that the Revenues of the City are immense; the Offices in their Disposal, so long ago as the Year 1721, were estimated at £. 152,000 and a very few Years will put the Citizens in the actual Possession of such Estates as must yield an Income much more than adequate to the Expences of its Government; and that, as the Sources of these Revenues are in general Royal Grants, many of them under the express Condition of well-governing the City, and are enjoyed by the Citizens in their Political and Corporate Capacity, the Revenues cannot be considered as Private Emoluments, in Reason and Justice they ought to be applied only for the Public Purposes; and, as the Petitioners conceive, the defraying the necessary Expences

U u of

21° Februarii

166

A. 17 65.

of Magistracy, the Erection and Repair of Gaols, Bridges, and other Public Edifices, are tome of those beneficial Purposes for which such Grants seem originally to have been intended, and to which the Revenues, thereby arising, are with the greatest Propriety applicable; for which Reasons, as also for divers of Weight and Importance, which the Petitioners have to offer, they do deny that the said Gaol ought to be rebuilt at the Expence of the City of London and County of Middlesex, in any Proportion whatsoever; on the contrary, that the Citizens are by Law bound, and ought, at the foie Expence of the City, to rebuild and repair the said Gaol whenever the same shall be necessary: And therefore praying the House, That the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the Matters contained in the said Petition, so far as the same may any way tend to impose a Charge on the said County.

River. the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunder!and, in the County of Durham, within the -Limits set to th in an Act of Parliament passed in the 20th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for the better Preservation and Improvement of the River Wear and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, assembled at a Meeting, pursuant to the said Act, on Thursda the 14th Day of February 2 765, was presented to the House, and read; Reciting the Petition of the Owners and Matters of Ships employed in the Coal Trade between London and Shields, Which was presented to the House upon the 4th Day of this Instant; and alleging, that all Ships of great Burthen trading to the Port of Sunderland are obliged to anchor at Sea, and take in their Loading at a great Distance from the Harbour, and, in bad Weather, such Ships are often driven from their Anchors, in which Emergencies the Port and Harbour Of Shields is the only Port to the Northward to which Ships can make for Safety; and therefore all Persons, trading with Ships of great Burthen to the Port of Sunderland, are particularly interested in the Preservation of the Port of Shields; and that the Petitioners are appre-hensive, that some Method, other than the Catting of Bnllatt fipon the dry Land, where the Tide or Water never flows or runs, is intended to be attempted in the said Port of Shields; and that the Petitioners conceive, that the permitting of Ballast to be unloaded from Ships in the Port or Harbour of Shields, otherwise than to be call upon the dry Land, might be of the most dangerous Consequence to the said Port and Harbour: And "Vol. 30.

therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and hope the House will not, by any new Law, permit any Ballad to be unloaded from any Ship or Vessel in the Port or Haven ot Shields, otherwise than so be call upon dry Land.

Mr Whitworth reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Persons, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, being Dyers, Callico Printers, and others, using Madder in their several Trades, in behalf of themselves and many others, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and haddirested him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In support of the Allegations of the said Petition, John Arbuthiot, Esquire, a Callico Printer, informed

your Committee, that Madder is a principal Ingredient, without which, many material Colours in Callico Printing cannot be fixed.

That he apprehends 1,500 Tons of Madder are annually consumed in Callico Printing alone#

Then an Act, passed in the 3 ill: Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, for encouraging the Growth and Cultivation of Madder in this Kingdom, by ascertaining the Tythe thereof, which was to continue in force for Fourteen Years, was read: And,

Mr. Arbuthiot said, That the belt Sorts of Madder, which are used in Callico Printing, have role since 17*58, the Year the said Act palfed, from Five Guineas to Seven Guineas per Hundred Weight.

That an inferior Sort of Madder, called Umbro, which is chiefly used by the Woollen Dyers, has role since that Time, Cent, per Cent. — That Sort is likewise used in Callico Printing, in inferior Work, which has induced many Printers to substitute Logwood instead of it for some particular Sorts of Work, which not being a fixed Colour, greatly discredits our Printing Manufactory abroad, where the create ft Encouragement is given to the Printing Bu-finels, particularly in France, where they are now able to undersell us; and the Witness said. That he law his own "Works copied and executed £.40 per Cent, cheaper than he could do it, in French Flanders.

That if the Act was continued, this Country could supply the whole Llufiness of Callico Printing with the best Sort of Madder; which is particularly adapted to this Climate.

That he has made Experiments of Madder of his own Growth, which the Witness prefers to foreign Madder.

And it appeared from some Samples produced to your Committee, that it requires Three Years before it can be brought to any degree of Perfection fit for Use.

That it is necessary to have it dried under Shelter, as it is subject to mildew, if exposed to the Air, which renders it not marketable.

That the Expence of building Houses necessary for a Plantation of 20 or 30 Acres, will coll about 100, exclusive of a Mill, which the Witness apprehends would cost about £. 100 more.

And he apprehends many Persons will be deterred, not only from beginning, but carrying on the Businessof Callico Printing, if the Act is not continued.

A Member present informed your Committee, that Mr. Andrews, a considerable Callico Printer, told him, he would decline his Business unless the Act was continued.

Mr. Edmund Farmer, Mr. Robert Jones, and Mr. Joseph ‘Tohvyn, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Arbuthiot.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for continuing an Act, made in the 31st Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, for encouraging the Growth and Cultivation of Madder in that Part of Great Britain called England, by ascertaining the Tythe thereof: And that Mr. Whitworth, the Lord Stran, the Lord Carysfort, the Lord Coleraine, and Mr. Mawbey, do prepare, and bring

in, the fame.

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Representing to the House, That the Petitioners and others are subjected to many Grievances, by lo much of Two several Acts, passed in the 3d and 4th Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, which lays an additional Duty on Cider and Perry, both with respect to the Tax itself, and to the Mode of collecting it, under the ' Power of the Excise Laws: And praying the

: House to take the Premises into Consideration,

and to give such Relief therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Motion wds made, and the Question being proposed. That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to repeal so much of an Act, passed in the 3d Year of His Majesty’s Reign, as lays a new Duty of Excise on Cider and Perry', to be paid by the Maker thereof; and also an Act passed in the last Session of Parliament, to explain and amend such Part of the said Act as relates to Cider and Perry made in this Kingdom;

The House was moved, that an Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act for granting to His Majesty several additional Duties upon Wines imported into this Kingdom; and certain Duties upon ail Cider and Perry; and for raising the Sum of Three millions Five hundred thousand Pounds, by way of Annuities and Lotteries, to be charged on the said Duties; might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

The House was also moved, that an Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to explain and amend such Part of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for granting to His Majesty several additional Duties upon Wines imported into this Kingdom; and certain Duties upon all Cider and Perry; and for raising the Sum of Three millions Five hundred thousand Pounds, by way of Annuities and Lotteries, to be charged on the said Duties; as relates to Cider and Perry made in this Kingdom; might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

Then the Question being put. That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to repeal so much of an Act, passed in the 3d Year of His Majesty’s Reign, as lays a new Duty of Excise on Cider and Perry, to be paid by the Maker thereof; and also an Act passed in the last Session of Parliament, to explain and amend such Part of the said Act as relates to Cider and Perry made in this Kingdom;

The House divided. The Yeas went forth.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to repeal an Act, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for the better preventing of clandestine Marriages; and to encourage and faciliate Marriages to be solemnized in Churches or public Chapels, under a Publication of Banns, or by Licences; and to remove all Doubts which have arilen, or may arise, concerning the Validity of certain Marriages solemnized since the making the said Act; and for the regulating Registers; and for preserving the Evidence of Pedigrees, Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into the said Committee.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The other Order of the Day being read;

The House resumed the adjourned Consideration of the Report, which was made from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for granting certain Stamp Duties, and other Duties, in the British Colonies and Plantations in America; and for applying the same towards further defraying the Expences of defending, protesting, and securing, such Colonies and Plantations; was committed.

And the Residue of the Amendments, made by the Committee to the said Bill, being severally read a Second Time, upon the Question severally put thereupon, One of them was disagreed to; and the rest were, with an Amendment to One of them, agreed to by the House.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that Warrants for Bounties shall be exempted from Duty.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill* to exempt Proclamations, Forms of Prayer, and certain other Things, from the Duty.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, to exempt lnllruments for purchasing Lands of the Indians from the Duty.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the I ioufe, to be made Part of the Bill.

Ordered, That Leave be given to offer a Clause to be added to the said Bill, to extend the Jurisdictions by the Act to be established, to the execution of an Act made in the Fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign relating to the Customs, and to the several dther Acts relating to the Revenues in the Colonies and Plantations.

And a Clause was accordingly offered to be added lo the Bill for that Purpose.

And the said Clause was Twice read, with Blanks, which being filled up, the said Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be m^le Part of the Bill.

The said Accounts are preserved amonest the other Papers of this Session j and the said Estimate is as followeth; viz.

An ESTIMATE of the Expence of maintaining the Children, received into the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of Exposed and Deserted Young Children, on or before the 25th Day of March 1760, from the 31st Day of December 1764, exclusive, to the 31st Day or 1765, inclusive.

The Number of Children living in the said Hospital, on the said 31st Day of December 1764, is Four thousand Nine hundred and Eleven, the Expence of maintaining whom, at Seven Pounds Ten Shillings each, amounts to Thirty-six thousand Eight hundred Thirty-two Pounds and Ten Shillings.

Note, Besides the above 4$tt Children, there have been taken into the Hospital 166 Children, most of whom were under the most distressed Circumstances, or Orphans of Soldiers and Sailors, whole Parents died in His Majesty’s Service, whereof 7 have been apprenticed, 4 claimed, and 36 dead, so that there are 119 Children now alive, which are wholly maintained and provided for out of the private Donations made to this Hospital, and are not, nor ever have been charged to Public Account.

Signed by Order of the General Committee,

Thomas Collingwood, Secretary.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Joshua Ringrofe, being examined, said, That the Roads mentioned in the Petition, from Welford, in the County of Northampton, to the Borough of are narrow

cester, and Parts adjacent, which do not grow enough for their own Consumption; and great Quantities of Coal and Lime, which are plentiful there, would be brought to Welford, and its Neighbourhood, where they are much wanted.

Mr. Henniker reported from the Committee, to whom Ramsgate the Petition of the Trustees for enlarging and main- Harbour, taining the Harbour of Ramsgate, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the feme was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act of Parliament, nude in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for enlarging and maintaining the said Harbour, and for cleansing, amending, and preserving the Haven of Sandwich, was read; and it appeared to your Committee, that the Trustees thereby appointed were impowered to settle and impose several Rates and Duties upon Shipping, which are subject to the Payment of any Sum to be borrowed by the said Trustees, not exceeding Seventy thousand Pounds, with Interest for the feme; and they were also impowered to grant Annuities for Lives, not exceeding in the whole the said Sum of Seventy Thousand Pounds, and that such Annuities should not exceed Eight Pounds Ten Shillings for every One Hundred Pounds, and the said Annuities are directed to be charged upon the said Rates and Duties, with this Restriction, that the Trustees should not subject the same to the Payment of any greater Sum than Fifty thousand Pounds, at any One Time, upon Annuities for Lives.

Then John Baker, Esquire, a Trustee for the Care of the said Harbour, feid. That the Trustees had, puf-suant to the Powers of the said Act, imposed Three Pence per Ton on all Shipping under Three hundred Tons Burthen, and One Penny per Ton on all Shipping above Three hundred Tons Burthen, the Amount whereof Communibus Annis, has been Four thousand Five hundred Pounds, or thereabouts.

That in carrying on the necessary Works of the said Harbour, the Trustees have expended Eighty thousand Pounds, or thereabouts, and the Annuities charged on the said Rates and Duties amount to Forty-six thousand Nine hundred and Ninety-nine Pounds Five Shillings and Four Pence.

And the Witness added. That the Money raised by virtue of the said Act, is not sufficient to complete the Works necessary to be done to the said Harbour, but he apprehends, about Twenty thousand Pounds more will complete the same, and he thinks the present Duties will be sufficient to pay Annuities for Twenty thousand Pounds more than are at present granted.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enlarge certain Powers, granted by an Act passed in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of King George the Second, intituled, An Act for enlarging and maintaining the Harbour of Ramsgate, and for cleansing, amending, and preserving the Haven of Sandwich: And that Mr. Henniker and Mr. Tucker do prepare, and bring in, the feme.

A Petition of the Owners and Mailers of Ships, uling the Coal Tiade, residing in North and South Shields, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Ships employed in that Trade, upon their Arrival in the Port of Shields, are obliged to throw their Ba.last upon Quays; and the unavoidable Wade which attends the Conveyance thereof, is of great Prejudice to the Navigation of the said Liver, and hath, as the Petitioners apprehend, been the Cauie of several Nuisances; and, as the Petitioners believe that the Conservators of the River of Tyne have received several thousand Pounds a Year for the Purpose of cleansing and keeping the said River navigable, which does not appear to the Petitioners to have been applied lor that Purpose, and in regard that the Navigation of the said River may be still further injured, unless some Remedy is immediately applied: Therefore praying the House will inquire what Sums of Money have been collected by the Conservators of the said River, for the Purpose aforesaid, and how the same have been applied; and that the said Conservators may be obliged to cleanle the said River forthwith, and to give the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises, as may be thought proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for the electing of a Burgess to lerve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Stafford, in the County of Stafford, in the room of the honourable William Richard Chetwynd, deceased.

A Petition of the Merchants and Owners and Matters of Ships, belonging to the Port of upon

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that a Petition of Owners and Matters of Ships employed in the Coal Trade between London and , hath been presented to the House, praying Relief against the present Method of unloading Ballast from the Ships in the Harbour of Shields, and River of Tyne-, and al-R»ngv that the Petitioners conceive the prohibiting'of Ballast to be unloaded from Ships in the Port or Harbour of Shields, otherwise than to be call upon the dry Land, where the Tide or Water never flows or runs, is of gjeat Consequence towards the Preservation, of the said Harbour, and the Navigation.of the River Tyne-, and therefore the Petitioners cannot but be alarmed at any Attempt to introduce a new Method of tinloading Ballast, in the said Port or River: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Confederation, and not make any Alteration in die Laws now in force, so as to permit Ballast to be unloaded from Ships or Vessels in the Port of Shields, or River of Tyne, otherwise than to be call upon the dry Land.

A Petition of the Owners and Mailers of Ships belonging to the Port of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That all Ships of great Burt lien trading to the Port of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, are under a Necessity of anchoring at Sea, and-df taking in their Loading at a great Distance from the Harbotlr; and, in bad Weather, such Ships age often driven from their Anchors; and, iq such Cases, the Port and Harbour of Shields is the only Port to the Northward to which Ships can make for Safety; and are therefore greatly interested in having the Port and Harbour of Shields preserved free and open; and that the particular Situation of the Entrance into the Habour of is

Rich, that it might be of the most fatal Consequence to the said Port and Harbour if Ballast was permitted to be unloaded from Ships in the said Harbour, not to be call on the dry Land, where the Tide or Water never Bows or runs; and also taking Notice of the said Petition df Owners and Mailers of Ships employed is the Coal Trade between London and Shields; and alleging, that the Petitioners are apprehensive, that an Attempt is intended to be made to introduce some Method of un-Vo is,30.

loading Ballast in the said Port of Shields, different from . catting the Cun© upon the dry Land, andi that thereby the Port of Shields may be in Danger of being totally blocked up: And therefore praying the; House, to take, the Premises into Confident ion, and not make any Alteration in the Laws now in being; so as to permit Ballast to be unloaded out of Ships or Vessels in the said Port Of Harbour of Shields, otherwise than to be call upon the dry Ladd, where the Tide or Water never flows or runs.

And the said Petitions were f severally ordered to be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Owners and Mailers of Ships employed in the Coal Trade between 4nd Shields, is referred.

That there is a little Hill in the Lower Road, but not steep; that if the Hills in the Upper Road were now made alike easy, the Under Road would be made something cheaper.

That he thinks it most convenient to repair the Under Road, as there are more Houses and Villages near that Road than the Upper Road.

Refo/ved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider what Rights of the Proprietor of the Isle of Man, under the several Grants of the said Island, it may be expedient to vest in the Crown, for the further and more effectual preventing the Mischiefs arising to the Revenue and Commerce of Great Britain and Ireland, from the illicit and clandestine Trade to and from the said Island; and what Compenfetion it may be proper to make to the said Proprietor, in respect thereof.-

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Rebuilding A Petition of the Churchwardens and Overseers of Newgate, j[ie poor> the Vestrymen, and other principal Inhabi-c' tants of the Parishes of Saint Margaret and Saint John the Evangelist, Saint Martin in the Fields, Saint George

Hanover Square, Saint Clement Danes, Saint Mary Le Strand, Saint Anne, and Paul Covent Garden, within the Liberty of Westminster, in the County of Middlesex, on behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants there, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that the Application of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of London, to Parliament, for pulling down and removing the Gaol of Newgate, in that City, is renewed; and that it is thereby alleged, that Two Thirds of the Prisonen committed to that Gaol arc County Prisoners, with a View, as the Petitioners con-, ceive, to put some Part of the Charge of that Work upon the Petitioners; and that the said Liberty of Westminster being ^>ne of the Divisions of the County of Middlesex, the Petitioners do contribute to the Maintenance of New Prison, and the Houses of Correction at Glerkemaell and Tot full Fields and that the Bates for rebuilding and repairing of Prisons and Bridges, and divers other public Uses, being raised out of the Poors Bates, the Taxing of the County of Middlesex, for removing and re-edifying of Newgate, will involve the Petitioners in a large Expence, proportionable to their Quota of the Poors Rates, which are already very heavy; that the Petitioners conceive themselves more remotely benefited by the Gaol of Newgate, than any other Inhabitants of the said County, the of

Westminster being the Common Gaol of the said Liberty, and more conveniently situated for the said Inhabitants; that, as the Petitioners are informed, that the Gaol of Newgale was originally built and always repaired by and for the Ease and Benefit of the City, without any Aid from the County of Middlesex: Therefore praying the Pro t eft ion of the House against any Charge that may be attempted to be thrown upon the said Inhabitants, towards such intended Re-edification.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, is referred.

And the Reverend Mr. Burroughs, and Collier,

Esquire, being severally examined, said. That they know the Roads mentioned in the Petition; that they are very imuch out of Repair, narrow in many Places, and cannot be amended and widened by the Laws in being: And,

" Mr. Thomas Shepherd said. That the Trustees for the Repair of the said Road, between Wisbech and March, have borrowed the Sum of £. 1,600 on the Credit of the said Acts, which, together with the Tolls collected, have been applied to the Repair of the said Roads; but is found to be greatly insufficient to answer the Purposes thereby intended; and that the said Roads cannot be effectually repaired, and the Money now due repaid, under the Powers of the said Acts.

A Petition of Thomas Patterfou, of , in

the County of Cambridge, Oil Merchant, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner and his Ancestors have, for the Space of Fifty Years last past, and upwards, possessed and held by Lease from the Dean and Chapter of Ely, certain Oil Mills called Hauxton Mills, with a Garden thereunto adjoining, and an Orchard; and that in the said Garden are Four large Fish Ponds well stocked with Fish, of considerable Profit to the Petitioner; and that the Hanks on the Sides of the said Garden have been occupied by the Petitioner in depositing Citterns for preserving his Oil from Fire, and are likewise quite necessary for the more convenient Stowage of the Petitioner’s Seed, Oil Cakes, and other Goods belonging to his Trade, which, if obliged to be carried and placed at a greater Distance from the said Mills, will be attended with much Loss and Detriment; and that the Petitioner, observes, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill is brought in for enlarging the Powers of several Acts, for repairing the Road from Stump , to Newmarket

Heath, and the Town of Cambridge, and from Foulmire, to Cambridge^whereby, the Petitioner apprehends, it is intended flr^uild a Bridge near his Mill Dam, and to turn the Road over some Part of his said Garden, Close, or Orchard, which, he alleges, would be a great Prejudice and Inconvenience to him: And therefore pray-ing. That he may be heard, by himself or Counsel, against the said Bill, so far as the same relates to his Garden and Close and Orchard; and that the House will grant him such Relief in the Premises, as shall be thought fit by the House, and as the Nature of the same requires.

Manufacturers of Great Britain; and also the Petition of the several Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, being Silk Throwfters and Persons concerned in Throwing Raw Silk, in behalf of themselves and the rest of the Silk Throwfters of this Kingdom; and also the Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Mercers and Traders in the Silk Manufacture, on behalf of themselves and others following the same Business; and also the Petition of several Hosiers, Frame-work-knitters, and Manufacturers of and Dealers in Frame-work-knitted Silk Stockings, Silk Gloves, and Silk Mitts, whose Names are thereunder written, living and residing in the Town of Nottingham, and in several Towns and Places being near to the fame, as well on behalf of themselves as many Hundred of poor Manufacturers and their Families employed in the same Trade; and also the Petition -of the Proprietors and Matters of the several Silk Works in thadffwn of Derby; and also the Petition of several Persons using Thrown Silk in their Manufacturers in the Town of Manchester, in the County Palatinp of Lan-easter, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of the Master, Wardens, Assistants, and Society of the Art or Mystery of Frame-work-knitters of the Cities of London and , and the Kingdom

t>f England, and Dominion of Wales, and also of divers Hosiers and Manufacturers in the said Trade, who live and reside in and about the said Cities, on behalf of themselves and all others concerned in the said Trade; and also the Petition of several Mercers and Traders in the Silk Manufacture, whose Names are subscribed, in behalf of themselves and others concerned in the same Business; and also the Petition of several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Silk and Worsted Weavers at K, in the County of Worcester, in behalf of themselves and others; were fc-verally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of Fact contained in the said Petitions; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the Silk Weavers Petition, Mr. John Baker, Mr. Charles Mr. John Sabatiere, Mr. John Lewis, Mr. Lewis Ogier, Mr. John Banyard, and Mr. John Lefouef.all Weavers of Englijfy Silks, being

severally examined, laid. That, for Two or Three Years last past, they have found a very great Decline in their Trade; that the Demand for made Silks was

- - greatly lessened; that Journeymen Weavers were every Day applying to them for Work, which it was not in their Power to give them; and that the Number of Men now employed by them is less than formerly, being gradually decreased for the Two or Three last Years, in some of the Houses 20, and in others 30, in 100; notwithstanding which, several of the Witnesses said, they had a large Stock on hand. Mr. Ogier said, he had £. 2,©oo of Stock on hand now, more than at the Time last Year; and Mr. Baker and Mr. Sabatiere said, they had a great Part of their last Winter’s Stock still by them.

Mr. Lewis Ogier, a Weaver of Flowered Velvets, laid. That in 1761, he had 17 Looms; in 1762, xa; in 1763, 7; in 1764, 3; and at present none. They all of them attributed this Decay to the legal and illegal Importation of Foreign Wrought Silks; and were of 'Opinion if that could be flopped, could

make enough to supply the Consumption of Great Britain, and what is exported from thence.

Mr. Triquett further laid, That there are same Men employed in the Silk-weaving at but they

arelikwife much reduced.

17

Mr. Baker and Mr. Sabatier, being examined with respect to their Knowledge of the illegal Importation of French Silks*, said. That they presumed the illegal Importation was very great. Mr. Sabatiere founded his Opinion on the Number of French Silks that he had known imported as Italian; and Mr. Baker, on the great Number of Seizures that he had known made, many of which he had been sent for to examine, and found them to be French.

The Mercers cross-examined these Witnesses, to shew that the Hands now out of employ worked in the Gauze and Silk Handkerchief Way, which could not be affected by a Foreign Importation. The Weavers admitted, that an Importation of Foreign Wrought Silks would not aflect these Two Branches, and that some Men were out of employ in them, but the Number could not be ascertained; and did not appear to the Committee to be very great.

Mr. Thomas Price, being examined to this Point, said, however. That he believed a good many Men, now out of Employ, had been employed in Handkerchiefs and Gauze, the former of which was in a great Measure gone into Flanders, and the latter into Scotland*

As to the present State of Trade in Spital Fields, he said. That in the present Month, and in January last, he made Inquiry, by himself and 10 others, in the Parish of Bethnal Green, and in Three Parishes only in Spital Fields, One of which he did not go Half over, and found 1,632 Looms unemployed, about 1,300 of which he believed were in the Silk Manufacture, exclu-five of Gauze and Handkerchiefs; and, that, upon Inquiry, he found they were unemployed merely for Want of Work; and that One Loom employs Four Persons, which makes the Number unemployed 5,200. He could not lay particularly in what Branch of the Manu? factory the Decay was, but believed it was in all, from the highest to the lowest

Your Committee, in oraer to fina out the true Cause of this Decay, examined all the above Witnesses, and also Mr. James Johnson, as to the particular Nature of the Manufactory, who agreed, that the Wages to Journeymen Weavers are not raised lately, and that good Workmen may earn from 11 to 15, and some 18 Shillings per Week.

That the Weights of Wrought Silks are as follow: Nine Yards of Ducape to a Pound; Eight Yards of Mantua Silk to a Pound, Eight Shillings the Yard; the lowest Brocade, without Gold and Silver, 7 Yards to a Pound, at Nine Shillings a Yard1; Brocade at Eighteen Shillings a Yard, 5 Yards to a Pound; the highest, at Two Guineas a Yard, Three Yards to the Pound; that in Damalks, of 14 Shillings a Yard, 5 Yards weigh a Pound; and Velvets at Twenty-three Shillings, Three Yards make a Pound.

That the Watte of every Pound of Raw Silk, of 24 Ounces, is in Winding, 5 in Boiling, and 2 in Manufacturing, in all 11 Ounces.

That in Thrown Silk, of 16 Ounces to the Pound, it is Six, viz.4 by Boiling, and 2 in Manufacturing.

That the Price of Raw Silk, on the Average, is 27 Shillings the Pound, and Thrown 32; and that the Duty paid on as much Raw and Thrown Silk together, as will make a Pound of Wrought Silk, is Four Shillings and Eight Pence the Pound, betides the Duty paid in Italy on Raw Silk exported, and Profit to the Middle Man.

That the Expence of varying the Loom for different Patterns upon Brocades, some laid was from to to£.20 according to the Richnefsof the Pattern; and One Wit-nets said it some times amounted to £. 50 and that if Orders could be given for a g-eater Number of each Pattern, the Silk would come cheaper.

That all Silks are sold by the Weavers Wholefile, and that at present very few Silks are exported.

That French Silks have been frequently found without Stamps; from whence they presume there is a great illicit Trade.

Your Committee then examined Mr. Robert Trey, Examiner, Searcher, and Stamper of Foreign Silk? at

the

1

5 Geo. III. 4° Martiu 209

the Custom House, as to the Practice of importing Frenth Silks under the Italian Duty; who said,

That it is very difficult to distinguish French from Italian Silks, particularly if the same Manufacture should be carried on at Genoa and Lyons, and the different Sorts mixed together.

That the Mercers have imported French Silks as lian, and have been permitted, on Application, to change their Entry; that Seizures have been several Times made of French Silks imported as Italian, One of which onlyi has been brought to Trial, and though thought by the Weavers and Mercers to be French, yet Persons have been found to swear, They were the Manufacturers in Italy, and the same have accordingly been adjudged Italian-, which has laid a great Difficulty upon the Officer, because, in many Cafes, he (lands the Expence of the Prosecution: that Seizures have often been given up, though he believes the Silks lb seized were French, and not Italian.

That he believes many Silks are imported from which are really such as they are said to be, and that the Traders enter fairly. He laid further, that he has frequently seized the Manufactures of France, in large Quantities, which have been run; that of late Years he has made more Seizures than formerly; and that Two Judgments have been obtained for £.200, on Seizures of foreign Wrought Silks, illegally imported, found in the Hands of Mercers; since which he has made fomt Seizures in the Shops of Mercers, and out of large Ships.

Your Committee then proceeded to read the Petition of the Mercers, in Opposition to the Weavers; and observing it was signed by 21 Persons, they inquired if the said 21 Persons belonged to so many distinct Houses of Trade; and were informed, that in some Houses, Two, and in others Three, Partners had signed the said Petition; and that the Petitioners upon she whole had no more than 10 Houses of Trade; and your Committee were informed by Mr. Peter Ogier, that besides these 10 Houses, who were Importers, there were above 100 Warehouse Men and Silk Mercers, not Importers, who buy more English Manufacture than those 10 Houses.

To prove the Allegations of this Petition,

Mr. John Peregol, a Weaver of Silks from the High tell, to the rpugheft, was examined, who said, That he employs'more Hands than be used to do, and is fully employed, but that is owing to the Nature of his Trade; which is not to keep a Stock of Goods by him for a general Market, but to work for particular Sftops, whose Patterns cannot be made for others; that this Method of Trade, which he calls a bespoke Trade, is a great Confinement; that if he made on his own Account, and for all the Mercers in general, he could not only make more Silks, but afford them cheaper, because 80 Hands would do the same Work, if he worked on his own Account, as 100 in the bespoke Trade; that the Reason why Silks are dearer in the bespoke Trade, is owing to the few Pieces which are taken of a Pattern (in rich Brocades only Four) which is a very heavy Expence, for the Charge tq the Mailer on every Loom is £.20, and when the Figure is changed, the whole is changed; whereas, as One Set of Harness would make from 18 to 20 Pieces, if he might be permitted to make that Quantity instead of Four, the Expence of the /.20 for the Loom would fall upon the greater instead of the lesser Number.

That this Confinement to Four Pieces of a Pattern is the Occasion of the Importation of Foreign Wrought Silks, because it makes ours dearer.

That he is more and more in the bespoke Trade, owing to the Mercers not choosing to have the Patterns which another Shop has; and that if he was not so confined to particular Shops, he could employ more Men, and with greater Ease.

Tirnt many Men have applied to him for Work, which he could not give them; that the Silk Weavery has been declining, gradually, for 2 or 3 Years; and that he supposes some Part of the Men now unemployed, are in the Gauze Way, but cannot lay what Proportion.

'That if no French Silks were imported, he thinks he should make more of every Pattern.

That the general Credit to the Mercer is 11 Months, and the Weaver abates One Yard and a Quarter in every 20 Yards and a Quarter.

That the Price of Labour is not risen; and that a good Workman may earn from 15 to i8r. a Week.

Mr. John Allen, a Mailer Weaver, laid. That he has now 100 Looms at work; that if he had a larger Capital, he could employ more Looms; that in his Trade, which is chiefly in Flowered Silks, there has, to his Knowledge, been no Decreale, nor does he believe in general there has been any Decrease for the lall Two Years, in the flowered Way; that the Gauze Manufacture has been removed to Scotland, and he thinks (but speaks from Conjecture) that the Journeymen Weavers out of Employ, are in that Way chiefly.

That he prefers a bespoke Trade to keeping a Stock of Goods for a Market, because in the former he would not be subject to have Goods left on his Hands, but should fell all he could make.

Carr and C*, in order to shew the Duty paid on French Silks imported, produced an original Invoice of French Silks, which had. been imported and paid the French Duty, by which it appeared that the Colt of the Silks in France was £.278. its. id. and the Duty £.134. <jr. which is as near as possible to 49 per Cent, on the Cod in France.

The Witness then said, that the Consequence of an Increase of Duty would be a Prohibition, because the few he imported was very small, on account of the Duty being so high.

That Persons conversant in the Business, may distinguish betwixt French and English Silks, though it has sometimes happened to the contrary.

That the Terms of buying Goods in France, are upon such Credit as the Mercers please to take, or if ready Money is paid, the French allow a Discount of 6 per Cent.

That he has heard of French Goods imported as , and seized, about Eight Years ago, but not since.

That he had known One English Pattern of Flowered Damask sent to Italy, to have the Silks made there from it, and then imported.

' That a Government Stamp put upon our own, as well as foreign Silks, would tend to distinguish them from j"uch as were smuggled; and that he thinks Smuggling would be more encouraged by an additional Duty, than a Prohibition.

Mr. Lavie, a Mercer, said, The Duty upon French Silks imported, is £.30 per Cent.

That a total Prohibition would be the Consequence of an Increase of Duty, because the Duties arc already so high, no Mercer could then import for Sale, which would produce a Monopoly amongst the Weavers.

That if there was no Importation of Foreign Silks, the Price of British would be raised, and that the Consequence would be, the Manufacture here would (land (till in the Fancy Way for want of Pattern Drawers, because Variety of Patterns induces People to buy double the Quantity they otherwise would do; and that French Silks would be worn, but they would be got another Way; that since the Prohibition of Gold and Silver Silks the 'Manufacture has decreased, that Prohibition having been attended with a Monopoly and bad Consequences; he declared be was daily wanting those Goods, and could not get them.

That lie has been lucky, and got a Profit upon the French Silks he has imported, though not so much as upon English-, that the Allowance in France is £$ per Cent, for short Measure, and 12 Months Credit, or per Cent, for ready Money.

That he has paid an Allowance lately of Sixpence on los. 6d. on account of Labour, which Advance being

upon the Whole* he cannot so Well judge of it in the Flowered as the Plain Way; but he now pays more than he did Four or Five Years ago.

That the Manufacture in Spital Fields has increased in Six Years fully in Proportion to the Increase of Wear; and that with respect to himself, he has at all Times found a Scarcity.

Mr. Fleetwood,a Mercer, said. That the Duty on

French Silks imported, is £-5 Per Cent.; that an Increase of Duty would amount to a Prohibition; and, in his Opinion, would be of more Detriment to the Silk Manufacture than a total Prohibition, because Smuggling would be thereby greatly increased, which he thinks now at a great Height in Wrought Silks, both with and without Gold and Silver; and that the same is a great Detriment to the Manufactory.

That if the Importation of French Wrought Silks was prohibited, no Designs or Patterns could be got, which w'ould occasion a Monopoly in the Weavers, who at this Time treat the Mercers as if they were their Servants; and though the Mercers lay out annually a large Sum of Money with the Weavers, the latter don’t look upon themselves under the lead Obligation, and refuse to execute their Orders in the Fancy Way.

That the Manufacture of Gold and Silver Silks in England is decreased.

That this Year he could have bought 20 or 30 more Pieces of Silks, if he could have been supplied; and, was it not for the Check of Importation, he thinks the Weavers might impose any Terms on the Mercers.

Being asked, Whether if the Weavers wrere to impose unreasonable Terms on the Mercers, more Weavers would not be induced to let up ? he laid, He thought not, for want of Patterns; and there is no Way of procuring Patterns from France, without permitting the Importation of French Silks.

Mr. Ashburner, a Mercer, said, A total Prohibition of

French Wrought Silks would create a Monopoly in the Weavers, who are now our Matters, and use us as they please; if we want any Thing in the Fancy Way, they either refuse our Orders, or a(k very high Prices.

That this is ow’ing to their being much in the bespoke Trade, which has confined the Business to Two Weavers chiefly; whereas formerly, all the Weavers kept large Stocks of Goods.

That he has not yet this Year been able to make his Assortments for want of Goo is, and has declined dealing with One House, on account of his being ill treated.

That he lays out here ,£.50,000 a Year, and his Orders were never refused by the capital Houi’es till within these 2 or 3 Years; that even Damalks, which are common Things, are not to be procured.

That Fancy Silks imported are for the Sake of Designs, which could not otherwise be got without the Expence of an Agent, who might not know whether they were new.

That he believes the new Method of bespoke Trade, was owing to the Mercers choosing to have Patterns to themselves, and the Ladies not lilung to buy Patterns, which were to be found in all Houses.

That the Mercers cannot establish Weavers, because, in the Fancy Way, they mutt fopport them, which he has tried, and loft Money by it; and they mutt likewise have Pattern Drawers, which is impossible, as the Trade are too jealous of each other to unite.

That the Trade in England is greatly confined for want of Taste, there being no Companion between the Taste of France and England; but that Brocades on white Grounds made in England, are greatly superior to those of France.

Your Committee observing through the Course of this Examination, that the Mercers laid great Stress on the Necessity of having French Patterns, and urged this as a principal Reason why the Importation of French Silks ought to be continued, alleging it to be very difficult to procure inch Patterns, if the Importation was not allowed, thought it proper to inquire particularly into this Fast; and for that Purpose examined the following Mercers on this Head.

Mr. William Pickart laid, That the few French Silks which are now imported, are more for the Sake of Patterns, for the Improvement of our Manufacture, than any Profit arising the reby.-

That for every Piece of French Silk he imports, he can get the Sight of ioo Patterns at least, upon which the Pattern Drawers here improve.

That small French Patterns are of very great Use, the few Pattern Drawers in Eng, who are disengaged, not being able to furnish Designs for all the Looms without them.

That he did not apprehend a Prohibition of French Silks would bring over other Pattern Drawers, as they look upon a Pattern Drawer at Lyons of such Consequence, and give him such high Wages; and that he never knew one born in France come over.

To this Point he was cross examined, and aiked. Whether he did not think a larger Salary would tempt a Pattern Drawer to come over ? To which he answered. He did not know: He was then aiked. If he knew what Salaries were given in France ? To which he like wile an-fvvered, He did not know.

Mr. Nathaniel Paterjon, a Throwfter in London, said, T-hat his Mills have in part flood still all this Winter, for Want of Raw Silk.

That Raw Silk comes from China, Bengal, many Parts of Italy, Spain, Sicily, some Parts of Genoa, and from Turkey; that the Bengal and Turkey Silk being very ordinary is used mostiy in the Button, and Twist, and Stocking Way; that it requires very little Labour to throw it, and is consequently of very little Affifiance tq the Throwfters.

- That the China and Italian Silk being extremely fine, Ten Times finer than Bengali in general, is the Species of Silk which employs the Throwfters, and has been the Means of letting up a Number of Mills in Imitation of those originally built by Sir Thomas Loom for Organzining Silk, that 100lb. of Italian or China Raw Silk will employ double the Number of Hands that Bengal or Turkey will; and that White China Silk is absolutely necessary for fine Gauze Silk Stockings.

That an Act of Parliament passed in the Year 1749 and 17.50, by which the Duty on China Raw Silk was reduced to that of Italian, in consequence of which great Quantities of China Silk was imported for the first 8 Years, and there being reason to imagine that the Importation would continue, it encouraged many People, and him in particular, to set up Silk Mills in Imitation of Sir Thomas Loom's, by which many Thousands of People were employed in Organizing Silk for Warp, and Throwing it for Trams.

That the Importation from China has been reduced to such a Degree that no more was brought in, in the Year 1764, than 6,741 lbs. whereas, upon an Average from the Year 1752 to j 760, there was imported from China 140,000 Pounds per Annum.

That the Exportation of Raw Silk is prohibited from Piedmont and Florence, and is loaded with a Duty of 25 per Cent, in the Kingdom of Naples, and One Shilling per Pound of 16 Ounces in the Milanese State, which produces a large Quantity , of Silk for Organzine and Trams; and in Spain it is never suffered to be exported, till their own Manufacturers have certified that they have had a sufficient Supply, and then the Surplus is allowed to be exported under a Duty of 16 per Pound of 16 Ounces. In the Roman State, which produces more Raw Silk than any other State, there is little or no Duty upon the Exportation, and if the Duty be taken off Raw Silk large Quantities would come Raw which now come Thrown; and that the King of Sardinia gives a Bounty of 6d. English per Pound on the Introduction of Foreign Silk, for the Sake of his own Mills; though the Growth of Silk in his County is very great.

That in Florence, from whence the best of all Silk conies for the Use of the Throwfters, the Exportation Yol. 30.

of Raw Silk is prohibited under thC Penalty of Death j which makes much against the English Manufacture.

That the Price of Working Organzine in Turin is 31. 9 d.Eng/ish per lb.; besides which the Throwfter Hands to the Watte, which reduces it to about 2 9 5

and that in England, exclusive of Waste, the same colls about $s. 6 d.; and that Trams are worked cheaper in proportion in Italy: Tram at Milan is worked lor 2 s. per Pound English, and would cost here 4f.; so that the said Difference of Labour in added to the Duty on Exportation there, is more than equal to the Difference of Duty between Raw and Thrown Silk on Importation here.

That it is owing to these Difficulties in getting proper Silk for the Use of the Throwfter the Trade is almost totally ruined, and though it may be true that there is an Increase of Turkey and Bengal Silk, yet the same Quantity of all Sorts will not l'upply the same Number of Hands; and besides these Difficulties there are such Disadvantages attending the English Throwfter, that it is out of his Power to fell the Silk when Organzined so cheap as it can be imported from the Italian States Thrown, for the Exportation being prohibited in some of the Italian States, and in others very high Duties laid, together with the Duty paid in England, it renders the Raw Silk imported here much dearer than in Italy, where they have no Competitors; besides this, the English Throwfters are obliged to buy from the Merchants here, who buy from the Heelers Abroad; fp the Profit of these Two are saved to the Foreigner; who having besides Mills of his own, purchases the Cocons, and has Filiatures of his own.

That by Recolta is meant the Crop of Silk, or the Time when the Worms finish spinning, and the Silk is-in Cocons, which is in the latter End of June: and by Filiature is meant the Silk reeled from the Cocons.

That Organzine Silk is first spun in a single Thread on particular Mills, which was never practised till Sic Thomas Loom's Invention, and when spun it is doubled and thrown hard Two Threads together; whereas Tram, which is only fit for Shute, after being wound double is flack Thrown.

That he estimates above 360,000 lbs. of Organzine Silk is used per Annum in England; and that all the Mills now erected in this Country could throw in Organzine about One Ninth Part of the whole Quantity; and if proper Encouragement could be given, he thinks a great many more Mills would be erected; that in his Building he has Eleven Mills, of which Five are now Handing Hill; and that the Remainder, he is afraid, will be employed to Loss, but he keeps them in Employ merely to keep the Hands from starving.

That the Organzining Silk has lain under great Disadvantages for many Years pad, as the Thrown Silk comes cheaper from Abroad, but People often embark in building Mills without considering these Disadvantages.

That he lived with Sir Thomas Loom when there was no Prohibition in Italy of the Exportation of Raw Silk; and^that Sir Thomas often told him, if he had known before he built his Mills that the King of Sardinia would have prohibited the Exportation of Raw Silk, he should not have done it; and that the Notion which prevailed of Sir Thomas getting his Fortune by his Mills, which was a Mistake, he believed was the Occasion of other People building Mills likewise; that he does not think upon an Average of 7 Years it has been a losing Trade, but that it certainly has this last Year or Two; and that Mr. Lloyd, who bought Sir Thomas's Mills, he believes, from his own Loss, loft £. 1,000 by a Sale last Week on 7,000 Pounds Weight of Silk; and he thinks the Trade will lose for the Time to come, if some Relief is not given.

That the Remedy he would apply is to give some Encouragement to bring in Raw Silk from those States in Italy which do not prohibit the Exportation of it, but

he does not think that those States which do prohibit the Exportation will be prevailed upon to allow it.

That Silk has been exported from hence and taken the Drawback, and then been manufactured and brought back here} and that it has likewise been sent Abroad to make Blond Lace, supposed to be brought back into this Country.

That he is about 5 Weeks Organzining 150 Pound Weight of Silk, going through the whole Process of it.

That the Organzine Mills can work Tram as well as Organzine, and that there ane a great Number of Silk Mills in this Kingdom which do not work Organzine, but having adopted the Italian Winding Engines, which is Part of Sir Thomas Loom’s Discovery, work large Quantities of fine Trams.

Upon the whole the Evidence laid. That the Italian Throwfter, by the Advantages which he has in providing upon the Spot the Raw Silk on much better Terms than the English Throwfter can, and by getting such

Silk in Italy thrown at is. to is. 6 per lb. left than the English Throwfter can, is able, notwithstanding the Difference here in the Duties of Raw and Thrown Silk, to furnish this Market with Thrown Silk, which cods him is. (id. to is. per lb. leis than Silk of the same Quality will stand the English Throwfter in; therefore the English Manufacturer of Thrown Silk cannot be near upon a Par with the Italian, unless the whole Duty be taken off

Raw Silk, or an Equivalent thereto granted in Favour of the English Throwfter.

That the Art of Sizing Silk in the Stocking Manufactory h is been lately found out, which is of great Ufo, and employs great Quantities of Thrown Silk.

That there are 7 Mills in England that work Organzine on Sir Thomas Loom’s Principle, and that such Wills can also work Tram.

Mr David Hall a Silk Throwfter at Macclesfield, said. He had been in Trade 5 Years; that in 176a he era-

Stayed 200 People; that he was obliged to leave off his lufiness for Want of Employ* and came to Town last Sunday Fortnight, and could not get any.

Mr. B/ackJone, a Throwfter, being examined, laid, That his Mills have been but Two Thirds employed for the last Two Years; and that he has now 3,000lb. Weight of Tram lying by him, which he imputed to the high Price of Italian and China Raw Silk, and the small Demand from the Weavers; that he formerly employed 380 Hands, and at present no more than 230; and that from his own Knowledge, and from Letters and Accounts which he had received from several Parts of England, which he produced to your Committee, and which are hereunto annexed, N° 1. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8.

S. 10. 11. 12, he apprehended the Trade to be greatly eclined in general.

That in proportion as this Business declines many People will be deprived of Work, who are not employed in Throwing Silk, as he believes from 12 to 15,000 People are employed in working up the Waste, which is made into Ferrets, Stockings, Knee Garters, Fringes, and Sewing Silks; which Trade would be ruined with the Throwfters; and that there has not been a sufficient Quantity of Waste lately to supply the Demand.

That English Tram bears the same Price now as for Two Years past, and that Foreign Tram is cheaper than English by 3 s.or 4 s.in 33*.

That the Number of Mills in England for Throwing Tram are upwards of 60; and he apprehends theft Mills are One Third unemployed.

Your Committee then proceeded to examine Evidence in Support of the Petitions of the Frame-work-knitters j And,

Mr. John Moirice, a Holier and Frame-work-knit-ter at Nottingham, laid, That this Trade has very much

decreased there of late Years; that it has declined about One Half; that in 1760 and 1761, 1,300 Frames were employed in Nottingham Town in the Silk Branch, and 20

in 1764 only 800; and that each Frame employs Three People, Men, Women, and Chiklren; and that the Decrease in Mitts and Gloves is Three Parts in Four; and that Frames, which in 17602nd 1761 Ibid.from £. 23 to £. 28, now fell only from 10 to 12.

That the Manufacturers have good Stocks on hand and little Demand, and that he imputes this Decrease to the legal Importation and Smuggling of Stocking, Gloves, and Mitts.

That the Duty is high enough at present to prevent the legal Importation, but that some are legally imported tP conceal the Smuggling of others; that the Witness has loid but 3 or Dozen of Stockings in the last Three Weeks; and that he has fold 50 or 60 Dotes in the same Time in former Years, at the same Time of the Year.

He laid. It was easy to distinguish French Stockings from English; but upon his Croft Examination he acknowledged the French might make them exact Iy the fame:

And that if the English Hosiers were to put any Stamp or Mark on their Stockings, the French might easily-counterfeit it.

That, at present the French Gloves and Mitts are not made upon a Frame, as the English ant, which makes-them very distinguishable.

In Support of the Petition of tire Frame-work-knitters of London and Westminsterthe Agent called,

Mr. Charles Tyrcle, a Holier and Manufacturer in Fleet Street, who said. That the Manufacture had increased for some Time, but that for or 5 Years last: it had declined, particularly in Gloves and Mitts; and that he imputed this Decrease to the Foreign Importation; but acknowledged he had always better Trade in War than Peace.

Mr. Obadiah Wright, a Holier in London, laid, He-believed all the Foreign Gloves and Mitts fold in London are run, and that 100 Foreign are fold for One English.

That many French Stockings are smuggled into London, and that a Person at Dunkirk would have lent him any Quantity of Stockings without paying the Duty, but he refused them, though the Person offered-to stand all the Hazard of their being seized, and to deliver them at his own Shop.

That it is very easy to smuggle these Goods, as the Captains of Ships take the whole upon themselves.

That he does not think Silk Stockings can be made so cheap here as in France, on account of the Duty and Price of Silk; but we make them better, and could make them as cheap if the Silk was as cheap.

That he does not think the French could make them like us if they had the Patterns, and that he could' hitherto, always distinguish them; and that if the French were to make the Clock, &c. like the English, they could not fell them so cheap as they do.

That the Price of French Mitts is 20 or nd. per Pair, and the English 30 s.a Dozen; and that the Silk in England without the Manufacturing, would come to as much as the French Mitts.

That this Manufacture in London has very much declined.

That the French Silk Stockings are not so well made as ours, but the Silk is excellent, and they wear well.

That he was applied to to make Silk Stockings to a French Pattern, which cost 5J. 3 and that he could not make them under 6s. 6d.and if we could foil such Stockings we could not make them so cheap.

Mr. George Alcock, being examined as to the Drawback on Exportation of Silk Stockings, said, It was i$d. per lb. and 3*. per lb. on the Silk Manufacture made by Weavers.

Mr. Burton, a Frame-work-knitter in London, laid. He formerly employed 20 Frames, now 9 or 10.

That, Quality and Price considered, he could make Stockings, as cheap as in France.

Mr. Thomas Moore, a Hosier and Manufacturer in London/as to the State of the Trade, said, He had been in the Bufirrefs near 27 Years: that when he first began, the chief Confiimption was Thread and Cotton Stockings, and feme few weighty Silk; that about 18 Years ago, some lighter Silk Stockings were introduced from France, since which Time that Manufacture has increased gradually, till within this last Year or Two; since which the Trade in general has declined, though his own Bufinelshas not; and he believes One Third of Frames in London now want Employment.

As to the Goodness and Price of the Manufactures of the Two Nations, he said. He never thought the French had much the Preference. As to the middling Sort, we exceed them in Goodness, and are not much above them in Price; that they make a (lighter Sort cheaper, and in the (lighted Goods of all the English have not done much yet; that he has seen some French Stockings, that tk> finer than Engljh, particularly One Pair, for which lie gave 33;. but that he could make (ueh, and as cheap, or cheaper than that; and on the whole, he said. He was certain* Price and Quality considered, the English are preferable to the French.

He give it as his Opinion, That the Importation of French Gloves and Mitts did more Prejudice to the English tliaft their Stockings; for as they are made with

Bobbins, and the English with Frames, the French are about One Fifth cheaper, and great Quantities arc fold in London.

That he never (aw any Gloves made with Bobbins in England; for though he applied to the Manufacturers in Buckinghamshire for this Purpose, a few Years ago, the Demand for Blond Lace was then so great, that they whidd not undertake it.

That in his Business he works about One Half for Exportation; that he has exported many Stockings to Portugal, but thinks that Trade dccreased.

Mr. Trott, being again examined, said, That many Gloves and Mitts are imported now; which are entered as Wrought Silk.

Being asked, If he could" devise any Method tbftamp Home Manufacture, or French, (b as the Stamp could not be counterfeited ? he said, No Doubt but all Stamps are liable to be counterfeited, but we have a Cheque to our Stamp at the Custom House, which we apply to, when we are apprehensive of any Counterfeit.

He then produced a Seal, which is affixed to Pieces of Silk, with a Cheque to it, which he was of Opinion could not be counterfeited.

He also produced a Stamp, that he cal* put upon Stockings, Gloves, and Mitts; and he said the Mark was a chymical Preparation, and would not easily wadi out.

And said, That 18,956 Pairs of Gloves and Mitts*, and 647 Pairs of Stockings, were stamped, from March to November last.

Being aiked. Whether, if there was a total Prohibition of Foreign Wrought Silk, and a Stamp Office established, to (lampthe British Manufacture, Smuggling

could be prevented

He said, they might then be known; and he thought Smuggling more likely to be prevented under a' Prohibition-, than under a high Duty.

That he thought a Prohibition of all Gloves and Mitts that are not knitted, would tend to establish the Manufacture in England, because the Officers would know them: But they might dill be run > for though Ribbands are prohibited, many are fmyggled.

SIR,

I would gladly have answered jours fully in every Point mentioned; viz. as to particular Number Mills, Swifts,.'and People, would they have come into it. Mr. Bennett and Stamford say they will lend a satisfactory Account, byt what Mr. Bennett does is through Mr. Lloyd, so that my single Account, I suppose, can be of no Use; it is certain that for some Time past not Half the Number of People hereinmentioned are, or can be employed, and those that are* are not employed whole Days; a melancholy Consideration, and calls loudly for

Mr. Paterson, according to Order, reported from the lfl of M*o.

Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider what Rights of the Proprietor of the Isle of Man, under the several Grants of the said Island, it may be expedient to vest in the Crown, for the further and more effectual preventing the Mischiefs arising to the Revenue and Commerce of Great Britain and Ireland, from the illicit and clandestine Trade to and from the said island; and what Compensation it may be proper to make to the said Proprietor, in respect thereof; the lle-solutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the feme were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That for the further and more effectually preventing the Mischiefs arising to the Revenue and Commerce of Great Britain and Ireland, from the illicit and clandestine Trade to and from the Isle of Man, it is expedient to vest in the Crown, upon a proper Compensation to be paid to the Proprietors of the said Island, the Isle, Castle, and Peele, of Alan, and all Rights, Jurisdictions, and Interests in and over the said Island, and all its Dependencies, holden by the said Proprietors, under the several Grants thereof, or under any other Title whatsoever, excepting only their landed Property, with all their Rights in and over the Soil, as Lords of the Manor, with all Courts Baron, Rents, Services, and other Incidents, to such Courts belonging, their Wastes, Commons, and other Lands, Inland Waters,

Fisheries, and Mills, and all Mines, Minerals, and

Quarries, according to their present Rights therein; *.

Felons Goods, Deodands, Waifs, Estrays, and Wrecks

at Sea, together with the Patronage of the Bishoprick,

and of the other Ecclesiastical Benefices in the said

Island, to which they are now entitled.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Sum of Seventy thousand Pounds may be proper to be paid, as a full Compensation to the said Proprietors, according to the Proposel contained in the Letter from the said Proprietors, dated the 27th Day of February 1765, to the Commissioners of the Treasury.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Annuities granted by Two Acts of Parliament, the One passed in the 33d Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, and the other passed in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, in respect of certain capital Stocks thereby established, amounting together to the Sum of £. 20,240,000, at the Rate of £. 4 per Centum per Annum, for certain Terms, of Years, and then to be reduced to £. 3 per Centum per Annum, which Annuities are, by the said Acts, made payable Half-yearly, on the 5th Day of July and the 5th. Day of January in every Year, and were, by the last mentioned Act, consolidated and made one joint Stock, shall, from and after the 5th Day of July next ensuing, with the Consent of the Proprietors thereof, be payable in the Manner following, that is to say; That one Quarterly Payment of the said Annuities shall be payable on the 10th Day of next; and that the said Annuities, from and after the said 10th Day of October, shall be payable Half-yearly, on the 5th Day of April and the loth Day of October in every Year; and that such of the Proprietors of the said Annuities who shall not signify their Diflent on or before the id Day of June next, in Books to be opened at the Bank of England for that Purpose, shall be deemed and taken to consent thereto.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Qeftion put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the several Rates established by an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her Majesty Queen Anne, for the Conveyance and Postage of Letters and Packets, between London and the Dominions in

America, and between any Places within the said Dominions, do cease and determine.

Resolved, That it b the Opinion of this Committee,

That there be granted to His Majesty, upon the Postage and Conveyance of Letters and Packets from London, to any Port in the British Dominions in America, and from any fixch Port in London, for every Single Letter One Shilling, for every Double Letter Two Shillings, for every Treble Letter Three Shillings, and for every Ounce Four Shillings Sterling Money; and so in proportion for every Packet of Deeds, Writs, or other Things.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That there be granted to His Majesty, upon the Postage and Conveyance of Letters and Packets, from any Port in the British Dominions in America, to any other Port in the said Dominions, for every Single Letter Four Pence, for every Double Letter Eight Pence, for Treble Letter One Shilling, and for ever}’ Ounce One Shilling and Four Pence Sterling Money; and so in proportion for every Packet of Deeds, Writs, or other Things.

and uling the Coal Trade, was presented to the House, and read.; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that several Petitions have been preleiited, relative to the Navigation of the River Tyne-, and that the Petitioners apprehend the River of Tyne and Harbour of Shields are now irt a much worse Condition for the Purposes of the Coal Trade, and particularly for the Colliers trading to London, titan the same were in Twenty Years ago; and, unless some effectual Methods are immediately taken to cleanse and scour the said River and Harbour, the Consequence will, as the Petitioners conceive, be very prejudicial to the Nation in general, and to the City of London in particular; and that the Petitioners, like other Owners, pay a Duty upon Coals and Ballail to the Corporation of Newcastle upon Tyne, to a very considerable annual Amount; and as the said Corporation daim the Con-iervatorship of the said River, and justify, (as the Petitioners are informed) the receiving the said Duties from an Obligation they are under to cleanse and scour the said River and Harbour, and to keep the same a Place of Safety for Ships to load and lie in: Therefore praying, That the Conservators may be compelled (by such Means as the House shall think proper) to cleanse and scour the said River and Harbour, and to keep the same clean and navigable; and to grant to the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premites, as to the House shall seem meet.

That for the more effectual Protection and Encouragement of the Trade to Africa, the Fort of Senegal and its Dependencies, and all Other the British Forts and Settlements upon the Coast of Africa, lying between the Port of Sallee, and Cape Rouge, be veiled in His Majesty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the British Forts and Settlements upon the Coast of Africa, lying to the Southward of Cape Rouge, do continue vested in the Company of Merchants trading to Africa.
