Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Persons interested in, or entitled unto, any Bill or Bills, payable in the Course of the Navy or Victualling Offices, or for Transports, which were made out on or before the 30th Day of June 1764, who shall, on or before the 26th Day of this Instant , carry the fame, after having had the Interest thereupon computed to the 6th Day of April next, and marked upon the said Bills at the Navy or Victualling Office respectively, to the Office of the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, shall have, in exchange for the fame, from such Treasurer, or his Paymaster or Cashier, a Certificate to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, for every entire Sum of One or more Hundred Pounds, of which such Bill or Bills, together with the Interest lb marked, shall consist, until the several entire Sums of One or more hundred Pounds, for which such Certificates are to be made forth, shall amount together to One million Five hundred thousand Pounds, and also One other Certificate for the Fractional Part of One hundred Pounds being the Remainder of such Bill or Bills; and the Persons who shall be possessed of such first-mentioned Certificates, of the entire Sum of One or more hundred Pounds, shall upon Delivery thereof to the said Governor and Company, be entitled, in respect of the fame, to the Annuities hereafter mentioned: That is to say; for Two Fifth Parts of the Sums therein mentioned, to an Annuity after the Rate cf Three Pounds per Cent, redeemable by Parliament, and transferable and paid at the Bank of England', for Two other Fifth Parts thereof, :to a proportional Number of Tickets of the Value of Ten Pounds, in a Lottery, to consist of 60,000 Tickets, every Blank to be of the Value of Six Pounds, the Blanks and Prizes to be attended with the like Three per Cent. Annuities; and for the remaining One Fifth Part, to a dike Annuity, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Cent. with Liberty to.convert the same into an Annuity for Life, after the same Rate, with Benefit of Survivorship, in manner following: That is to say; that every Person who shall become possessed, in Right of One hundred Pounds Capital Stock of an Annuity of Three Pounds in such last-rnentioned Annuities, and shall produce, on or before the 5th Day of April 1766, a Certificate thereof, attested by the Cashier of the Bank of England, to the Auditor of the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, shall, in lieu thereof, be entitled, from the said 5th Day of April 1766, during the Life of the Nominee whom he shall appoint, to a Life Annuity of Three Pounds payable at the Exchequer, out of the Sinking Fund; and the several Nominees to be appointed in respect of such Life Annuities, to be divided into Clas. fes, the whole Annuity belonging to each Clals not to be less than One thouliind Five hundred Pounds, if Life Annuities to that Amount shall be lb subscribed; and, upon the Death of every Nominee, the Annuity so fallen in to be distributed among the Survivors of the same Class: And the Annuities, in respect of the said first Two Fifth Parts, shall be immediately added to, and made a Part of, the Joint Stock of Annuities, reduced from to 3 per Cent, and consolidated, pursuant to certain Aifts of Parliament, made in the 25th and 26th Years of the Reign of his late Majesty; and the Annuities attending the said Lottery, together with such of the Annuities in respect of the said One Fifth Part as shall not be exchanged for Annuities on Lives, with the Benefit of Survivorship, in manner above mentioned, shall also be added to, and made a Part of, such Joint Stock, from the 5th Day of April 1766; and all the said Annuities, transferable, and paid at the Bank, shall Commence from the said 5th Day of April i 765, and be payable Half-yearly, on the 10th Day of October and the 5th Day of April in every Year, out of the Sinking Fund: But, in case the several entire Sums of One or

more hundred Pounds, for which Certificates are to be granted by the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, orjjis Paymaster or Cashier, in respect of such Bills lo to be delivered in, on or before the 26th Day of this instant March, and of the Interest marked thereon, shall not then amount in the Whole to the Sum of One million Five hundred thousand Pounds,-all- Persons possessed of the above-mentioned Certificates for the fractional Part£ of One hundred Pounds, or of Navy, Victualling, or Transport Bills, which were made out on or before the 30th Day of June 1764, and do not amount, together with the Interest thereupon, computed, to the 6th Day of April next, to One hundred Pounds, may, on or before the 5th Day of Aprilnext, after having had the Interest upon such Bills marked in such Manner as is before mentioned, bring the same to the Office of the Treafilrer of His Majesty’s Navy, and shall have, in exchange for the fame, from such Tmal'urer or. his Paymaster or Cashier, a Certificate to the said Governor and Company of the Bank of England, for the Sums contained in such Certificates, and for the Amount of the Principal and Interest of which such Bills shall consist; and, upon Delivery thereof, and Payment of lo much Money to the said Governor and Company as shall, with the Sunt so certified, amount toOne hundred Pounds, shall be entitled to the Annuities and Advantages before mentioned: And if any such Certificates for fractional Parts shall not be delivered in, and subscribed as aforesaid, on or before the said 5 th Day of April next, they shall be paid according to the course of the Navy, in such Order as the Bills in Part of which they were granted were payable; and such of them, as were granted in part of Bills bearing Interest shall, from the said 5th Day of April next carry the like Interest to which such Bills were entitled.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be granted to His Majesty, an additional Duty ot Four Shillings for every Chaldron of Coals, Newcastle Measure, which shall be shipped for Exportation to any Part beyond the Seas, except to Ireland, the Isle of , or the British Dominions in America; and after the fame

Rate for any greater or leis Quantity. )

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee; That there be granted to His Majesty, upon all Wrought Silks, Bengals, and Stuffs, mixed with Silk or Herba, of the Manufacture of Persia, China, or East India, and upon all Calicos, printed, dyed, painted, or stained, there, which shall be exported from this Kingdom, except to Africa, or the British Dominions in America, a Subsidy of Poundage, after the Rate of Twelve Pence for every Twenty Shillings of the Value of such Goods, according to the grols Price at which the same were Ibid.at the public Sales thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon the Exportation from this Kingdom of any sort of White Calicos or Mullins, except to Africa or the British Dominions in America, there be retained, besides the One Half of the Rate or Duty commonly called The Old Subsidy, which now remains, and is not drawn back for the fame, the further Sum of Two Pounds for every Hundred Pounds of the true and real Value of such Goods, according to the gross Price at which they were sold at the Sale of the United Company of Merchants trading to the East Indies; but that such Calicos, which' shall first have been printed, stained, painted, or dyed, in Great Britain, shall not be subject to the said Duty of Two Pounds, to be retained as aforesaid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be granted to His Majesty, a Stamp Duty of Two Pence for every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, on which shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, any Policy of Assurance, which shall be made or entered into, within the Cities of London or Westminster, or elsewhere within the Limits of

the Weekly Bills of Mortality, over and above all other Duties.

The Agent for the Petitioners produced Three Acts, passed in the 7th of Queen Anne and the 7th and 14th of King George the Second, which were read: And then,

Mr. John Senior, a Cloth Maker, being examined, laid. That Cloth, though it varies 3, 4, or 5 Inches in Breadth, is generally stamped 1 Yard 13 Inches and an Half, which is the Standard Breadth:

That Cloth, which is only 1 Yard 9 Inches in Breadth, h frequently stretched to the Standard; that Commissions are sometimes given for Cloth under the Standard Breadth, which Orders they must either return, to their great Disad vantage, or subject themselves to the Penalties of the Standard:

That it is impossible to weave Cloth to a given Breadth* on account of the Difference in Wool and its Dirtiness, and also in the Milling, Carding, and Stiffening the Warp when the Air is moist:

That Two Cloths equal in every Respect, as to Materials, when milled. One will come out several Inches narrower than the other, occasioned by the different State of the Stocks:

That when Cloth is(milled to the Standard Breadth, it is frequently found greasy, and then is obliged to be milled over again,‘and consequently loses in the Breadth:

That Coarse Cloths mill swiftly, and will, in 5 Hours, <fun up 30 Inches in Breadth:

That if a Mill-man is ever so diligent.it is impossible for him to mill a Cloth exactly to any given Breadth, so as to make it marketable:

That if he mills 50 Coarse Cloths, and the Wool is of the same Sort, which is almost impossible to get, yet there will be Four or Five Inches Difference, or more, in the Breadth of some:

That it is impossible for the Clothier to stretch his Cloth without being discovered by the Merchant who buys it, because the Merchant will wet it, and the Cloth, when it has lain Hours in Water will run up to its original Breadth:

That when a Cloth is milled narrower, by lying longer in the Stocks, it is generally the stouter:

That the Witness was summoned before a Justke of the Peace for a Cloth 2 Inches under Standard, and the Justice being informed it was owing to the Milling, he remitted the Penalty, and ordered him to agree with the Searcher, which Agreement cost him 7*. 6 and he could not name any other Instance of any* one being punished for making Cloth 2 Inches under the Standard Breadth:

That when a Clothes under the Standard Breadth, it is fold 4 d.or 6d, per Yard cheaper, in proportion to the Price and Goodness of the Cloth:

That when the Merchants finds the Cloth narrow, he infills on an Abatement of 3 Yards in 50 in the Length, and sometimes more; and lie keeps a Stoppage in his Hands, out of which he makes these Abatements, and then does not prosecute the Clothier:

That Prosecutions have been commenced within these or 5 Months for Cloth under the Standard Breadth.

And that more Cloths are now made under the Standard Breadth than there were 20 Years ago, owing to the ready Market for narrow Cloths:

That Cloth sometimes comes out of the Mill a greater Length than the Maker desires, owing to the Warp: That if the Wool is short, the Cloth holds out in Length, but if it be long, it widens and contracts in Length,

When Cloth is strained it looks much worse.

That if a Method was found out to have the Cloth truly stamped, and to prevent over-stretching, it would be an Encouragement to the making Cloth broad, as the Maker would in that same be paid for every Inch of his Cloth.

That if the Searchers were to attend at the Mills and stamp the Cloth truly, it would be a Means of prevent-in the Cloth from beingover-stretched.

That the Witness has been applied to for Cloths 5 Quarters wide, but refused the Order, because he would have been, liable to the Penalty, and the Person told him he did not care, as he could get such Cloth in Lanca-Jkire.

That if the Maker was to put his own Stamps upon his Cloth, the Maker and the Merchant might agree together, so that the Maker might Stamp his Cloth more than it really was, and the Consequence would be, that the Merchant would be left at liberty to over-stretch.

That the Maker in effect is at present the Stamper, because the Miller will stamp the Cloth as the Maker directs, notwithstanding the Maker is answerable to the Merchant for the Width of the Cloth.

That if a General Inspector was appointed, the Witness. apprehends the Maker and the Merchant might llill combine together, and prevent the Inspector seeing the Cloth.

That the Merchant’s Remedy is against the Clothier, and the Clothier's Remedy is against the Searcher, and that the Merchant has an Interest, if he has bad Designs, in wishing the Clothier to make Cloth under the Standard, and the Clothier has an Interest in desiring the Searcher to mark his Cloth the full Breadth.

That if there was nit any Standard, the Clothier

That if the Cloth fells short of the Standard the Merchant’s Remedy is against the Clothier; and if the Searcher marks the Cloth wrong, the Clothier’s Remedy is against the Searchers.

Benjamin Craw/kaw, a Miller, being examined, said. That Cloth, cannot be made or milled to a particular Standard Breadth. '

That Cloths will take more or less Time in milling, from to 29 -Hours, according to the Quality of the Cloth, and lie cannot tell by 5 or 6 Hours how long a Cloth will be in milling when he puts into the Stocks; that he. can tell when Cloth is milled enough by the Feel of it.

That the reason why he cannot mill to a particular Breadth is on account of the Sharpness of the Stocks, and Wool being carded on new or old Cards; but he can’t distinguish by the Appearance of the Cloth, whether the Wool is carded on new or old Cards.

That the Miller stamps the Cloth himself, but not truly,' because of the Penalty on the Clothiers, he stamps it 1 Yard 13 £, if not above 1 Yard 9 or 10; and there is no Penalty on him, he does it to oblige the Clothiers.

That there is a regular Searcher at his Mill, who comes Twice a. Day, and ;stays Half an Hour each Time, but seldom stamps any Cloth.

That Cloths appearing well made, and of proper Mar terials, sufficient for the Standard Breadth, are frequently and unavoidably milled several Inches under it.

That he only remembers One Information by the present Searcher, which was several Years since, for; a Cloth of 1 Yard 9 Inches.

That the Witness mills some Cloths 48 Yards long, and forpetimes mills Two Cloths, each 34 Yaids long, in the same Stock, which frequently stretches, and sometimes . bursts the Stock, and cuts Holes in the Cloth; and that a Cloth of 48 Yards long cannot be well milled in a Stock that has been strained.

That the Clothiers desire to have Two Cloths milled in One Stock, and, if that is refused the Clothier will go to another Mill, and the Miller mud lose his Bread; though he receives no more for 2. Cloths ef. 34 Yards each, than he does for a Cloth of 48 Yards.

That the Witness’s Wages is 6 for One Stock full of Cloth, and his Matter receives Two Shillings, which is generally the Price at all Mills.

Mr. David Farrer, Clothier at being examined,

laid, That when he buys Wool he cannot tell what Quantity of Cloth it will make, but when spun into Yarn, can tell within aij Inch or Two in Breadth and 1 Yard in Length, in a Piece of Cloth of 60 Yards that should be the Standard Breadth. f That, the Spinning of the Yarn harder or foster, will make a Difference of an Inch or Two; that it is in some Measure in the Power of the Weaver to remedy that Pcfech ' ,:

That if Two Cloths of equal Quantity of Materials are sent to the Mill, they will, if proper Care is taken, in general come out nearly alike.;

That Clothiers fend a Note to the Mill-man, describing, the Length and Breadth wanted, which he frequently completes, if he does not, it isowing to his Neglect.

When a Cloth is found greasy, it is sent to the Mill to befcowered, and it is thereby made both longer and broader.

That the Manufacture of Cloth is conducted by Weight till the Wool is spun, and afterwards by Measure* That the Merchant does not always pay for the Cloth delivered, but he never found he wasabated to the Value of the Deficiency in the Breadth of the Cloth.

That the Mill-Searcher is not the proper Person to stamp the Cloth, as it will alter by laying wet, for want of Weather to dry it.

That* he measures the Cloth before it is put on the Tenter as to Length and Breadth, and thinks that is the proper Time to stamp it.

That^when he dries it on the Tenter, he can let it to the Breadth and Length he intends it to be; and if ho had the Power of stamping it himself, he should have no Advantage by stretching it.

That he is not deceived as to the Produce of the Wool above a Yard in Length, or an Inch or Two in Breadth.

That a Cloth is a longer or shorter Time ifi milling according to the Quality of the Cloth and the Sharp-nels of the Stocks; that he has known one Cloth pulled in Six Hours, and another has not been milled in left than 40 Hours; that Stocks are sharp when new made or new lined.

That there will be that Difference in milling Cloth# of equal Quality; that if a Cloth be of a thriving Wool, it will mill quick; but if of a poor hungry Nature, will mill flower.

That it is the Maker’s Interest to have Cloth duly stamped, but it is not always stamped of the Breadth the Maker requires; that he never knew a Mill-man stamp Cloth unfairly above Half a Y ard in Length.

That the Miller frequently, though he has no Orders, stamps the Cloth 1 Yard 13^, though'not of that Breadth,-

That it happens sometimes that the Maker has a Cloth Three or Four Inches under Breadth, and wiil not have the full Breadth stamped on it.

That die Maker has the Cloth stamped under thp Standard to prevent the Searcher finding it, and lodging an Information against him for not having it of th? Standard Breadth; and he informs against himself to save Half the Penalty; that he has lain an Information against: himself for a Cloth of x Yard 10 Inches; that the oftener a Cloth is wetted, the more it loses in Length and Breadth.

That if a Cloth is measured when it comes from the Mill, and has lain Three cr Four Days or a Week without being dried, and then measure it again, it will be both shorter and narrower, but can’t say how much; and if over milled, will lose both fh Length and Breadth.

That Cloth is always less in Length and Breadth when Twice rnilled.

That the Merchants abroad know that Cloth is made, in TorkJJiire to a particular Breadth, and expect to have it so; but thinks it would not be for their Advantage if Cloth was duly stamped; though he believes all Buyers of Cloth, if it is narrow, endeavour to let it to the Standard Breadth, and that stretching makes the Cloth worse.

That the Witness thinks the Trade would not Be well regulated, if the Makers were at Liberty to make Cloths of such Breadth as their Correspondents require.

That the Benefit of the Stamp is to secure the Credit of the Manufacture abroad.

Mr. JoftniaSmith, a mixt Clothier, being exatnihed,

said. That he never found it difficult to make Cloth of the Standard Breadth.

That he is sensible of the Advantage to the Manufacture of Broad Woollen Cloth, from having it made to the Standard Breadth, because he never liad Orders for Cloth under the Standard Breadth.

That the Clothier’s Advantage by.stretching his Cloth before he carries it to Market is, thiit it takes out the Mill Wrinkles, and makes it come up to the Standard Breadth whether it is so or not. and by that Means induces the Merchant to buy it.

That the properest Time to stamp Cloth is immediately before it is put on the Clothier’s Tenters.

That he thinks the Act passed in the Year 172J was of great Use to the Manufactory of Cloth, as the Clothiers made their Cloth fuller and broader, and the Trade was carried on to the mutual Sathfudion of all Parties.

That he met the Clothiers previous to the present Application, and drew up a Plan of a Bill with a Standard, but without a Penalty for Breach of it.

That he never had a Cloth under Standard, except by some Accident at the Mill, and that not One in Ten; and that he has more Cloth above than under the Standard.

That he never delivers Cloth under the Standard and does not find any Difficulty in complying with his Orders.

That the Merchants can discover whether Cloth is stretched by wetting it, which they always do In order to dress it.

That if the Witness makes Cloth above the Standard, he fells it in proportion to the Quality and Breadth , and does not think there are any Inconveniences attending the present Law; that he drew up the Bill to quiet several People in the Trade, who complained they lay under Difficulties.

That if a Mill-man does his Duty Cloths will in general come out of the Mill alike; and he laid. That he does not fail One Cloth in Ten.

That there is a great Difference in Wool, and some Cloth will run up more than others at the Mill; that he often finds great Difference in a Quantity of WoqI, as to the Hardness or Softness, and Greafiness. of it; but he does not buy bad Wool at all.

That many Cloths come into Market t Yard 9 Inches, to the Detriment of Trade; that he supposes both Merchant and Clothier spoil the Cloth; that if a Cloth is I Yard 9 Inches, the Clothier is deficient, and the Merchant is obliged, though unwillingly, to spoil that Cloth, to bring it up to the Breadth, to comply with his Orders.

That he thinks it his own and every Clothier’s Interest to make Cloth to the Standard Breadth; that the; Clothier’s Advantage, by stretching, is to carry it up to the Standard, and make it faleablej and the Stamping at the Mill, previous to the Stretching, gives them that Advantage.

That if the Stamp is put on the Cloth to Be of the Standard, though really not before it is stretched on the Clothiers Tenters, the Stamp in that same enables the Clothier to fell the Cloth as being Standard when it i4 not j and that the Stamp; as now fixed dn the Cloth, tends to discredit the Manufacture Abroad.

That he thinks it for the Credit of the Manufacture to stamp true Length and Breadth; Clothier deceives the Merchant when he fells Cloth that is stretched, and the Merchant deceives the Foreigner by felling Cloth, that he has stretched»

That if a Stamp could be put to prevent Clothier deceiving the Merchant, and Stamp put to prevent

That he generally stamps Cloth i Yard 13 Inches and {, and let it be measured at what Time he will, it will be deficient Half a Yard in Length, and perhaps art Inch in Breadth; but can’t say he ever measured a Cloth after it had lain a Week wet.

That he does not think it the properest Time to stamp Cloth when it has lain Hours wet after it is taken out of the Stock, because if it is bad Weather and a thriving Cloth it will grow, and in a Week run up Half a Yard in Length, and an Inch in Breadth; and that Clothiers sometimes come to the Mill for new Stamps, though the Cloth had been stamped, but had grown up.

Mr. William Cowell, a Merchant at Leeds, being examined, said. That he is of Opinion the Standard is of great Use, and abolishing of it would be of bad Consequence.

That he never had any Order for Cloth under Standard, nor does he believe any regular Merchant ever had.

That before the passing of the last Act, the Trade was in a languishing State, but afterwards flourished much.

That he remembers Prosecutions on that Act, and many heavy Penalties inflicted on Millers and Clothiers.

That Mill Searchers were appointed in 1741 to take off the Penalty from the Millers.

That he, as a Merchant, has no Remedy against the Mill Searcher for false stamping.

That he had too frequent Complaints from Abroad, for fending Cloth under the Standard Breadth.

That if the Clothiers manufacture their Goods up to the Standard Breadth they have no occasion to stretch it, therefore the Stretching is to deceive the Merchant.

That the Cloth brought to the Market is in general too narrow for Exportation; and therefore the Merchants are obliged to stretch it further than they are willing, or is lawful for them to do.

That it would be greatly for the Benefit of Trade to have Cloth under the Standard Breadth; that the most effectual Method to prevent stretching, is for the Maker to put a Seal when the Cloth is tentered, containing its true Length and Breadth, and would propose an Inspec-for, who should keep several Register Offices; and if the Cloth is false stamped, the Register to stamp it and i'eal it again, and that to be the Rule of Payment.

That it would be of bad Consequence if the Parties were to agree without the Inspector’s Knowledge.

That it is expected in foreign Markets, that Cloth should be of the Standard, though there is great Quan* tities of Cloth in Leeds under that Breadth; that he thinks stretching, as now allowed by Law, is detrimental, and that it would be better if they W'ere allowed to stretch only § a Yard in a Score; and that the Standard Breadth should be 1 Yard 15 Inches.

That the Merchants at present allow /. 5 per Ce'nt. ort the Length, but he is in Hopes that they might be prevailed on to take 2 f per Cent, as the Goods would than go so much the honester, and clear from shrinking.

That it Would be more difficult to ascertain the Breadth without a Standard than with one, because lo long as a Standard is properly supported all wife and capable Ma-nufaftuters will endeavour to come to any Orders or any Measure, which they find is wanted by the Merchant.

That he frequently buys Goods under Standard, but has a proper Market to apply to where there is no Standard, and can have Goods of any Lengths or Breadths.

That he sometimes prefers a Market without a Stand-atd to suit a variety of Orders, which a Market where there is a Standard would not do.

That it is a Convenience to have a Market where there is no Standard; but does not go there to buy Broad Woollen Cloths.

That in some Sorts of Cloths a Market without Standard is a Convenience.

That a wife Merchant, though a dishonest One, would nojt have any interest in wishir.g his Cloth really to be under Standard, and yet marked Standard to stretch it the more, because he would lose by it in the End.

That the Clothier frequently stamps Cloth Standard Breadth, though short, to the Prejudice of the Buyer.

That the Merchant’s Remedy is against the Clothier, which Merchant’s interest may be that the Clothier should do wrong, and the Clothier’s interest that the Searcher should do wrong.

That he thinks if the Clothier could not deceive the Merchant, he would not have any interest in false stamping, if there was no Standard.

Mr. Thomas Lee, Merchant at Leeds, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Cowell.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Refblutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Laws now in force, prescribing particular Standards of Width and Length, for the several Woollen Cloths, respectively made within the West Riding of the County of Yorkr, have been ineffectual even to the Purposes proposed to have been secured by the said Acts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Establishment of the said respective Standards, by Act of Parliament, as a Regulation of the Manufacture, has been found inconvenient, in many Respects productive of Frauds, and in no degree advantageous to the Manufacture.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for repealing so much of the said several Laws as relates to the Standard, and substituting other Regulations of the Cloth Trade within the West Riding of the County of York, by proper Cheques, Inspections, and Measurements to be made, and Stamps to be affixed at the proper Stages of the Manufacture, for preventing the several Frauds, for certifying the teal Contents of the Cloth, and for preserving the Credit of the said Manufacture at the foreign Market.

The Two Eirft Resolutions of the Committee being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The last ftesolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repealing so much of the several Laws now in force as. prescribes particular Standards of Width and Length for the several Woollen Cloths made within the West Riding

A Petition of the Mill-owners, their Farmers, and Mill-men, within the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, it there be no Standard for the Length of coloured Broad Cloth, it will be highly prejudicial for the Trade in general, and to the Petitioners in particular, for the Reasons set forth in the said Petition: And therefore praying. That the Clothiers may have a certain Length limited them for the coloured Broad Cloths 3 and that, the Act of Queen Anne being obtained at the foie Expence of the Mill-owners, and by the Approbation of both Merchants and Clothiers, and never since altered, save to Forty-eight Yards, and then to the good Liking of both Merchant and Clothier, that the One of these Acts shall be the Rule as to the Length of the said coloured Cloths, or to what other reasonable Length the House shall think most proper, not to be oppressive to the Petitioners in the Value of their Estates, and their1 Farmers for their great and flavilh Labour, working Night and Day.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That a Ship has failed, under the Direction of the Commissioners of Longitude, from Po in Great Britain, to

Barbadoes in the West Indies; and that, by Means of a

Machine, Watch, or Time-keeper, invented by Mr. John Harrison, thej said Ship did not lose its Longitude beyond Ten Geographical Miles.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Method for finding the Longitude at Sea, within Half a Degree of a Great Circle, or Thirty Geographical Miles, by Means of the said Watch or Timekeeper, invented by the said Mr. John Harrison, may be made generally practicable, and of general Utility, if the Principles, upon which the said Machine is constructed, are fully discovered and explained, and other Watches or Time-keepers of the same Kind can be made.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That One Moiety of the greatest Reward, which is di-redledbyanAcl, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for providing a Public Reward for such Person or Persons as shall discover the Longitude at Sea, to be paid to the Author or Authors, Discoverer or Discoverers, of a proper Method for finding the said Longitude, be paid to the said Mr. John Harrison, as soon as the Principles, upon which his Machine, Watch, or Time-keeper, is constructed, are fully discovered and explained, and so soon as the said Mr. Harrison hath assigned the Property of his Time-keepers to the Commissioners of the Longitude, for the Use of the Public, according to the Conditions «n which divers Sums of Money have been advanced to 9

hlrrt by Order of the said Commissioners; deducting the reout the SumofTwo thousand Five hundred Pounds, already advanced to him; and the other Moiety of the said Reward be paid to him, when other Watches or Time-keepers of the same Kind are made, and, upon Trial, found to be of a sufficient Correctness to determine the said Longitude within Half a Degree of a Great Circle, or Thirty Geographical Miles.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That great Progress has been made towards discovering the Longitude at Sea, by a Set of Lunar Tables, constructed by Tobias Mayer, deceased, late Profelfor at Goetinghen in Germany, in which he was considerably assisted from Theorems furnished by Professor Eu/tr, of the University of Berlin', and that the said Tables are of considerable Use to the Public.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Tables may be further improved, and made of more general Utility.

Resolved, 'I hat it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Widow, or other Representatives, of the said Professor Mayer, arc deserving of a Public Reward, upon their assigning the Property of the said Tables to the Commissioners of Longitude, for the Use of the Public; and also, that the said Profelfor Euler is defers ing of an honorary and pecuniary Acknowledgment of his uteful and ingenious Labours towards the Discovery of the Longitude, and for the Improvement of Navigation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Powers of the said Act of the Twelfth of Queen Anne, and also of an Act passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for rendering more effectual the said Act, be explained, and made effectual, as well for receiving the Discovery and Explanations of the Principles upon which the said Machine or Watch is constructed, and for making Trial of other Watches to be made in consequence thereof, and for paying the said Reward to the said Mr his Executors, or Administrators, as for giving propet Rewards to Professbr Euler and to the Widow or Representatives of the said Professor Mayer, and to such Person or Persons as shall improve the said Tables of the Moon, or have contributed to the Construction of the said Tables; as also to such Person or Persons as shall make other Discoveries useful to Navigation, (b as the Reward to the said Professor Euler, and to;the said Widow or Representatives of the said Professor Mayer, do not exceed the Sum of Five thousand Five hundred Pounds, and the other Rewards do not exceed in the Whole the Sum of Five thousand Pounds; the said Rewards to be paid out of any Money in the Hands of the Treasurer of the Navy, unapplied to the Purposes of the Navy.

Glove Mr. Boulton reported from the Committee, who were Manufacture, appointed to examine into the present State of the Manufacture of Leather Gloves and Leather Mittins; and to report the lame, as it should appear to them, to the House; That the Committee had examined accordingly; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards- delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Mr. William Majfey, a Glover, informed your Committee, That the Trade -of Leather -Gloves and Mittins is in a declining State, owing to the great Quantities of French Leather Gloves and Mittins lnruggled into this. Kingdom.

That he believes there are 50,000 Dozen and upwards of Leather Gloves and Mittins annually smuggled into this Kingdom; that the Trade cannot be furnished but with such foreign Goods as have been seized and sold at the Custom-«House, owing to Foreigners manufacturing their Skins into Gloves and Mittins, and smuggling them into this Kingdom.

That there is a great Decrease in the Duties on the Importation of Kid and Lamb Skins; that One House Vol. 30.

in London paid more Duties formerly than all the Trade together pay now.

That if the Importation of foreign Gloves and Mittins was prohibited. Skins would be imported into this Kingdom for want of a Market abroad; and that if Skins were imported into this Country, they could manufacture them into Gloves and Mittitis better than the foreign Manufacturers.

That the Demand for Gloves and Mittins in France has been lb great, that the French have bought up Skins in Italy, which has been a Means of distressing the Trade here for want of them; and that the French have likewise manufactured those Skins into Gloves and Mittins, and have smuggled them into this Country.

That Smuggling prevents the Trade employing so many Hands as formerly, for want of Leather to work up into Gloves and Mittins; and that many of the Trade are in great Distress at this Time for want of Employment, particularly Women and Children.

The above Evidence was confirmed by Mr. John Walter, Mr. Richard Griffith, Mr. John Pitt, Mr.

George Jennings, and Mr. William Rowe, who are all Dealers in Gloves and Mittins.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thttrfday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

Mr. Kyttaston, according to Order, reported from the

Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of an Act, made in the 26th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for permitting the Importation of Wool, and Woollen or Bay Yarn, from any Port in Ireland, to any Port in Great Britain, the Resolu-lutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Import from Ireland of Wool, Wool-fells, Short-lings, Mortlings, Wool-flocks, Worsted, Bay, or Woollen Yarn, Cloth, Serge, Bays, Kerseys, Says, Frizes, Druggets, Cloth Serges, Shalloons, or other Drapery Stuffs, or Woollen Manufactures, made up with Wool or Wool-flocks, hath of late greatly decreased.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, intituled, An Act for taking off the Duties upon Woollen and Bay Yarn imported from Ireland to England, and for the more effectual preventing the Exportation of Wool from Great Britain, and of Wool and Wool manufactured from Ireland, to Foreign Parts, passed in the 12th Year of King George the Second, as permits the Exportation of the said Commodities from all the Ports of Ireland to Great Britain, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 26th Year of the Reign of Lis late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Von. 30,

Act fof opening the Port of Exeter, for the Importation of Wool and Woollen Yarn from Ireland, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, intituled, An Act for permitting the Exportation of Wool, and Woollen or Bay Yarn, from any Port in Ireland, to any Port in Great Britain, passed in the 26th Year of King the

Second, as permits the Exportation of Wool, Woollen or Bay Yarn, Wool-fells, Shortlings, Mortlings, Wool-flocks, and Worsted Yarn, from any Port in Ireland, to any Port in Great Britain, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the future, Dublin, Waterford, Hew Ross, Toughall, Kingsale, Cork, Drogheda, Newry, Wexford, Wicklow, and Dundalk, shall be the only Ports in Ireland, from which Wool, Wool-fells, Shortlings, Mort-lings. Wool-flocks, Worsted, Bay, or Woollen Yarn, Cloth, Serge, Bays, Kerseys, Says, Frizes, Druggets, Cloth Serges, Shalloons, or any other Drapery Stuffs, or Woollen Manufactures, made up with Wool or Wool-flocks, shall be exported, to be brought into Great Britain; and that Bideford, Minehead,

Bridgewater, Bristol, Milford Haven, Liverpool,

Lancaster, and Whitehaven, shall be the only Ports in Great Britain, into which the said Commodities shall be importedexcept that Bay and Woollen Yarn be permitted to be imported into Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk.

The Two First Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Third Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That the said Resolution be re-committed;

It passed in the Negative,

Then the said Resolution was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The subsequent Resolutions of the Committee being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of the several Cutting Butchers of the Cities of London and Westminster, and Borough of Southwark, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was prefen ted to the House, and read; Setting forth, that the Petitioners are informed, a Bill is depending for repealing so much of an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of Queen Anne, for explaining and making more effectual that Part of an Act, passed in the 5th Year of Queen Anne, concerning the Buying and Selling of Cattle in Smithfield, and for giving Leave for bringing up Calves dead to London as formerly, as relates to the Selling of Sheep and Grass Lambs dead, by one Butcher to another; and alleging, that the Farmer and Grazier consign their Sheep and Lambs to their respective Salesmen in Town, who fell the feme to another Set of Men, called Carcase Butchers, wbq are about 28 in Number; and that the Carcase Butchers have been long labouring to engross to themselves the whole Power of supplying the Town with Mutton and Lamb; and each of them, upon an Average, buy weekly of the Salesmen 400 Head a-piece, which they retail out to the numerous Body of Cutting Butchers; the Salesmen and Carcase Butchers, therefore, have it in their Power to combine together, and buy and sell at what Price they please, and thereby subject both the Grazier and House-keeper to such Price as they think fit; and representing to the House, that the great Source and principal Caule of the present Dearnels of Provisions is chiefly owing to the Carcase Butcher having the foie Pbwer of

The said Copy is preserved anaongst the other Pa--pers of this Session; and the said Translatioa and Certificate are as followeth; viz.,

Translation of a Convention between His Majesty and the . moll Christian King, concluded and ligned at,

the 27th of February 1765,

CONVENTION. -The Courts of Great Britain and France having reciprocally delivered several States, or Accounts of Advances made by them, respectively, for the Subsistence and Maintenance of the Prisoners of War of each Nation, in Cpnformity to the Stipulations of the Third Article of the Definitive Treaty of Peace, concluded at Paris, the Tenth, of February, One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-three; and his mostChristian Majesty, to manifest his ftneere Delire to fulfil, with all possible good Faith and Exaftnels, the several Engagements, which he has entered into by the last Treaty, having, by his Ambassador, the Sieur Count de Guerchy, made Propositions, with a View to prevent the very intricate and difficult Difcuffioivs -which might protrait the final Adjustment of the Accounts delivered, and to he delivered, JHij>.'Britannic Majesty has thought fit to accept thereof, in the Manner proposed by the Count de Guercliy, in his Declaration of the Fifth of January, One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-five, delivered by Order of his Court; In’ Consequence whereof, it has been pautually agreed between the Two Courts, to secure the Performance of

C .*

the said Agreement by a foletnn Act, reducing the Propositions, and the Acceptance of them, into the Form of* a Convention, to be concluded and ligned by dieir respective Ministers: For which Purpose, their said Mar jellies have appointed and authorized; viz. His Majesty the King of Great Britain, the Earl of , One of

His principal Secretaries of State, Knight of the most noble Order of the Garter, &c. and his most Christian Majesty, the Sieur Count de Guerchy, Knight of his Orders, Lieutenant General of his Armies, Colonel of his Regiment, and his Ambassador to His Britannic Majesty; who, alter having communicated their full Powers to each other, and having conferred together, have agreed to the fallowing Articles.

ART. I.

Whereas it has been represented on the Part of his most Christian Majesty, that, after the imperfect Examination, which it had, as yet, been possible to make of tire Account delivered by the Court of Great Britain, containing Demands for the Maintenance and Subsistence of the French Prisoners, comprised in the Account^., which amounts to the Sum of One million One hundred Seventy-four thousand Nine hundred and Five Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Nine-pence Three Farthings Sterling, to the Eleventh Day of November One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-two, it appeared, that, besides the Sum of One hundred Six thousand Nine hundred Seventy-three Pounds and Five Shillings Three Pence Three Farthings Sterling, (after deducting that of Six thousand Four hundred Thirteen Pounds One Shilling Two-pence Sterling, charged under the Head of Extraordinary Expences incurred by his laid most Chril-tian Majesty) for the Subsistence and Maintenance of British Prisoners of War, according to the Account delivered by the Court of France, which Sum of One hundred Six thousand Nine hundred Seventy-three Pounds Five Shillings Three-pence Three Farthings Sterling, ought to be set against the said Demands of Great tain, the Sum of One hundred Twenty-one thousand Nine hundred Ninety Pounds One Shilling One Penny Sterling, charged under the Head of Extraordinary Expences in the said Account delivered by tire Court of Great Britain, could not be admitted, agreeably to the Terms, and within the Sente of the late Treaty; and that several other considerable Sums ought to be taken off*from what remains charged to France in the said British Account, and that the Adjustment of thotc Difficulties would be liable to very intricate Discussions, which, would be drawn into great Length: In order, therefore, to prevent those Difficulties and Delays, it is agreed, that his most Christian Majesty, conformably to the Proposal contained in the above-mentioned Declaration of his said Ambassador, llralI pay, and that His Britannic Majesty will accept the Sum of Six hundred and Seventy tlrou-sand Pounds Sterling, for the Discharge and total Extinction of all the Pretentions and Demands on the Part of Great Britain, for the Subsistence and Maintenance, and other Expences whatsoever incurred on Account of French Prisoners, contained and specified in the Account above-mentioned: It is moreover agreed. That his most Christian Majesty (Hall make the said Payment in the Manner, and at the Periods following, that is to lay. That his most Christian Majesty shall pay the Sum of One hundred Seventy-six thousand Pounds Sterling, immediately after the Signing of this present Convention; the Sum of One hundred Thirty-two thousand Pounds Sterling, in the Course of the present Year One thousand Seven hundred Sixty-five, in Four equal Payments, at the End of each Quarter; and the remaining Sum of Three hundred Sixty-two thousand Pounds Sterling, in Eight Payments of Forty-five thousand Two hundred Fifty Pounds Sterling, at the End of each Quarter, in the Course of the Two subsequent Years One thousand Seven hundred Sixty-six, and One thousand Seven hundred Sixty-fcyen; the Whole amounting together to the said Sum of Six hundred Seventy thousand Pounds Sterling, which Hull be remitted to Great Britain, without

any

﻿Militia.

any Delay, upon any Pretence whatsoever, at tho different Periods above mentioned, and according to the Course of Exchange whifch shall subsist between the Two Nations at the Times of making the said Remittances.

A R T. II.

It is agreed, and his most Christian Majesty expressly declares, That no Demands of the Court of Great Britain are comprised in the preceding Stipulation, except those which are contained and specified in the said Account of £. 1,174,905 19J. 9 Sterling, to the 1 sth November 1762, as it is above set forth.

ART. III.

His most Christian Majesty promises, and engages, that the Account for the Subsistente and Maintenance of French Prisoners of War, since the 11th of November 1 762, and the Accounts delivered, and to be delivered for the Subsidence and Maintenance of French Prisoners in the East Indies, shall be examined, liquidated and settled, and that the Balance of the said Account shall be paid as expeditiously as possible; and it is agreed, that, in all Events, the Payment of the said Balance shall not be delayed, on any Pretence whatsoever beyond the following Periods; that is to say, supposing the Balance of the said Accounts should not exceed the Sum of Four millions of Livres Tournois, it shall be paid, at farthest, in the Course of the Year 1768, in Four equal Payments; and in case it shall exceed that Sum, the Surplus shall bedif-charged in the same Manner, in the Course of 1769; it being understood, that the Demands on the Part of the Court of France, for the Subsistence and Maintenance of the British Prisoners in the East , and in the French

Colonies, which have not been delivered to the Court of Great Britain, shall be examined, liquidated and settled, and in like manner set off and balanced against the Two last Heads of Demands on the Part of the Court of Great Britain, as far as the Balance, which Avail be due thereon, shall amount,

ART. IV.

The present Convention shall be approved and ratified by His Britannic Majesty, and by his most Christian Majesty; and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged at London within the Space of Three Weeks, or sooner? if it can be done, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing.

In* Witness whereof. We the under-written Ministers, Plenipotentiaries of His Britannic Majesty; and his most Christian Majesty, by virtue of our full Powers, have signed the present Convention, and caused the Seal of our Arms to be affixed thereto.

Done at London the Twenty-seventh Day of February, One thousand Seven hundred Sixty-five.

(L. S.) Dunk Halifax. (L. S.) Guerchy.

Mr. Kynaston reported from the Committee, to whom the several Accounts and Estimates, which have been presented to this House, in this or any former Session of Parliament, relating to the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of exposed and deserted young Children, were referred; and who were to consider of the present State of that Hospital, and of the most proper Means for the future Support and Employment of the Children who have been received into the said Hospital; and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had considered the present State of the said Hospital; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

It appears from the several Accounts and Estimates laid beforeyour Committee, That the Number of Children belonging to the Foundling Hospital, and maintained at the Expence of the Public, on the 31 ft of December 1764, were 4,911, of which there were under the Age of Six Years 1,594, of the Age of Six Years 1,414, of the Age of Seven Years 1,268, of the Age of Eight Years 472, and above that Age 163; of which Children of the Age of Six Years and upwards 1,612 were under the Care of several Inspectors in the Country, and the remaining 1,705 of that Age were lodged and maintained in the several Foundling Hospitals of London, Ackworth, bury, Aylesbury, Westerham, Chester, and Barnet. It further appears, that of the above Number of 1,612 Children under the Care of Inspectors, there are but 46 whose

And it further appeared to your Committee, That the whole Number of Children placed out in the last Year, amounts to 89, of which only 22 have been under the Age of Ten Years; and that Several have been kept in the said Hospitals till the Ages of 14, 15, or 16 Years.

And it further appeared to your Committee, That from the Year 1756 (at which Time Parliament first granted Money to the Hospital for receiving Children) ro the Year 1760, the Expences of purchasing, building, and furnishing the said Hospitals, have been as follows; viz. at London £. 2,044 15*. 5 at , £. 11,071

Whereupon your Committee came to the following Resolufions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Lodging and educating of Foundling Children within Hospitals has a tendency to make such Children less fit for laborious and useful Employments.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such of the said Children, as are of the Age of Seven Years, or upwards, ought to be forthwith placed out as Apprentices to Husbandry, Manufactures, or to the Sea or other Service; and that the rest of them ought to be placed out in like manner, as soon as they shall attain that Age, or earlier, if proper Matters can be provided for them.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Governors and Guardians of the said several Hospitals, and also the said Inspectors in the Country, under the Direction of the said Governors and Guardians, be empowered, with all convenient speed, to place out the said Children to proper Matters or Mistresses.

Refo/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there may be allowed to every Master or Mistreft, who shall take any such Apprentice upon the Terms hereafter mentioned, a Sum of Money at the Discretion of such Governors and Guardians, having regard to the Age, Sex, and Ability of each Child, not less than Five, and not exceeding Ten Pounds, to be paid at such Time or Times as shall be agreed upon between the Governors and Guardians, and the Master, for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Child should be bound longer than until his or her Age of 21 Years; and that the Master or Mistress should be obliged, by proper Covenants, to find and afford the Child all necessary Clothes, Provisions, and Instructions during the Term.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all the Lands and Buildings purchased, erected, rented or hired, and the Stock and Furniture provided at all or any of the said Hospitals, except that at,

ought to be sold or disposed of to the best Advantage, as soon as the Children in the said Hospitals can be placed out; and that the Money arising therefrom be applied in such manner as Parliament shall direct, for the Benefit of the said Charity.

A Petition of James Dalby, of Tetbury, in the County of Gloucester, Gentleman, was presented to the House,

‘and read; Taking Notice of the Bill depending in the House, for rebuilding the Parish Church and Chancel of Tetbury aforesaid; and setting forth, That the Ancestors of Jane, the Petitioner’s Wife, and Mary and Anne her Sifters, were heretofore seised of, and entitled unto, a very considerable Estate, called the Graunge, within the said Parish; and many Disputes having arose between them, and the Parishioners of the said Parish, touching the Claim of the Parochial Rights and Duties due unto the said Parish Church from the said Estate, and touching the Rights and Privileges belonging to the Ancestors of the Petitioner’s said Wife, and her Sifters, in the said Church, by virtue of certain Premises within the said Parish belonging to them, it was, by an Instrument in Writing, bearing Date the 23d Day of October 1624,

agreed by and between Richard Gajlrell, Gentleman, One of the Ancestors of the said Petitioner’s Wife, and her Sifters, and the then Church Wardens and other the Parishioners of the said Parish, with the Content of the then Vicar thereof; that the said Richard Gajlrell, His Successors and their Family, should, at all Timts thereafter, relbrt to the said Parish Church, to hear Divine Ser-yice and Sermons in the Ille and Seat, where they then lat, to receive the Sacrament, and to marry, bury, and baptize, and use all other Parochial Rights, without any Molestation whatsoever; he and they paying, in regard of the Premises, the Sum of Ten Shillings yearly, towards the Repairs of the said Parish Church; and in case he or any of his Family should be buried in the same Ille, or any other Part of the Church, the Sum of Six Shillings and Eight Pence, for every such Breaking of the Earth; and that afterwards, by a Faculty, bearing Date the 28th Day of May 1684, granted by the then Vicar General of the Bishop of Gloucester, the said Seat was confirmed to James Gajlrell, another of the Ancestors of the Petitioner’s Wife and her Sifters, in order that he and his Family might have and enjoy the fame, at all Times, without any Interruption whatsoever; and that the said Richard Gajlrell and James Gajlrell respectively, during their Lives, solely enjoyed the said Seat, and all other the Rights so agreed to belong to them as aforesaid; and from Time to Time, pursuant to the said Agreement, paid the said yearly Sum of Ten Shillings;, towards the Repairing of the said Parish Church; and after their Deaths, were respectively buried in the said Isle of the said Parish Church; after which, a Part of the Estate belonging to them was fold; and though the said Seat, and all other the said Rights were reserved upon such Sale, yet it was agreed, that a Moiety of the said yearly Payment of Ten Shillings should be made by the Purchaser thereof, which has accordingly ever since been, and now is done; and the said Seat, and all other the said Rights, always have been, and now are, solely enjoyed by the Petitioner’s laid Wife and her Sifters; and the said other Moiety of the said yearly Sum of Ten Shillings has also ever since been, and now is, paid by them; and they have also always, when Occasion required, exercised such Rights of Burial within the said Parish Church as aforesaid; And therefore praying. That, in case the said Bill passeth into a Law, Provision may be made therein for lccuring to the Petitioner’s laid Wife and her Sifters their laid Rights and Privileges, and establishing them therein, in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet!

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the

A Petition of the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa, being offered to be pre-lenled to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend, that it Will be difficult, if not impossible, to preserve and maintain the Settlements on that Part of the Coast near Cape Appolonia, unless a Fort should be built there; the building whereof would tend to increase the Trade on the Gold Coast; and that the Petitioners are unable to complete so necessary a Work, without the Assistance of Parliament: Therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to conlkler further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Which Resolution and Order thus signified and published by me, are to be sufficient Notice of the Re-payment of One Fourth Part of the Principal Sum, for which the said Annuities were established, and of the Redemption of so much of the said Annuities as are attending on the said Fourth Part.

A Petition of several Merchants and Traders of Chnjlchurch, Ringwood, Winbour War eh cm, Weymouth, Bridport, the City of Briflal, the City of Exeter, Dartmouth, and Sidmouth, on behalf of themselves and many others concerned in the Cod and Seal Fishery, and Fur Trade, carried on by His Majesty’s Sutye&s, oh that

Part of the Coast of Newfoundland, lying between Cape Bonavifta and Point Riche, as also on the South and South-West Parts of the said Island of

and of several T adel'men and Manufacturers connected with, or dependent on, the said Trade and Fishery, was preferred to the House, and read; Setting forth. That since the Conclusion of the late Treaty of Peace, the Subjects of His Moll Christian Majesty have interrupted the Britishi Subjects in their Fishery j and that, although, in the Year 1763, by Orders from the British Governor* the Effects left by the French on the Coast of Newfoundland were declared to be forfeited, and the Britishi Subjects impowered and required to seize and take to their own Use, or destroy all French Boats left there, yet, to the great Surprise and Disappointment of the Petitioners, these Practices and Proceedings were, by the present Governor’s Orders, strictly forbid for the future; and that the Britishi Subjects are, by the Orders of the present Government, liable to, and in great Danger of being dispoffeffed by foe French of all their Settlements there, which they have made and erected at a great Expence, under the Sanction of an Act of Parliament of the 10th and 1 ith Years of King William the Third, and the Determination of former Governors; by which precarious Situation, they will be reduced to the hard Necessity of abandoning their Settlements, and leaving the French in the entire Pollession of that Coast and Fishery; and that the French have not only presumed to fish in the very Harbours on the South-Well Coasts of the said Island of Newfoundland, but also to land there, and cut and carry away great Quantities of Timber, and have also carried on a considerable Trade in those Parts, by introducing French Goods and Manufactures, in Exchange for which they take and carry away Fish, Oil, and Furs, to the great Detriment of the British Subjects trading the re, and of the Manufacturers of this Kingdom; and representing to the House, that, unless the Subjects of Great Britain are maintained in the Possession of their Settlements, and protected from the above-mentioned Encroachments and undue Practices of the French Subjects, it will be impossible to carry on the Fishery there, whereby that moll valuable Branch of Commerce will infallibly be loll, to the great Injury and Damage of these Kingdoms, and the French Nation become possessed of an exclusive Fishery: And therefore praying the House will be pleased to take the above Premises into Consideration, and grnat such Relief as foe Nature of the same and Importance of the Object may require.

The House was moved, that the 13th Article of the Treaty of Peace, between her late Majesty Queen Anne and his Mod Christian Majesty, concluded and signedat Utrecht, the 31st Day of March 1713, might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

The House was also moved, that Part of an Act, made in the 10th and 1 ith Years of foe Reign of King William the Third, intituled, An Act to encourage the Trade so Newfoundland, might be read.

And same was read accordingly.

Mr. Paterson, according to Order, reported from the clandestine Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to Marriage*, repeal an Act, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for the better preventing of Ciandestine Marriages; and to encourage and facilitate Marriages to be solemnized in Churches or Public Chapels, under a Publication of Banns, or by Licences; and to remove all Doubts which have arisen, or may arise, concerning the Validity of certain Marriages solemnized since the making the said Act; and for the regulating Registers; and for preserving the Evidence of Pedigrees; was committed; the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take into Consideration the Report, which was made from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Owners and Mailers of Ships employed in the Coal Trade, between London and Shields; and the several other Petitions relating to the River Tyne; were severally referred.

And the said Report was read; and is as followeth;

viz.

To prove the Allegations of the First, Second, Fourth, and Eleventh mentioned Petitions;

Captain James Wilson, being examined, said, That he has used the Coal Trade Fourteen or Fifteen Years, but that he had not been at Newcastle these Seven Years; that there are 500 Sail of Ships employed in the Coal Trade, between London and Newcastle, and that they carry, upon an Average, 60 Ton of Ballast each, and make about 6 or 7 Trips in a Year; that the Method used to discharge their Ballast, when they arrive at Newcastle, is, by putting it into Keels; and sometimes Ships go to IVillington and Jarrow Quays, to discharge their Ballast; and after it is thrown on the Quays, it is carted away from the Face of the Quay, about 100 or 150 Yards Distance.

That the Ballast is subject to be blown off the Quays, and washed into the River, by hard Rains, and that the Channel has been growing worse from Year to Year; that formerly Ships drawing 13 Feet Water might load within a Mile of Newcastle, and come down the River; but when the Witness was there last, it was impossible for a Ship of that Draught of Water to fail down from the same Place, owing chiefly to the London Ballast in the River; and at that Time South Shields was blocked

up;

Marriagts.

Supply Bill; Exchequer Bill*.

Weights and Measures.

River.

up; and there was no Place for large Ships to load at but at North Shields.

That he knows the Soundings from Tinmcuth Bar, into 14 Fathom Water; that they are very regular into to Fathom, and then run ©ff steep into 20, 30, and lo on; that it has been the Custom for Ships coming into the Harbour to call their Ballad in 14 Fathom Water, before they come in, and that he has seen 20 Ships at a Time do it.

And being asked, Whether Ballad thrown into 14 Fathom Water can be of any Detriment to the Harbour?

He laid. He is convinced that there is no Motion at the Bottom of that Depth, the Tide running no deeper than 9 Fathom; and that Ballad dropt in 11 Fathom can never return to the Harbour.

That it has been the Cudom formerly for Ships to go to the Quays to discharge their Ballad, when there was Room, but they now can only go in Spring Tides.

That he has seen Ships of 20 Keels of Coals at Jarrow Quay; and that Ships that could go to that Quay formerly at Neap Tides, could, when he was there lad, go only at Spring.

And being asked, he said. It would not be convenient for Ships to go high up the River to discharge their Ballad, except they loaded there; and that the general Place of loading is at Shields.

That Ballad thrown without the Bar cannot return; but if thrown within, or near the Bar, on the Outside, it would damage the Bar; that he has never heard of Maders of Ships being punished for throwing Ballad in 14 Fathom, but has heard of their being punished for cading it in less; and that the Didance from the Bar, into 14 Fathom at Low Water, is near Miles, into 5 Fathom { a Mile, into 10 Fathom a Mile; and from 14 to 20 Fathom f a Mile; and that Ballad thrown a Mile to Seaward of the Bar, cannot hurt it.

That the Names of the several Quays in the River are;

Burden's Quay, Broad Landing and s Quays;

Jarrow Quay, fVillington, St. Anthony's, South Shore,

Fryar Goose, Ewjburn, Skinner's Burn, Fellon, and bren.

That he has known Keels, after they have taken in the Ballad, detained 3 Days at Shields, before they could go to the Quays to unload; and that Nuisances created on the Outside of the Bar cannot be removed lb easy as if within the River.

Captain John Sligktholme, being examined, said, That

he has been Mader of a Ship 40 Years; that he was at Shields about a Month ago, and he went up to Newcastle in a Wherry; that not so many Ships by a considerable Number can lay afloat now in Shields Harbour, as could have done within his Memory; that Ships of Twenty Keels cannot take in their full Loading at South* Shields or off Burden's Quay, owing to the Shoalness of the Water, occasioned by the Ballad washing off the Quays, and dropping from Ships throwing Ballad upon the Quays; that he has seen the Inhabitants of North and South Shields throw Dirt and Soil into the River, which he thinks mud hurt the River, but never heard any Complaint of it; that there is not Water for Keels to come down the River, at lad Quarter Ebb, without grounding, which formerly they might; and is the Means of preventing Ships from loading so soon as they otherwise would, and prevents Ships from making so . many Voyages as they could do, if they could get Coals in proper Time.

That he has seen Ten or Twelve Ships at a Time loading at the upper End of Jarrow Quay, which is now dry.

That 40 Years ago Hay Hole was the general Place for Ships of 13 or 14 Keels to load, but they cannot load there now at the Fird of the Flood; and that if Ships could load there now, it would save ao a Keel.

Mr. William Gibson, a Sea Pilot, said. That be has

been a Pilot 30 Years; that he has known Haven ever since he was Pilot; that he has known the Middle Ground ever since he went to Sea; that the Bar, -the Middle Ground, and the Inn Sand, are better now than ever he knew them; that, there were 400 Sail of . Ships in the Harbour at one time last Winter, and if more had come, there was Room for them; that he does not think the Harbour is filling up, and that the River in general is as good now as ever he knew it, and as much Room for Ships to load; that he saw 3 Ships, of Fourteen Keels, go over the Middle Ground abreast, about a Month ago, at Spring Tide, and that there were then 22 Feet Water, and that he never saw Anchors dry on the Outside of the Girt.

Mr. Samuel Marriott,a Farmer and Surveyor of Land, said. That he is acquainted with the River Tyne from the Conjunction of North and South Tyties down to Cow-bridge-, that he knows the DeviPs Water a little above Cowbridge; that in the Year 1763, according to his Calculation, there was about 35,000 Cubical Yards of Ground washed away from the Banks of the River Tyne and Devil’s Water; that it chiefly confided of a light Soil with some Gravel; that he imagines some Part of it might have been carried into the Sea; but that the coarse Gravel lies in Heaps in several Places; that the Sand would go down the River, and will lodge.

John Tweddale, Esquire, informed your Committee,

That he knows the River Tyne-, that there has been very great Land Floods there lately, which have damaged the River; that in December 1763 there was a remarkable one, which carried away great Quantities of Earth. A Paper containing an Account thereof he produced to your Committee, and is hereunto annexed, marked +; that he has not observed any particular Sand Banks have arisen in the River above Hexham since that Earth was carried away; none that bear the lead proportion to the Earth and Gravel taken away.

Sir Thomas Clavering, being examined, laid, That by Tyne River the Flood in 1763, when he went a Shooting upon the Moors, the lad Year, he observed a Moss at the Head of the River Derwent (which runs into the River; 5 or 6 or more Acres of it was entirely waftied away 2 or 3 Feet deep, which had lodged in the Sides of the River, and came down the whole Length to the; that the Flat Land upon the River Side, near to where the Der- , went goes into the Tyne, was covered with Sand in some Places a Foot thick, so that the Tenants were under the Necessity of removing it with Carts.

Mr. Joseph Robson, an Engineer, who lives at Sunderland, being examined, said, That he has known Tin-mouth Haven Forty Years, particularly for Ten Years; that the Sands in the River are as great Obdrudions now as they ever can be; that they are occasioned by the Sands being brought down by the Great Land Floods; but while the Receiver (or Bed of the River) continues in its full Extent, that Haven.will always be capable of receiving Ships of the feme Draught of Water as use that Port now; that in all Rivers that have great Receivers the Tide runs into those Rivers with great Rapidity, and the Stream that comes from the Land meets the influx of the Sea, and swells it to a considerable Height; that about Ten or Twelve Miles up the Tyne, when the Influx recedes (or goes back) the Reflux runs out of the River with a greater Force than it came in, and consequently will scour out the Sands brought down by the great Land Floods, and will keep that Port open and capable of receiving Ships of as great a Draught of Water as use that Port now; and that the River Tyne, in his Opinion, will be capable of receiving as many such Ships as use the Port, as long or longer than the Coal Mines upon that River will lad.

That he knows the Inn Sand; that there are Quays built above it, which project into the River and keep the Stream from having Effect upon the Inn Sand; that he knows the Middle Ground; that there are Two Points,

One on each Side the River, against which the Reflux falls very strong, and projects the Stream from each.

Point in an oblique Direction across the River; they therefore mutually destroy the Force of each other, and also destroy the Force of the direct Stream, and make an Eddy below, which he apprehends to be the Cause of the* Middle Ground.

This Middle Ground is of a moveable Nature, and appears to him to be very difficult to remove so as not to be formed again; but that taking Sand from it will make the Water better; he founded it, and found from 12 to 6 Feet; and he produced to your Committee a Paper, being an Eye Sketch of the River Tyne, which is hereunto annexed, N* 4.; and he further laid. That he knows Durtwich Sand, it is much narrower than when he fird knew it; what has come off from the South Side has made it narrower, and is lodged at the Lower End nearer to North Shields, and makes a Point of Land there; and therefore the Channel is much broaderby that Sand being narrower; that he founded off the Durtwich Sand, and found from 6 Feet gradually to 17 at the Lower Point of it in the bed of the Channel; at the South Side of that Point, opposite a dry Dock, there is 13 Feet at Low Water; and that the Breadth of the River, from Quay to Quay, at the Upper End of South Shields, is 460 Yards; below that and opposite the Inn Sand is 371 Yards; that there are more Sands brought down the River within this i£ Year or Two Years, by the great Floods, than have been for many Years; that he does not think the Sands in the River are chiefly owing to the London Ballad; but, as he apprehends, by the Sands coming down with the Floods; that every Ton of gross Matter put into the River mud be in a Degree prejudicial; that the Floods bring down Sullage and Sand, which is apt to form into Heaps, and in Time to form Obstructions; that he has known great Sands driven down Rivers by Floods, and in the Time he has been preparing to remove them they have gone away with the
