Rivet. Stream; and has known Sands caused by the Flux and Reflux; that the Navigation of the River appears to him as practicable as formerly.

In the present State of D Sand it may be feme small Obstruction, but, as he apprehends, there is foffi-cient Room for Ships to go pad that Sand; and, as it is his Opinion, it will not continue there long; the Obstruction it may caui'e appears to be very inconsiderable; that if there had been a great Expence bellowed to take away the Sands in the River , as has been upon the River Wear before the late great Freshes within these Two Years, he apprehends it would, notwithstanding that Expence, have been in the same State as it is now, for where any new Sands have been made within these Two Years by the late Freshes, they would have been made again by these Freshes, even if there had been as great an Expence bellowed as there had been at Sunderland; for if a Tree, Root, or a Bush with Earth to its Roots, is brought down by the Land Floods, and is stopt in a wide Part of the River, it is great Odds but a Sand Bank will be made there; that mofl of the Sand that comes down the River goes over the Bar, otherwise the River would have been filled up many Years ago; the Sand which is gone from the South Side of Durtwich Sand has made lo much Room there, that, in his Opinion, it fully compensates for the Obstruction made by the Low End of Durtwich Sand; and that as many Ships may lay at South Shields as formerly, and the Preservation of the Harbour depends upon keeping the Bar clear.

That Colliers dispose of their Ballast at Sunderland, by putting it into Keels, which carry it to and call it upon the Quays; some few Ships at particular Times fend it out to Sea, but the Commissioners put a Stop to it, apprehending it was a Prejudice to the Port of Sunderland', the Sand and Soil taken out of the River Wear, was some time ago carried behind a Point of Land on the North Side of that River, and threw it out behind a large Shelf of Rocks; but the Commissioners apprehending it to be also prejudicial, ordered the Witness to fend no more Ballast to Sea.

The Quantity of Coals mentioned in the Petition of the Aldermen, Sheriff, and Common Council, of New-cajife, to have been exported was admitted.

Your Committee closed their Examination with the Evidence of

Mr. Thomas Aubone, Secretary to the Trinity House at Newcastle, who said. He has been at Two general Soundings in the River Tyne, one in the Year >752, and the ether in the Year 1765; that the Method of Sounding is by the Master and Brethren of the Trinity House in a Barge, and the Pilots in Two Boats, One on the South Side and the other on the North, and found the River all the Way down; that the Barge keeps in thebeft of the Channel, and the Pilots on board of her are dhrested to

make the Soundings; and that the Soundings were put down in the Barge as they occurred. Copies of which are hereunto annexed, N* 5 and 6. That the Soundings in 175a was taken at Low Water Spring Tides; and those in 1765, at or near Low Water Mark, as near as could be guessed, and not quite Spring Tides; and that they allowed 6 Inches for the Difference of Tide; that the Channel of the River opposite to Black Steatk is on the North Side, but in the Year 1752 it was on the South; that there is 6 Feet Water in the Channel opposite Black St eat h at Low Water; and there is 7 and 8 Feet all the Way down to Willington Quay; that he knows Durtwich Sand, which is grown up to the Northward, but it has made a better railage for Shipping to come up and down on the South Side; that he founded the Bar in 1764, and found on the South Side 7 Feet Water, on the North Side 9 Feet; near the Sparrow Hawk 9 Feet, and with the Lights half open 9 Feet.

And he further said. That the River is better now than formerly; and that it is for the Interest of the Con-fervators, who are (the most Part of them) great Coal Owners, as well as for the Benefit of the Public, to keep the River open, and as free from Nuisances as possible; that he remembers Captain Cole being Mailer of the Trinity House, and that there was a Plan proposed, feme Part whereof he believes wai to throw all Ballad upon Quays, and to abolish the Use of Keels.

And being asked, Whether Captain Cole did not advise that the Conservators should cleanse the River up to farrow and Willington Quays; that large Ships might throw their Ballad at Burden's and Simpson'% Quays, and smaller Ships at farrow and Willington Quays ? he said. That has been the Opinion of the Trinity House in general; that the Witness had seen Captain Cole the other Day, who told him he was summoned by an Order from the Committee, to be examined on behalf of the Petitioners, and that he was discharged from attending here, for that he told the Witness Mr. Letteney said he would be of no Service to them; that there always is Room and Depth of Water sufficient for large Ships to go to Burden's Cookson's, and Simpforis Quays at proper Times of Tide; that he thinks the Channel of the River is rather contracted; but by his Observation in Soundings in the Years 1752 and 1765 he thinks the Bed of the River is rather better; that he is a Freeman of Newcastle, and that he was unanimously chose Secretary to the Trinity House, and is re-e!ected annually, according to the usual Form of the House, and is also Receiver of the Town Dues; the River jury are composed of Seamen and Tradesmen, but he believes the Majority are Trades-men; that there are great Freshes in the River feme-times, and particularly in the Year 1763 the Water role 10 Feet above the ordinary Course of the Tide.

N* I.

Netvcajllc 7 At a Court held for the Conservation of the River Tyne, at the Guildhall of the said Town, by Custom,

upon Tyne, 3 Time out of Mind, on Monday the 22d Day of October, in the 27th Year of the Reign of our Sovereign Lord George the Second, by the Grace of God of Great , and Ireland, King,

Defender of the Faith, and so forth, and in the Year of our Lord 1753, before the Right Worshipful Henry Eden Esquire, Mayor, Matthew Ridley, Cuthbert Smith, and William Peareth, Esquires and Aldermen, and Conservators of the said River Tyne.

WHEREAS several Mailers of Ships trading and resorting to this Port, do take upon them, on their Arrival here with their Ships or Vessels, to call such Ballad, Rubbish, Gravel, Earth, Stones, Wreck, or Filth, as they bring in with them, into any Keel, Boat, or Lighter, that will receive the same, without any Warrant for that Purpose; or examining or enquiring whether such Keel, &c. is properly authorized and appointed to be employed in that Service.

And whereas divers and sundry Keelmen, and others, do take upon them to receive the Ballad, &c. out of such Ships or Vessels into their Keels, Boats, or other Vessels; although the Maders of such Ships have no Warrant to cad their Ballad into such Keels, &c. as in the like Cafes has been always used and accudomed.

And whereas several Keelmen, to whom Liberty is granted to take the Ballad, &c. out of Ships at Shields, and to carry the same to the Ballad Shores, do frequently cad the said Ballad, &c. at other Places than they are appointed and directed to do, by the Warrants so granted them for that Purpose; whereby great Damage is done to the River Tyne.

And whereas several Proprietors of Shores and Keys upon the River Tyne, do frequently permit and suffer Ballad to be cast on their Shores, &c. although the Persons cading the same do not produce and shew a proper Warrant directing such Ballad to be cad thereon, as in the like Cafes is usual.

And whereas several Proprietors of Shores and Keys upon the River Tyne, do also frequently allow Ballad to be cad and thrown on their Keys, &c. notwithstanding such Keys, &c. are not properly authorised, appointed, and set apart by this Court to receive the same; all which Practices are deemed highly prejudicial to the River Tyne, and contrary to the several Orders of this Court, and ought not to be permitted and differed. In Order therefore to remedy such Abuses and Nuisances for the future, and for the better Preservation of the Navigation of the said River, this Court doth think fit to order, and doth hereby accordingly order,

That no Mader or Matters of Ships or Vessels, or other Persons intruded with, or having the Government of any Ships or Vessels trading or resorting to, or frequenting this Port, shall at any Time or Times hereafter cast any Ballast, Rubbish, Gravel, Earth, Stones, Wreck, or Filth, into any Keel, Boat, Lighter, or other Vessel whatsoever, unless such Matter or Matters, or other Person intruded with the Care of such Ship, &c. as aforesaid, be thereunto duly licensed, as hath been antiently accustomed, by Warrant from the Water Bailiff, or his Deputy for the Time being; upon Pain of forfeiting for every Keel Load of Ballad, fice. which such Matter or other Person intruded as aforesaid, shall cast contrary to the Tenor and true Intent and Meaning of this Order, the Sum of Twenty Shillings.

And it is further Ordered, That no Keelman or Keelmen shall hereafter take any Ballast, &c. out of Ships or other Vessels, until such Time as they shall see the Warrant or Authority granted to the Matter of such Ships, &c. as aforesaid, for so doing; upon Pain of forfeiting the Sum of Thirteen Shillings and Fourpence for every Keel Load of Ballast, &c. which they shall so take out of such Ship or other Vessel, contrary to the Directions of this Order.

And it is further Ordered, That if any Ballast be from henceforth cast out of any Keel, upon any other Ballast Shore than what they are appointed and directed to cast the said Ballast at, by the Warrant to be granted them as aforesaid, then the Skipper and Men belonging to such Keel shall forfeit and pay the Sum of Ten Shillings for every Time they, or any of them, shall be guilty of the said Offence.

And it is further Ordered, That if any Proprietor or Owner of any Key or Shore, on the River Tyne, (properly licensed and appointed for the Reception of Ballast) shall and do hereafter permit and suffer any Ballast, &c. to be cast on such Key, &c. without a proper Warrant for that Purpose, every such Person shall forfeit and pay for every Keel Load of Ballast so cast, without such Authority, the Sum of Twenty Shillings.

And it is further Ordered, That if any Proprietor or Owner of any Key or Shore, on the River Tyne, (not properly licensed and appointed for the Reception of Ballast) shall, notwithstanding such Incapacity, permit and suffer any Ballast to be cast thereon, without giving Notice and Information thereof to this Court; every such Proprietor or Owner so offending, shall forfeit and pay the Sum of Five Pounds for every Keel Load of Ballast so cast upon any such their Key or Shore as aforesaid.

And whereas, it is suggested to this Court, that many of the above Offences are done through Ignorance, because the several Orders heretofore made by this Court, to remedy such Abuses, are not sufficiently made public and known: It is therefore hereby Ordered, That Copies of this Order be printed and fixed up at all public Places in this Town, and at North Shields and South Shields, to the End that the same may be the better known to all Mailers of Ships, Keelmen, See. and that they may pay due Observance to the fame, as they will answer the Contrary, &c.

By the Court,

CUTHBERTSON.

Tyne Town and County of) At a Court held for the Conservation of the River Tyne, by Custom, Time out of Mind, River. NeucaJlle-upon-Tyue.3 in the Guildhall of the said Town, on Monday the 5th Day of November, in the Fifth

Year of the Reign of our Sovereign Lord George the Third, King of Great Britain, &c. and in the Year of our Lord 1764, before the Right Worshipful Sir Walter Blacket, Baronet, Mayor; the Worshipful William Peareth, Henry Partis, William Matthew Bell, and Aubone Surtees, Esquires and Aldermen, Conservators of the said River . Calling Ballad on 7 /'"'lOM P L A I NT having been made to this Court, that the River hath for some Ballall Keys. \ y >> Time pad been greatly prejudiced, by the carelessly calling Ballad upon Ballad Keys, and neglecting to trim or Ihovel such Ballad back from the Face of the Keys, after the same hath been so cad thereon; by which Carelessness and Negligence, great Quantities of Ballad have fallen from the said Keys into the said River, to the Impediment of the Navigation thereof.

It is therefore Ordered, That every Mader of any Ship or Vessel, who shall hereafter bring his Ship or Vessel to any Ballad Key of the said River, to have his Ballad cad thereon, shall, before the cading thereof be begun, oblige the Caders and proper Persons to be employed therein, by Contract or Agreement, to undertake to cad all such Ballad, Gravel, or other Rubbish, upon every such Key, as far back from the Face or Edge thereof as they possibly can, and with the lead Prejudice to the River that may be. And al.so during the Time of the Cading thereof (if necessary) and immediately afterwards, to trim or diovel the same back Three Feet at lead from the Face or Edge of the Key: And that every such Mader shall be obliged to cause the same to be done at his own Expence and Peril; and shall not employ, nor suffer to be employed, in the Cading such Ballad, any Person or Persons but only those who shall actually undertake to cad and trim the same as aforesaid. And in case of any Neglect or Default therein, an Information shall lie against every such Mader for the fame, to be made and taken either in this Court, or before any one of the Conservators of the said River out of Court: And if taken before a Conservator, he shall issue his Summons to the Mader, to appear at the then next Court, to answer such Information, which the Conservator shall present to such next Court: And if upon the Hearing thereof, the Fact shall be proved, to the Satisfaction of the Court, every such Mader shall forfeit and pay, for every such Offence, such Fine as the Court shall order in that behalf, not exceeding the Sum of Five Pounds. And upon Nonpayment thereof, or Refusal to pay the same upon Demand, the same shall be levied by the Warrant, or Order of this Court, upon the Tackle, Apparel, or Furniture, of the Ship or Vessel out of which the Ballad, Gravel, or Rubbidi was cad. And in case of any wilful Breach, Neglect, or Default in the Premises, by any of the Caders, or Persons who shall be so employed as aforesaid, contrary to their Agreement with the Mader in that behalf, then upon the Complaint or Information of the Mader, either to this Court, or to one of the said Conservators (who shall summon the Offender or Offenders, and present the Information to the then next Court as aforesaid) and upon proving the Agreement, and the Breach, Neglect, or Default of the Person or Persons offending, to the Satisfaction of the Court, every such Offender shall forfeit and pay, for every such Offence, such Fine as the Court shall order in that Respect, not exceeding the Sum of Forty Shillings a-piece: And upon Non-payment thereof, or Refusal to pay the same upon Demand, the Offender or Offenders shall be otherwise punished as the Court shall order. And it is further Ordered, That if any Skippers of Keels, Keelmen, or others, shall hereafter cad or throw any Ballad, Gravel, or Rubbish, out of any Keel or smaller Vessel, upon any of the said Ballad Keys, carelessly or negligently, and not as far back from the Face or Edge of the Key as they possibly can, and with the lead Prejudice to the River that may be, all such Skippers, Keelmen, and others, or any of them so offending, shall, for every such Offence, forfeit and pay such Fine as this Court shall order, not exceeding the Sum of Forty Shillings a-piece, to be recovered against them in this Court, by such Proceedings and in such Manner as aforesaid: And in case of Non-payment thereof, or Refusal to pay the same upon Demand, the same shall be levied by the Warrant or Order of this Court, upon the Tackle, Apparel, or Furniture of the Keel or Vessel, out of which the Ballad, Gravel, or Rubbish was cad; or else the Offender or Offenders shall be otherwise punished as the Court shall order. And it is further Ordered, That the Ballad Conveyers, of every Ballad Key adjoining upon the said River, shall, as often as any Ballad, Gravel, or Rubbish, shall be cad upon their respective Ballad Keys, from out of any Keel or smaller Vessel, immediately after the Cading thereof, cause the same to be trimmed or shovelled back Three Feet at lead from the Face or Edge of every such Key: And in case of any N eg I eft or Default therein, every such Ballad Conveyer shall forfeit and pay, for every such Offence, such Fine as this Court shall order in that behalf, not exceeding the Sum of Five Pounds, to be recovered against them in this Court, by such Proceedings and in such Manner as aforesaid: And in case of Non-payment thereof, or Refusal to pay the same upon Demand, every such Ballad Conveyer shall be otherwise punished as this Court shall order. Amd it is further Ordered, That printed Copies of this Order be put up at the most public Places in this Town, and at North and South Shields, to the Intent that the same may be the better known to all Maders of Ships, Skippers of Keels, Keelmen, Ballad Conveyers, and others whom it may concern, who are hereby required to take Notice thereof, and to pay due Obedience o the fame, as they will answer the Contrary at their Peril.

By the Court,

GIBSON.

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty.

Ar.d being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had attended His Majesty in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Assent to the several Public Bills following; viz.

An Act to confirm all Leases already made by Arch-bishops and Bishops, and other Ecclesiastical Persons, of Tythes and other Incorporeal Hereditaments, for One, Two, or Thtee, Life or Lives, or Twenty-one Years; and to enable them to grant such Leases, and to bring Actions of Debt for Recovery of Rents reserved, and in Arrear, on Leases for Life or Lives.

An Act for enlarging the Times limited for executing and performing several Provisions, Powers, and Directions, in certain Acts of this Session of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker also reported, That His Majesty was afterwards pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The tender Concern which I feel for My faithful Subjects, makes Me anxious to provide for every possible Event, which may afifeft their future Happinel's or Security.

My late Indisposition, though not attended with Danger, has led Ale to consider the Situation, in which My Kingdoms, and My Family, might be left, if it should please God to put a Period to My Life, whilst My Success’or is of tender Years.

The high Importance of this Subject to the Public-Safety, good Order, and Tranquillity; the Paternal Affection, which I bear to My Children, and to all My People; and My earned Desire, that every Precaution should be taken, which may tend to preserve the Constitution of Great Britain undisturbed, and the Dignity and Lustre of its Crown unimpaired; have determined Me to lay this weighty Bufinet's before My Parliament: And as My Health, by the Blessing of God, is now re-llored, I take the earliest Opportunity of meeting you here, and of recommending to your most serious Deliberation the making such Provision as would be necef-t'ary, in case any of my Children should succeed to the Throne, before they shall respectively attain the Agjt of Eighteen Years.

To this End, I propose to your Consideration, Whether, under tffe present Circumstances, it will not be expedient to veil in Me the Power of appointing, from Time to Time, by Instruments in Writing, under My Sign Manual, either the Queen, or any other Person of My Royal Family usually residing in Great Britain, to be the Guardian of the Person of such Success’or, and the Regent of these Kingdoms, until such Successor shall attain the Age of Eighteen Years; subject to the like Restrictions and Regulations as are specified and contained in an Act, passed upon a similar Occasion, in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of the late King, My Royal Grandfather: The Regent so appointed to be assisted by a Council, composed of the several Persons, who, by reason of their Dignities and Offices, are constituted Members of the Council established by that Act, together with those whom you may think proper to leave to My Nomination.

A Message from the Lords, by the Lord Chief Justice s Pratt and the Lord Chief Baron Parker:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed upon an Address to be presented to His Majesty; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

And the said Address was read; and is as followeth;

viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, in Parliament assembled, presume to approach Your lacred Person, with our warmest Acknowledgments of the peculiar Goodness expressed in Your most Gracious Speech from the Throne.

We humbly entreat Your Majesty’s Acceptance of our heartiest Congratulations upon Your Recovery from Your late indisposition. Your Majesty’s Return to Your Parliament has difiipated all those anxious Sensations, which the Occasion of Your Absence had excited: And as the Re-establishment of Your invaluable Health is an Object to Your faithful People of the sincereft, Joy and Exultation, Your Majesty has shewn a most affectionate Regard to their Satisfaction, in condescending to take the earliest Opportunity of giving them so pleating a Proof of it.

This great Mark of Your Majesty’s Attention demands our most sincere and dutiful Thanks: But we have before us a (till more engaging Instance of Your watchful Solicitude for our future Security and Happiness.

Vol. 30.

The constant Tenor of Your just and constitutional Government, distinguished and endeared to Your Kingdoms by an unwearied Application to the Advancement of their Interests and Prosperity, had already filled our Minds with a most cordial Sense of Gratitude. The new Proof, which Y our Majesty is now pleased to give us, of Your truly Paternal Tenderness, by extending Your Concern for the Stability, Dignity, and Lustre of Your Crown, with all the happy Effects of Your Love to Your Royal Children, and to \rour faithful Subjects, beyond the Period of Your own Continuance among them, mud inspire us with fti'l higher Degrees, if poflibie, of Reverence and Affection.

Whiift we contemplate, with Admiration, that Magnanimity which enables Your Majesty to look forward, with a cool Composure of Thought, to an Event, which, whenever it should please God to permit it, must overwhelm Your Loyal Subjects with the bitterest Detraction of Grief; we cannot but be deeply affected with that compassionate Sentiment of Your Royal Heart, which iuggefts a Provision for their Comfort under lb severe an Alflidtion.

May it nleafe the Divine Providence to exempt us from the fatal Necessity of such a Consolation ! Your Majesty has shewn, from the First Day of Your au-fpicious Reign, so conlcientious a Regard to the Laws and Liberties, the Religious and Civil Rights, of Your Kingdoms; that we should be insensible and unworthy of the Happiness we ourselves enjoy, if we did not ardently with to transmit it under the same gracious Care and Protection to our Children.

Yet, feeling, as we do, the infinite Importance of every Measure that may tend to the perpetuating, in all Events, our happy Constitution; in Deference to Your Majesty’s Recommendation, and under a full Conviction of that consummate Prudence, and beneficent Intention, which were the Motives of it, we will not fail to apply ourselves to the immediate Discussion of the high and momentous Object, which Your, Majesty has been pleased to propose *to our Consideration.

Our Deliberations concerning it will be animated by the Hopes of securing to our Posterity, under the Blessing of Almighty God, and in Concurrence with Your Majesty’s salutary Designs, the inestimable Blessing of a legal Protestant Succession to the Crown of theie Realms in Your Royal Family; and will be influenced by a just Confidence in Your Princely Wisdom, and Paternal Concern for Your People.

We shall go into this Conlultation with a sensibl.e Anxiety, arising from the Subject of it; but we humbly assure Your Majesty, that we will conclude it with all the Dispatch compatible with its Angular Importance; repeating at the same Time, our earned Supplications, that, through the Mercy of God upon this Protestant Church and Nation, a Precaution so expedient in Pro-spedt, may become useless in the Event; by Your Majesty’s living to ferm, under Your own Instruction, a Successor worthy to inherit the Allegiance and Affections of a free People, by a long and mature Attention to the Example of Your Royal Virtues.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Lords in the said Address.

Mr. Bacon reported from the Committee of the whole Manufacturt, House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Report, which was made from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Bailiffs, Wardens, Assistants, and Commonalty of the Trade, Art, and Mystery, of Weavers of London, in behalf of themselves and the Silk Manufacturers of Great Britain; and the several other Petitions, relating to Silk; were severally referred, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an additional Duty of Eight Shillings per Pound Weight, be laid upon all Plain Wrought Silks, and Plain Velvets, of Foreign Manufacture, imported into Great Britain; except such Plain Wrought Silks, and Plain Velvets, as are of the Manufacture of France.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an additional Duty of Eight Shillings per Pound Weight, be laid upon all Brocaded, Flowered, Figured, or Clouded Silks and Velvets, of the Manufacture of France.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an additional Duty of One Pound Thre^Shillings, be laid on every Pound Weight of all Brocaded, Flowered, Figured, or Clouded Silks or Velvets, of Foreign Manufacture, imported into Great Britain, except such Brocaded, Flowered, Figured, or Clouded Siiks or Velvets, as are of the Manufacture of France, and except such Wrought Silks or Velvets, as shall be manufactured in, and imported from, the East Indies.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Provisions made by an Act, of the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for encouraging the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom, and for securing the Duties pa) able upon the Importation of Velvets, Wrought Silks, and Silks mixed with other Materials, be further extended and enforced.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Provisions made by an Act, of the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act to prevent unlawful Combinations of Workmen, employed in the Woollen Manufactures, and for better Payment of their Wages, bo extended to the Workmen employed in the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Duties now payable upon Raw Silk, imported into Great Britain, do cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That in Lieu of the said former Duties, there be granted to His Majesty, a Duty of One Shilling and Three Pence, upon the Importation into Great Britain of every Pound of Raw Silk, each Pound containing Twenty-four Ounces.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That there be granted to His Majesty, a Duty of Sixpence upon every Pound Weight of Thrown Silk, imported into Great Britain, each Pound containing Sixteen Ounces; over and above all other Duties now payable for the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Drawback of One Shilling be allowed, upon every Pound Weight of Raw Silk, exported from Great Britain to Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Drawback of the said additional Duty, of Sixpence per Pound Weight of Thrown Silk, be allowed upon all Thrown Silk, exported from Great Britain to Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That for the better encouraging the British Manufacture of Silk Stockings, Silk Mitts, and Silk Gloves,

Be allured, I have not a more sincere Concern, or a more earnest Desire, than to secure to My faithful People, both now. and hereafter, the Religious and Civil Blessings of our invaluable Constitution.

Mr. Hewett reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for repealing so much of the several Laws now in Force, as prescribes particular Standards of Width and Length for the several Woollen Cloths made within the West Hiding of the County of York, and for substituting other Regulations of the Cloth Trade, within the said West Riding, for preventing Frauds in certifying the Contents of the Cloth, and for preserving the Credit of the said Manufacture at the Foreign Market, was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table.

And a Motion being made. That the said Report be now read;

A Petit ion of the Clothiers of the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That, by the said Bill, the Standard Breadth of Woollen Broad Cloth, in the said West Riding, is to be abolished, and the Clothiers to have Leave to make Cloth of what Length and Breadth they chuse; and that the Petitioners have found, by long Experience, that the Standard now existing has been of great Utility to this Manufactory, and are convinced, that every Clothier can, with great Facility, conform to the present Standard, or any other Breadth this House may think proper; and therefore praying for the Continuance of the established Standard, as beneficial to the Kingdom in general, and this County in particular; and as the Matter Clothiers in the West Riding of the County of Yorkconfift of not lei's than Twc Thousand; and the Petitioners apprehend, that there is not sufficient Time to collect the Opinion of so large a Body; therefore praying, that the Law now in Force may continue till another Session, to give the Petitioners Time to consult the Persons concerned , and that they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Leeds, in the County of York, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and setting forth, that the public Market for the Sale of all Broad Woollen Cloth, manufactured in the West Riding of the County of York, has Vol. 30

always been held within the Town of Leeds; and that the said Broad Woollen Cloths, when fully manufactured, are chiefly sent Abroad to Foreign Markets, to the great Advantage of the Kingdom in general; and that, from the Infancy of this Manufacture to the present Time, there always has been a Standard for the Width of those Broad Cloths; and alleging, that it appears, from the Accounts of the Treasurers of the said Riding, that double the Number of Broad Cloths are now manufactured in the said Riding, than were in 1725; and that most of the Cloths now made are made many Yards longer than heretofore; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the abolishing the present Standard in the Width of Cloths, or even the towering thereof, will be highly injurious to the Merchants and Manufacturers, and ruinous to the Credit of the said Manufacture; and that the continuing the present Standard in Width, and obliging the Clothier to keep up the fame, is the most probable Method' for preventing the undue stretching and {training of Cloth; and therefore hoping, the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and pass no Law for the lowering of the Standard in Width of Broad Cloth, but will make all due Regulation for securing to this Kingdom so valuable a Branch of Trade.

Then several Members, returned upon new Writs, having taken the Oaths and made and subscribed the Declaration, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration; and having delivered in to the Clerk of the House, Accounts of their Qualification, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Qualification; according to the Laws made for those Purposes;

The said Report was read.

And the Amendments made, by the Committee, to the said Bill, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, with several Amendments to One of them, agreed to by the House.

Then the said Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House* to consider of the present High Price of Corn;

A Petition of the Mayor, Magistrates, Manufacturers, and Principal Inhabitants of the City of Norwich, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, for the present, and for some Time past, there hath been lb little Demand for the Manufactures of that City* that great Numbers of Journeymen and Labourers employed therein are destitute of sufficient Employment, fot1 the Maintenance of themselves and Families, and many of them unable to obtain any Employment at all; and that the Distress of these labouring Poor is aggravated by the High Price of Wheat, which is already risen to Fifty-four Shillings per Quarter in the Market, and is likely to continue riling every Market-day; that the Petitioners are apprehensive that the present Scarcity is likewise increased by unlawful Combinations amongst the Growers, to starve the Markets, and deprive the Poor of that Supply which the Country really affords; and that the Petitioners have been credibly assured, that Wheat may be imported from Holland and elsewhere, and, notwithstanding the Expence of Importation, be still fold much cheaper in our Markets, than the present Price there, if the same might be imported free from Duties; and praying, that a Bill may be brought in, for permitting Wheat to be imported from Holland and elsewhere, free of any Duties on the Importation thereof, for the Supply of the Markets of this Kingdom; or that the Petitioners may have fuel) other Relief in the Premises, as the Nature of their Grievance shall require, and to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Paterson, according to Order, reported from the Ways and Committee of the whole House, to whom it was re- Means, ferred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Bounties and Drawbacks, now paid upon the Exportation, from this Kingdom, of Refined Sugars and Ground Sugar, be discontinued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, upon the Exportation from this Kingdom of Refined Sugar, in the Loaf, compleat and whole, being Net, that is to lay, of one uniform Whiteness throughout, and which has gone through the Operation of Three Clays at the least, and been properly and thoroughly dried in the Stove, according to the prefertt Practice of Refining, a Bounty be allowed after the Rate of Fourteen Shillings and Six Pence, for every Hundred Weight thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, upon the Exportation from this Kingdom of Refined Sugar called Bastard, and of Ground and Powdered Refined Sugar, and of Refined Loaf Sugar broke in Pieces (the said Sugar having been Twice Clayed, and properly dried in the Stove) a Bounty or Drawback be allowed, after the Rate of Six Shillings and Four Pence, for every Hundred Weight thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Liberty be granted, for a limited Time, to carry Rice from the Province of North Carolina, di redly to any other Part of America, Southward of South Carolina and Georgia, subject to such Duty as is now payable upon Rice, carried from South Carolina and Georgia, to any Part of America, to the Southward thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Duties which shall avise in respect of Rice, so carried from North Carolina, and the Duties which shall arise in pursuance of an Act made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for granting, for a limited Time, a Liberty to carry Rice, from His Majesty’s Provinces of South Carolina and Georgia, directly to any Part of America, to the Southward of the said Provinces, subject to the like Duty as is now paid on the Exportation of Rice from the said Colonies to Places in Europe situate to the Southward of Cape Finisterre, be paid into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, and there reserved, to be, from Time to Time, disposed of by Parliament,

Mr. Paterson, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Instrument, Letter, Entry, Minute, Memorandum, or other Writing, whereby any Officer is admitted, in any Court whatsoever, to serve or to hold his Office, shall be deemed and taken to be an Admittance of such Officer, within the Meaning of an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, and of another Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of King William the Third, and also of another Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, whereby the several Duties of Forty Shillings are charged and imposed upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Admittance of such Officer is ingrafted or written.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duty of One Shilling, charged by an Act made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, and the Duty of One Shilling, charged by an Act made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of King William the Third, upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, and upon every Sheet and Piece of Paper upon which any Admission into any Corporation or Company shall be ingrossed or written, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, instead thereof, a Stamp Duty of Two Shillings be charged and payable upon the Entry, Minute, or Memorandum, which shall be made of such Admittance in the Court Book, Roll, or Record, of every such Corporation or Company.

Vo jl. 30.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Allowance made by the several Statutes passed in the First, Ninth, Tenth, and Twelfth Years of the Reign of Queen Anne, and in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King George the First, and in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of King George the Second, to every Person who shall, at any One Time, bring to be Stamped, or buy of the Commissioners of the Stamp Duties, Paper or Parchment, the Duties whereof shall amount to Ten Pounds or upwards, after the Rate of Six Pounds in the hundred Pounds, per Annum, for Six Months upon the present Payment of the said Duties, be discontinued and no longer payable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, instead thereof, there be allowed to every Person, who shall, at any Time, bring to be Stamped, or buy of the said Commissioners, Paper or Parchment, the Duties whereof shall amount to Ten Pounds or upwards, after the Rate of Four Pounds in the Hundred Pounds per Annumi for Six Months, upon the present Payment of the said Duties.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Stamp Duty of Twenty Shillings be charged upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrafted, or written any Policy of Assurance, in which the Properties of more than One Person, in any Ship, Cargo, or both, or of more than a particular Number of Persons in general Partnership, or of more than One Body Politic or Corporate, to a greater Amount in the Whole than the Sum of One hundred Pounds in any Ship, Cargo, or both, shall be allured.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three hundred and Eight thousand Pounds, of the Monies agreed to be paid by a Convention between His Majesty and the French King, concluded and signed at London the 27th Day of February last, for the Maintenance of the late French Prisoners of War, be applied towards making good the Supply granted to Elis Majesty.

Montagu:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Amendments made by this House to the Bill, intituled, An Act to provide for the Administrarion of the Government, iA case the Crown should descend to any of the Children of His Majesty, being under the age of Eighteen Years; and for the Care and Guardianship of their Persons: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for granting Annuities, to be attended with a Lottery, to fotisfy and discharge certain Navy* Victualling, and Transport Bills; and for charging the Payment of such Annuities on the Sinking Fund, without any Amendment; And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to alter certain Rate9 of Portage; and to amend, explain, and enlarge several Provisions in an Act made in the Ninth Year of tire Reign of Queen Anne, and in other Acts relating to the Revenue of the Port Office; with* out any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on the Exportation of Coals, and of several East India Goods, and upon Policies of Art u ranee; for retaining, upon the Exportation of White Calicoes and Muslins, a further Part of the Duties paid on the Importation thereof; and for obviating a Doubt with respect to Stamp Duties imposed upon Deeds by Two former Acts; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to amend, and render more effectual in His Majesty’s Dominions in America, an Act passed in this present Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for punishing Mutiny and Desertion, and for the better Payment of the Army and their Quarters, without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for more effectually supplying the Export Trade of this Kingdom to Africa, with such Coarse Printed Calicoes, and other Goods of the Product or Manufacture of the East Indies, or other Places beyond the Cape of Good Hope, as are prohibited to be worn and used in Great Britain-, for encouraging the Importation of Bugles into this Kingdom, for the better Supply of the Export Trade thereof; and for discontinuing the Bounty payable in Great Britain, and all Bounties and Allowances in Ireland, upon the Exportation of Corn, Grain, Malt, Meal, and Flour, from thence to the Isle of Man; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to impower the High Court of Chancery to lay out, upon Government Securities, a Sum of Money, therein mentioned, out of the Common and General Cash in the Bank of England, belonging to the Suitors of the said Court; and to apply the Interest arising therefrom towards augmenting the Income of the Masters of the said Court; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing and widening the Road from the Turnpike Road in Banbury, in the County of Oxford, through Daventry and Cottefbatch, to the South End of Mill-Field, in the Parish of Lutterworth, in the County of Leicester, without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing and widening the Road from the Great Bridge, in the Borough of Warwick, through Southam and Daventry, to the Town of Northampton; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for amending and widening the Road from the North End of Old Malt011 Gate, in the Town and Borough of New Malt on, to the Town of , in the County of York, without any Amendment: And also,

Ditto. A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty

of the City of Oxford, in the County of Oxford, in Council assembled, and of others, the Owners of Houses and Lands within the said City of Oxford and the Suburbs thereof, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Value of Houses and Lands within the said City and Suburbs have, from Time to Time, so much decreased, as to make the Land Tax, when settled at the Rate of Four Shillings in the Pound for the Kingdom in general, to arise, in some Parishes in the said City and Suburbs, from Five Shillings and Sixpence to Six Shillings in the Pound; and that, for thel'e Nine Years last pad, during which Time the Land Tax in general has been Four Shillings in thd Pound, all the Houses and Lands within the said City and Suburbs, at an Average, have been assessed to the Land Tax at the- Rate of Four Shillings and Eleven Pence in the Pound, and upwards; an.! that all the Houses and Lands within the County of which

are not within the said City or Suburbs, do not, at an Average, pay Three Shillings in the Pound, when the Land Tax is at Four Shillings; and alledging, That by a Clause in an Act in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the several Laws now in being relating to the railing and training the Militia within that Part of Great Britain called England, it is enacted, That in, all Cafes where the Militia has not been raised for any County or Riding, within which any City, Town or Place shall not be rated to the Rate called the County Rate, the Payment of the Sum ol'Tive Pounds per Man upon the whole Number of private Militia Men, directed to be raised within every County or Riding, shall be divided arid apportioned between each respective County or Riding, and each such respective City, Town, or Place within the same, as shall hot contribute to the said Rate, called the County Rate, in such Proportion as the respective Quotas paid to the Land Tax, by each respective County or Riding, and by such respective City, Town, and Place, bear to each other; and that the Militia has not been raised in or for the County of Oxford-, and that the said City of Oxford has never been rated to the Rate called the County Rate; and as the Houses and Lands within the said City and Suburbs have, from Time to Time, hitherto been assessed, and do now pay to the Land Tax

in such greater Proportion as aforesaid, than the rest of the Houses and Lands in the said County, which are not within the said City or Suburbs) the Petitioners therefore apprehend themselves to be doubly grieved by the said Clause, which seems not only to confirm the present Inequality in the Land Tax, under which the Petitioners now labour, but to extend that Inequality to other new raised Taxes, which, the Petitioners apprehend, was never intended by this House; and expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that the House will take the Premises into Consideration; and that the said Clause may be either repealed, explained, or altered, so that the Petitioners may not pay for their Houses and Lands within the said City and Suburbs towards the Militia for the said County, in greater Proportion than the Owners of other Houses and Lands within the said County; and that the Petitioners may have such other Redress in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put.

That the said Bill be re-committed;

It passed in the Negative.

His'; Mr. Whitworth reported from the Committee, ap-Appi. 1 pointed to inquire into the Management and Applica-of Mo- tion of all such Sums of Money, as have been collected, within Twelve Years last past, by virtue of any Act of Parliament for repairing any particular Highway; and to report the Matters, as they should appear to them, together with their Observations and Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had inquired accordingly; and had considered the Petition of many Gentlemen, Freeholders, and others, use-ing the Western Road, from and to Bath, through

Bridgewater, Taunton, and Exeter, to Plymouth, and other Parts of the West of England, to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the ' Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; vix.

Your Committee being of Opinion that it would be most satisfactory to the House, to give them feme Information of what had been done, in pursuance of the Repo rt which was made to the House in the last Session of Parliament, and the Resolutions thereupon;

In the First Place proceeded to inquire into the State of Kensington Trust; and thereupon ordered the proper

Officers to attend, with their Accounts of Receipts and Disbursements for the Year 1764, which were produced to your Committee (Abstracts whereof are in the Schedule hereunto annexed); and it appeared, upon the Evidence of Mr. Boyd, one of the Surveyors, that 3,500 Load of Gravel has been laid last Year on that Part of the Road from the End of Clarges Street, Piccadilly, to bridge, which is only I of a Mile, the expence of which has amounted to £.978 although at the same Time, the Witness laid, that nothing extraordinary had happened to occasion it; but that it was owing to the low and flat Situation of the Road, and the continual Wear of it by Numbers of Carriages, which go into Hyde Park and Tyburn La#*; — and the Witness likewise delivered it as his Opinion, that it would amount to the same Sum annually to keep that Part of the Road in Repair. — Your Committee cannot help making an Observation on the foregoing Evidence; that either there appears great Mismanagement in expending so large a Quantity of Ballast upon so small a Distance of Road; or that the said Road should have been done with other Materials, which would occasion a less annual Expence; wherein they are confirmed by the Opinion of Mr. John Philips, the Treasurer, and Mr. Scott, one of the Trustees, who severally said, that the Road might be kept in Repair at less Expence by 50 per Cent, and should advise that Part Voi. 30.

429

of it, from Clarges Street to Hyde Park Corner, to be pav- Highway.*; ed, under the Management and Direction of the Com- Application missioners for Paving the Streets of Westminster, who 0 oney' could perform it in a much better and cheaper Manner than the Trustees of the Turnpike can polftbly do. —

Your Committee beg Leave to take Notice, that, as this Part of the Examination proceeded upon the Opinion which Mr. Philips delivered last Year to the Committee, it was accordingly read to him, and is as follows.- —

That a considerable annual Sum should be taken from " the Trust, to prevent the amazing Quantity of Mat- ter, which, he apprehended would, by the present " Trustees, be continually putting on and taking off the " said Road, whilst they are in Possession of lb large an " Income." Mr. Philips hereupon confirmed the above, except that he meant, instead of the present Trustees, the present Surveyors.

Your Committee then proceeded to inquire what Quantity of Gravel had been laid upon the Road by each Surveyor. — And it appeared, that there had been in Mr.

Boyd's Department, 7,027 Loads.-In Mr. Monk's 4,418*

In all 11,445 Lo®ds, which, your Committee apprehend, is owing to some of it not lying above a Month before it is taken off, and others not above Two or Three Months — which was according to Mr. Boyd’s own Declaration, and corrobates Mr. Philip’s Opinion delivered last Year, and mentioned above. — Upon inquiring what Persons supplied the said Trustees with Gravel, it appears to have been chiefly furniflred by Mr. Scott, an acting Trustee. — Whereupon the Committee ordered the Resolution of the House of last Year to be read, which mentions, — " That no Persons for the future shall act " as Trustees, for any Turnpike Road, who are employ- ed or interested in Works carried on by the said Trust."

And Mr. Scott being present — declared, that he did not know there had been such a Resolution of Parliament;

— and your Committee think it Justice to observe, that the Surveyor mentioned, in his Examination, that Ballast could not be got so conveniently of any one else. —

Mr. Boyd was then asked, in what Manner the Smith’s Work belonging to the said Trust was performed. —

Who said it was done by the Pound Weight; and that the ioweft Price was 6 d.except for setting Grates, which was at j\d. f per Pound. And upon Inquiry who performed the Carpenter’s Work, — he replied, Mr.

who appears to be Partner with Mr. Timbrel, an acting Commissioner. — Mr. Philips being again tailed, desired he might represent to the Committee, as Treasurer, that the Trustees never keep any Money in the Treasurer’s Hands; but at their annual Audit, when they find a Surplus in the Hands of their Banker, they pay off Part of their Debt; and have this Year discharged £.400 so that there only remains £.1,000 Debt, on a Revenue of £.4,737. And as so small a Sum might soon be reduced from the Savings upon so large an Income, your Committee beg Leave to represent, that a considerable Sum might be well applied to the Benefit and Advantage of those who pay the said Toll; and in order to find out how far Part of it might contribute to new-paving and keeping in Repair the Town of Kensington, which has constantiy been in a very bad Condition, and very inconvenient to Passengers, owing to the great Expence which would fall on the Inhabitants of the Great Street, if they were to put the same into proper Order, — Your Committee inquired, whether any Part thereof was under the Power of the Kensington Trust; but find, that the Town is not included in the present Act, but that each End only is paved by the Trustees.

After which His Majesty was pleased to make a most: Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Dispatch which you have given, with lb much peec Zeal and Wisdom, to the Public Business, enables Me now to put a Period to this Session of Parliament.

No Alteration in the State of Foreign Affairs has happened, since your Meeting, to disturb the General Peace; and it is with Pleasure that I inform you, that the present Dispositions of the several Powers of Europe promise the Continuance of this BielTing.

I have seen, with the moll perfect Approbation, that you have employed this Season of Tranquillity in promoting those Objects which I had recommended to your Attention; and in framing such Regulations, as may belt enforce the just Authority of the Legislature, and at the same Time secure and extend the Commerce, and unite the Interests of every Part of My Dominions.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Cheerfulness and Prudence which you have shewn, in providing for the necessary Expences of the

?resent Year, deserve My particular Acknowledgments.

'he many Bills which you have formed for the Improvement and Augmentation of the Revenue in its several Branches, and the early Care which you have taken to discharge a Part of the National Debt, are the most effectual Methods to establish the Public Credit upon the surest Foundations, and to alleviate by Degrees the Burthens of My People.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Provisions which have been made for the Administration of the Government, in case the Crown should deicend to any of My Children under the Age of Eighteen Years, whilst they add Strength and Security to Our present Establishment, give Me the kindest and most convincing Proof of your Confidence. The Sense which I have of the important Trust reposed in Me, and My Desire to repay this Mark of your Affection, by discharging My Part, agreeably to your Intentions, in the Manner most beneficial to My People, have concurred to make Me execute without Delay the Powers with which you have intrusted Me. This is already done; and you may be allured, that, as far as it depends upon Me, those (alutary Provisions shall never be ineffectual. It is My ardent With, and shall be My constant Endeavour, on this and every other Occasion, to perpetuate the Happiness of My Subjects, and to transmit to Pof-terity the Blessings of Our Invaluable Constitution.

After which the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, said:

Parliament My Lords and Gentlemen,

July next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the nth Day of July next.

Mr. Speaker reported, that the House had attended His Majesty in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most- gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The present general State of Tranquillity in Europe gave Me Hopes, that it would not have been necessary to assemble my Parliament sooner than is usual in Times of Peace.

But, as Matters of Importance have lately occurred in some of My Colonies in Am, which will demand

the most serious Attention of Parliament; and as further Informations are daily expected from different Parts of that Country, of which Ishall order the fullest Accounts Vo*. 30.

to be prepared for your Confederation; I have thought fit to call you now together, in order that Opportunity may thereby be given to issue the necessary Writs on the many Vacancies that have happened in the House of Commons, since the last Session; so that the Parliament may be full, to proceed, immediately after the usual Recess, on the Consideration of such weighty Matters as will then come before you,

His Majesty’s Happiness and that of His People are one; and every Increase of His Majesty’s illustrious Family is considered by His faithful Commons as a further Security to that Religion, and those Liberties w*e enjoy under His Majesty’s most auspicious Government.

appointed Yesterday to draw' up an Address to he preferred to His Majesty, that the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s moll; dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, Wg Leave to return Your Majesty the Thanks of this House, for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne: And to allure Your Majesty, that, we will not fail, when this House shall he supplied with its Members, to apply ourselves with the utmost Diligence and Attention to those important Occurrences in America, which Your Majesty recommends to our Consideration; and to exert our most zealous Endeavours for the Honour of Your Majesty’s Government, and the true Interest of Your People, in all Parts of Your extended Empire.

Permit us, at the same Time, to congratulate Your Majesty on the late Increase of Your Royal Family, by the Birth of a Prince. Your Majesty’s Happiness and that of Your People are one; and every Increase of Your Majesty’s illustrious Family is considered by Your faith-fill Commons, as a further Security to that Religion, and those Liberties we enjoy under Your Majesty’s most feufpicious Government.

We also beg Leave to offer to Your Majesty our fin-cere Condolence on the great Loss, which Your Majesty and this Kingdom have sustained by the Death of his late Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland-, whose private and public Virtues, whose Duty and Affection to Your Majesty, and whose distinguished Merits, and Services to this Country, as they made his Person dear to this Nation while he lived, so they cannot fail to render his Memory sacred to the latest Posterity.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

The Satisfaction you express in the Increase of My Family, and the atfe&ionate Share you take in the great Loss I have sustained by the Death of the Duke of Cumberland, are fresh Proofs of your Zeal and Loyalty.

Your Resolution at the same Time, to support the

Honour of My Government, and to provide for the'mm Interest of all My People, cannot but be moil acceptable to Me. My Conduct shall always iliew, that I consider their Interest as infeparuklc from My own.

♦ spefch Mr. S|>eaker reported, , that the ttoilfe had attended *Pone ijis Majesty in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Miilakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House and is as followed; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

When I met you lait I acquainted you, that blatters of Importance had happened in America, which would demand the most lerious Attention of Parliament.

That no Information which could serve to direct your Deliberations in so intereding a Concern might be wanting, I have ordered all the Papers that give any Light into the Origin, the Progress, or the Tendency of the Didurbances which have of late prevailed in some of the Northern Colonies, to be immediately laid before you.

No Time has been loit, on the first Advice of these Didurbances, to issue Orders to the Governors of My Provinces, and to the Commanders of My Forces in America, for the Exertion of all the Powers of Government in the Suppredion of Riots and Tumults, and in the edectual Support of lawful Authority.

Whatever remains to be done on this Occassion I, commit to your Wisdom; not doubting but your Zeal for the Honour of My Crown, your Attention to the jull Rights and Authority of the British Legidature, and your Aflection and Concern for the Welfare and Prosperity of all My People, will guide you to such found and prudent Resolutions, as may tend at once to preserve those Conditutional Rights over the Colonies, and to redore to them that Harmony and Tranquillity, which have lately been interrupted by Riots and D;if-orders of the most dangerous Nature.

If any Alterations should b^wanting in the Commercial Economy of the Plantations, which may tend jto enlarge and secure the mutual and beneficial Intercourse of My Kingdoms and Colonies, they will deserve your most lerious Consideration. In effectuating Purposes so . Worthy of your Wisdom and public Spirit, you may deend upon my most hearty Concurrence and Support, he present happy Tranquillity, nowfubfiding in Europe, will enable you to pursue l'uch Objects of Our interior Policy with a more uninterrupted Attention.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the proper Edimates for the enrrent Service of the Year to be laid before you. Such Supplies as you may grant shall be duly applied with the utmod Fidelity, and shall be dispensed with the drifted Economy. s

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I earnedly recommend to you to proceed in your Deliberations with Temper and Unanimity. The Time requires, and I doubt not but your own Inclination will lead you to those salutary Dispositions. I have nothing at Heart but the Assertion of legal Authority, the Pre-fervatiotij-Of the Liberties of all My Subjects, the Equity and good Order of my Government, and the Concord and Prosperity of all Parts of My Dominions.

The Lord Villiers reported from the Committee appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to His Majesty, that the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him'tb report to the I louse; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return Your Majesty our moll humble Thanks for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

It is with the higheftSenfe of Your Majesty’s Goodness we acknowledge that Care for the Welfare of Your People, and that Confidence in the Loyalty and Affection of Your faithful Commons, which Your Majesty shews in the early Communication Your Majesty has been pleased to order of the necessary Informations relative to the Disturbances in . Your Reliance

on the Wisdom and Duty of Your Parliament in a Matter of so great Importance, and the Attention shewn by Your Majesty, in referring to our Deliberation and Advice, the joint Concern of Your Majesty’s Royal Authority, the Rights of Your Parliament, and the Happiness of Your Subjects, are at once Objects of our highest Admiration and Gratitude.

It is our Duty, as it shall be our Care, to imitate that Temper and Equanimity which appear in Your Majesty’s Conduct, by mixing with our Zeal for the Honour of Your Majesty’s Government, and with our just Regard for the Dignity and Authority of Parliament, the utraoft Attention to the important Objects of the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms, and the tenderell Concern for the united Interests of all Your Majesty’s People.

It is with inexpressible Grief we are again called upon to condole with Your Majesty on the Death of another Prince of Your Royal Family, whose amiable Disposition, and whose early Virtues in the first Dawn of Life, while they shew him worthy of the illustrious Race lie sprang from, mull now double our Regret for his untimely Loss.

The general State of Peace and Tranquility, so happily reigning in al 1 Part s of Europe, mud give the greatest Satisfaction to every one, who has any Concern for the true Interest of this Country, or who feels for the general Happiness of Mankind.

Our Assistance shall not be wanting to aid Your Majesty with our Advice, and to strengthen Your Authority, for the Continuation of that Harmony so happily

We allure Your Majesty that we mall, with the greatest CheCrfulness, grant Your Majesty the Supplies necessary for the current Service of the Year having the firmed Reliance on the Promise Your Majesty is gractoufiy - - pleased to make, of seeing them duly applied, with that Oeconomy which Your own Wisdom will direct, and which the Circumstances of this Country lb strongly demand.

The Unanimity and Dispatch which Your Majesty is

Eleased to recommend, we shall, from Motive? both of >uty and Inclination, endeavour to make the Rule of our Proceedings; being sensible that nothing can more immediately tend to add Weight to the Deliberations of Parliament, or Efficacy to their Resolutions.

And, as the constant Tenor of Your Majesty’s Conduct shews that the Happiness and Prosperity of Your People are the foie Objects of Your Concern, we should be equally wanting in Duty to our Sovereign, and Care for our pwn Honour, did we a Moment neglect our Part, in promoting all such wife and Salutary Measures as may tend to reflect Dignity on Your Majesty’s Government, and fix the Welfare of Your People on the most solid Foundations.

High Price A Petition of the Court of Mayor and Aldermen of of Corn, the City of London.

And then lie withdrew'.

And the said Petition Was read; Reciting, That, by an Act, made in the 31st Year of his late Majesty, for the due making of Bread, and to regulate the Price and Assize thereof, and to punish Persons who shall adulterate Meal, Flour, or Bread, Returns are required to be made weekly to the said Court of Mayor and Aldermen, by the Meal Weighers of the said City, upon Oath, of the Prices which Whgat, and the several Kinds of Grain, Meal, and Flour, fit for Bread, fell for in the Markets of the said City; and the Assize and Price of Bread is, by the said Act, required to be from Time to Time set by the said Court, if fitting, or by the Mayor of the said City, if the said Court should not fit, to be in Force for the said City of London and the Liberties thereof, and the Weekly Bills of Mortality, except as in the said Act is excepted; that, in pursuance of the said Act, such Returns have been, from Time to Time, regularly made upon Oath, by the Meal Weighers of the said City; and the Assize of Bread, to take Place and be in Force as aforesaid, hath been duly set by the said Court, or by the Mayor of the said City for the Time being, according to the said Act, and according to the Right and Custom of the City of London, and the Practice there used to set the fame; and that the Petitioners think it a Duty they owe to the Public, in the Exercise of this great Trust, humbly

Vol. 30.

to represent to the House, that it appears to the said Court of Mayor and Aldermen, by such Returns made upon Oath as aforesaid, that the Price of Wheat fit. for Bread hath been, for Three Months pall, from Thirty-nine to Forty-two Shillings Quarter; and that the Petitioners observe, that, notwithstanding these high x Prices, a large Quantity of Wheat and Wheat Flour hath, within the aforesaid Time, been exported from London; and that, it being evident that the old Stock of Wheat was nearly exhausted when the new Wheat came to Market, and there being Reason to believe that the Consumption of the new Wheat will be increased in some Parts of this Kingdom, by the almoll general Failure of the last Crop of Barley, the Petitioners beg Leave to express their Fears, that if the Exportation should continue, this Nation may be so drained of Corn, as to be again reduced, as in the last Summer, to the Necessity of having Foreign Supplies; or at least, that the Price of Bread Corn will greatly advance, to the Distress of the Poor, and to the Prejudice of the Manufactures of this City and Kingdom in general; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the prohibiting the Exportation of Wheat, and other Grain, and Flour, for a Time, may be a Means of preventing this Evil: Arid therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into ConsideratioU; and to grant such Relief therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That the several Streets, Squares, Yards, Courts, Alleys, Passages, and Places, within the City of London and Liberties thereof, are in general ill paved and cleansed, and not duly lighted; andare also greatly encumbered with Potts, and annoyed with Signs, Spouts, and Gutters, projecting into and over the fame, w hereby they are rendered incommodious, and in feme Parts dangerous, not only to the Inhabitants, but to all others passing the fame, or resorting thereto; and that, by an Act passed in the 2zd and 23d Years of the Reign of King Charles the Second, the foie Power of ordering, designing, and regulating the cleansing and keeping clean of all the Streets, Lanes, and Passages, within the said City and liberties} and the pitching and paving, with the Order and Manner thereof was vested in the M ay or, Commonalty, and Citizens, of the said City, to be managed, executed, and done, by such Persons as the Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the said City, in Common Coun-.cil assembled, should' thereunto authorize and appoint, or by any Seven or more of them (being all Members of the said Court) and in such Sort and Manner, as from Time to Time should by them be found most convenient, for the public Benefit of the Inhabitants; and that the said Inhabitants having, ever since the pafttugof the said Act, continued in the Practice of paving the said Streets themselves, and the several Water Companies very improperly repairing the frequent Breaches made by them, the Provisions made by the said Act, as well as by several subsequent Acts of Parliament, for improving and cleansing the said Pavements, have not been of Force sufficientto obtain the salutary Purposes thereby intended; and that, by an Act passed in the 17th Year of King George the Second, for making more effectual Provision for enlightening the Streets of the City of London, certain Rates are directed to be assessed and levied, in Manner therein mentioned, for defraying the yearly Charges of erecting, lighting, supplying, and maintaining such a convenienfand sufficient Number of Glass Lamps, within

the said City and Liberties, as the Mayor, Aldermen, and Commonalty of the said City, in Common Council assembled, should think proper; but several of the Powers granted by the said last recited Act have been also found defective; and that the several Businesses of paving, cleansing, and lighting of the said City and Liberties, andpreventing and removing the said several Annoyances therein, might he carried on to more Advantage, and 1 letter answer the Intentions of the Legislature, if the same were managed and executed by the same Persons, duly authorized for that Purpose; and it would also tend to facilitate that Execution, as well as prove fonie Ease to the Inhabitants, if the several Rates and Assessments necessary for defraying the Charge thereof wereconfoli-dated and collected together, and made one joint and general Fund; and that the said Inhabitants, being burthened with a Variety of Taxes, cannot of themfeb es afford to raise a sufficient Fund, for so expensive an Undertaking; and therefore the Petitioners conceive, that it would be a Means of facilitating and expediting the said useful Works, if they were impowered to raise a Sum, by a Small Toll upon the Roads immediately communicating with the Liberties of the said City, or by such other Ways as the House flia.ll think proper: Therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief therein, and such other Aid and Assistance, as to the House shall seem meet.

Sir John Sebright reported ffotn the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, of the City of Bath, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Richard Roberts, Deputy TownClerk of the said City, being examined, said. That the principal Markets within the said City are at present held in and near the High Street',whereby tile Passage through the same is

greatly obstructed, and great Nuisances happen; and if Power was given to remove the said Markets, to some more convenient Place or Places, under proper Regulations, it would be of great Use and Convenience.

That several of the Streets, Ways, and Passages, within the said City and Liberties, and the Precincts thereof, are too narrow and incommodious; that these Inconveniences might be remedied, and several new Streets and Passages made, to the great Ease and Safety of Passengers, if proper Powers were given to widen or alter the said narrow Streets and Passages; and for those Purposes to purchase such Houses, Buildings, and Grounds as may be necessary.

That the several Acts passed for paving, cleansing, lighting, and regulating the Streets and other Places, within the said City and Liberties, have hitherto been defective; and it would tend greatly to the Convenience

and Safety of the Inhabitants of the said City, and Persons reforming thereto, if proper Povvoin were gi>e;i to

save, cltun’b, light, watch, and regulate the Streets,-,anes, Ways, and Pillages, within the said Ciry, Liberties, and Precincts, an 1 to remove ail Nuisance and Obstructions therein, and to regulate the Pa! luge of Carts and Carriages through the fame.

That many Porfons frequently contrail small Debts, within the said City, Liberties, and Precincts, and refuse to pay the same, presuming upon the Difficulties-ami Expences their Creditors are put to in filing for the fame, under the present Laws; and that, the establishing a Jurisdiction for the more cafy and speedy Recovery of small Debts would be very beneficial.

That the present Law is ineffe -jual for supplying the said City, Liberties, and Precincts with fresh Water, although the Corporation are possessed of Springs, and have built a Reservoir sufficient for that Purposu; and that they might be very amply supplied, if proper Powers were given to the said Corporation, for com eying Water to and through the said City, Liberties, and Precincts.

Ordered, That Dave be given to bring in a Bill to remove and regulate the public Markets in the City of Bath; for widening certain Streets, Ways, and Passages, within the said City, and the Liberties and Precincts thereof, and for opening certain new Streets and Ways within the same; for better paving, cleansing, lighting, watching, and regulating, the Streets, Lanes, Ways, and Passages there, to remove all Nuisances and Obstructions therein, and to prevent the same for the future; and for better supplying the Inhabitants of the said City, Liberties, and Precincts, with Wa*er: And that Sir John Sebright, Sir Jarrit. Smith, and Mr. Pitt, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of John Hudson, Esquire, Lord of the Manor of BeJJingby, in the East Riding of the County of York, Patron of the Vicarage and Parish Church of BeJJingby aforesaid, and also the Owner of the greatest Part of the Lands and Grounds within the said Township or Parish , and also of the other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors of Lands, or otherwise interested, in the Open Fields, Grounds, and Wastes, of BeJJingby aforesaid, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Lands and Grounds within the said Fields and Wastes, being intermixed and dispersed' in small Parcels, are attended with much Loss and Inconvenience to the Proprietors thereof, and, in their presentState, are incapable of much Improvement; and that dividing and inclosing the said Fields and Walles would be advantageous to all the_ Parties interested therein, and of Public Utility:

T9

And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes abovementioned.

Ordered, That.Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir George Savile and Admiral Holborn do prepare, and bring in, the fame.
