Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Mr. Alderman Harley reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition olf the Churchwardens and Over-seers of the Poor, and of several other Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Botolph, Aldgate, in the City of London, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Fi/her, Vestry Clerk of the said Parish, being examined, said. That the Parish is very populous, and the Houses are in a great Measure occupied by poor VOL. 30.

/ Manufacturei\s and labouring Persons, whereby tlid Poor are become very numerous; and that the Charge Of maintaining such Poor hath amounted for several Years pall to £. 1,600 per Annum, or thereabouts.

Mr. Thomas Sabe, Churchwarden, and Mr. Griffith Stephens, one of the Overseers of the Poor of the said Parish, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. and

further said, That they apprehend the principal Cause of the great Number and Burthen of the Poor arises from the Number of Houses within the said Parish which are let into Lodgings of separate Apartments, there being upwards of 600 of such Houses, which do not pay to the Poors Rate, and not above 550 which do pay.

That if Power Was given for the better regulating, maintaining, and employing the said Poor, and toeharge the several Landlords, who so divide the said Houses, with the Payment of such Rates, it would be a Means of more equally taxing the Parish, lowering the said Rates, and tend greatly to their Benefit, and to the Welfare and Preservation of the Poor therein.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring iri a Bill for the better maintaining, regulating, and employing the Poor within the Parish of Saint Botolph, Aldgate, in the City of London: And that Mr. Alderman Harley and Mr. Gascoyne do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

Sir Robert Ladbroke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Maycr, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the lteport in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Edward GroJ'e, Esquire, being examined, said, That the several Streets, 1-a.ncs, Squares, Yards, Courts, Alleys, Passages, and Places, within the City of London and Liberties thereof, are in general ill paved, dirty, and not sufficiently lighted; that the Signs throughout the said City are very numerous and large, and not only obstruct the Light of the Lamps, but are very dangerous in windy Weather, when several Signs and Shew Boards have been blown down, and the Polts are a general Annoyance; that several Bulks, Penthouses, and Shops gre erected, which encroach upon the Streets; that the Penthouses are aNuifance, being frequently crowded with Flower Pots, by the watering of which the Clothes of Passengers are spoilt, and that he has seen a Flower Pot fall from a Penthouse; that the Gutters and Spouts are a very great Annoyance in their present Situa-

Yol. 30.

tion in rainy Weather; that the Wheelbarrows and Wheels driving along the Foot Pavements, and Shopkeepers fcxpofing their Wares, are great Inconveniences and Nuisances.

That the Practice lately introduced of making Bow Windows to Shops is a great and growing Evil, as the Ia(i Builder of such a Window always projects his Window beyond all the rest, so that if this Practice is suffered to continue, the Witness apprehends that in a little Time there will be no Spaces at all left for Passengers on Foot, and that he is very well satisfied, by Experience, that the Number of Foot Passengers is increased, and that they have much less Room than formerly.

That the Method at present used in exercising Horses at Livery Stables, where they frequently gallop out into the Street suddenly, is very dangerous to Foot Passengers, which the Witness saw an Instance of last Week in Coleman Streets and that this Evil might be prevented, if a Bar was put up at the End of each Ride, next the Street.

Then an Act passed in the 2id and 23d Years of the late King Charles the Second, Chap. 17, was read; whereby it appeared, that the foie Power of ordering, designing, and regulating the cleansing and keeping clean of all the Streets, Lanes, and Passages, within the said City and Liberties, and the Pitching and Paving, with the Order and Manner thereof, was vetted in the Mayor, Commonalty, and Citizens of the said City, to be managed, executed, and done, by such Persons as the Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the said City, in Common Council assembled, should thereunto authorize and appoint, or by any Seven or more of them (being all Members of the said Court) and in such Sort and Manner, as, from Time to Time, should be found most convenient for the Public Benefit of the Inhabitants. Then,

William Tyfir, Esquire, being examined, said, That,

since the passing of the said Act, the Inhabitants have continued the Practice of paving the Streets themselves, but that the several Companies, who furnish the City with Water, frequently break up the Pavements to relay and mend their Pipes, which Pavements they repair again at what Time, and in what Manner they please; that he has known Places so broken up, lie unpaved Three, or even Six Weeks, and when paved, the Stones are laid in Allies, Rubbish, or other insufficient Materials, which soon breaks up again in Holes; that the Witness has known Persons pave their Doors very sufficiently, at an Expence, from Eight to Twelve Pounds, which has been immediately ruined by theburfting of a Water Pipe, and the Pavement has become as bad as ever; that the Paviours for all the Water Companies are equally blamable; that frequent Complaints are made to the Commissioners of Sewers, but that the Evil can never be remedied, without adopting some other Method of paving, than that used at present.

Mr. GroJ’e, being further examined, confirmed Mr. Tyfir's Evidence in every Particular; and added, That when any Person relays the Pavement before his Door, it is the common Practice to raise it higher than the rest, which is One of the greatest Inconveniences attending the present Mode of paving, and can never be remedied but by paving the whole Street at Once, and placing the Power of repairing it in Persons, who shall take Care that such Repairs are made in a proper Manner; for that at present, if a Piece of bad Pavement happens to lie between Two Houses, only one Half of it can be mended at a Time, unless both Parties can agree, which they" frequently do not.

That the only Method of removing of Nuisances is by Indictment, which is troublesome, expensive, and dilatory, since if the Party is rich and obstinate, he may remove the Indictment by Certiorari, from Court to Court, for it is impossible to say how long aTime, to the infinite Trouble and Expence of the Party pursuing such Indictment; that it would be much more eligible to lodge

A Petition of the Freeholders and other Inhabitants of Petition the Colonies of the MaffadiuJ’etV s Bay, Rfiode Island and from

Prutf<fe?f«Plafttatiotis, NewJerfby, Pe MaifechufetV vemrpettts of the COunties of Newcastle, Kent, and Suffer, upon Dclcticare, and Province of Min America, signpd by James Otis and Oliver Partridge, Committee from the House offtepresentatives of Bay;

by Metcalfe Bowler and Henry Ward, Committee from the General Assembly of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations; by H. Fisher and J Committee from the Province of Nero Jerfby; by (J. Bryan and J.

Morton, Committee from the Province of Pensylvania;

ThomasM‘Kean and Cafar Rodney, Committee from the Government of Counties of Newcastle, Kent, and Suffer on Delaware; and by William Murdock, E. Tiglman, and T. Ringgold, Committee from the House of Representatives Of the Province of Maryland; wras offered to be presented to the House; stating the burthensome Rcstrictions under which the Trade and Commerce of the Colonies labour by several Acts lately passed, particularly by the Stamp Att; recognizing their Allegiance to the Crown, and acknowledging all due Subjection to line Parliament of Great Britain; expressing their most humiliating

500 27° JanuarA. 17

Petition bating Sorrow in finding the mrelves lately deprived of from the Right of granting their own Property for His Ma-algachJ et 1 jesty's Service, which on His Royal Requisitions they have been ever ready to contribute; complaining also, that the Penalties and Forfeitures, mentioned in the Stamp Act, and in divers late Acts of Trade, are, at the Election of the Informer, recoverable in any Court of Admiralty in America; that they are under great Pain to fee this manifest Dillin6tion made between the Subjects of their Mother Country and those' in the Colonies; in thus being unhappily deprived of Two Privileges essential to Freedom, and which all have evercon-

fidered as their bell Birth Rights, " that of being free from " all Taxes, but such as they have consented to in Per-" son or by their Representati ves, and of Trial by their " Peers;" that their remote Situation and other Circumstances render it impracticable, that they should be represented but in their respective subordinateLegillatures; that the Parliament, adhering strictly to the Principles of the Constitution, have hitherto never taxed Ireland or any other of the Subjects without the Realm: But though it were ever so clear, that the Colonies might in Law be reasonably deemed to be represented in the House of Commons, yet they conceive, that very good Reasons 0 from Inconvenience, from the Principles of true Policy, and from the Spirit of the Constitution, may be

adduced to shew, that it would be for the real Interest of Great Britain, as well as her Colonies, that the late Regulations should be rescinded, and that the several Acts, imposing Duties and Taxes on the Colonies, and extending the Jurisdiction of the Court of Admiralty beyond its ancient Limits, should be repealed; submitting, that Money is already become scarce, and is Hill decreafingin the Colonies; that an immense heavy Debt is yet due from the Colonies for British Manufactures, that from the Nature of American Business and several other Circumstances, a Stamp Duty mull ever be very burthensome and unequal; humbly submitting whether there be not a material Distinction, in Reason and found Policy at lead, between the necessary Exercise of Parliamentary Jurisdiction in general Acts for the Amendment of the Common Law, and the Regulation of Trade and Commerce through the whole Empire, and the Exercise of that Jurisdiction, by imposing Taxes on the Colonies; that the severalsubordinate Provincial Le-gillatures have been moulded into Forms as nearly re-lembling that of the Mother Country, as by His Majesty’s Royal Predecessors was thought convenient; that under these Forms they have been born and settled; that there, as every where else, the People retain a great fond-ness for their old Customs and Usages; that they eileem their Conne&ion with, and Dependence on6’reat Britain, as One of their greatest Bleifings; and apprehend the latter will appear to be sufficientlyfecure, when it iscon-fidered, that the Inhabitants in the Colonies have the most unbounded Affection for His Majesty’s Person, Family, and Government, as well as for the Mother Country; and that their Subordination to the Parliament is universally acknowledged: And therefore most hum-, bly entreating, That the House woqld bepleafedto hear their Counsel in support of this Petition, and take their most diitreffed and deplorable same into their serious Consideration; and that the Acts and Clauses of Acts, so grievously redraining their Trade apd Commerce, im-poling Duties and Taxes on their Property, and extending the Jurisdiction of the Court of Admiralty beyond its ancient Limits, may be repealed; or that the House would otherwise relieve the Petitioners as they should think meet. Mr. Houblon reported from the Corhmittee, to whom stort Rivtf the Petition of Charles Dingley, George Jackson, and Navigation. William Maflerman, Esquires, and also the several other

Persons, whose Names a"- thereunto subscribed, Commissioners named in an Act of Parliament therein mentioned, for making navigable the River Stort, in the Counties of Hertford and Essex, and for putting in execution the Powers for that Purpose by the said Act given, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as iblloweth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read; and the Clerk to the said Commissioners produced the original Minute Book of the Proceedings of the said Commissioners, by which itappeared,

That since the passing the said Act, the Commissioners have, in pursuance thereof, had several Meetings, if» order to put the same in execution; but from the Difficulty of procuring the Loan of a sufficient Sum of Money, upon the Security in the said Act provided, for carrying on and completing the said Navigation, and from other Causes of Impediment appearing to the said Commissioners, no Progress has hitherto been made tb effect the said Navigation; and the said Act hath proved wholly ineffectual for that Purpose.

That a Proposal had been made to the said Commissioners, by the Petitioner, Charles Dingley, on behalf of himself and the other Petitioners, George Jackson and William Maflerman -, that in case the said Commissioners would concur in obtaining another Act of Parliament, whereby the said Charles Dingley, George Jackson, and William Maflerman, should be inverted with fit Powers and Authorities, and whereby proper Tolls and Duties should be vested in them and their Heirs and Assigns, as aConsideration, that they would undertake, at their own Expence (exempt from all Expences theretofore incurred) and risk the making ofi supporting, maintaining, and rendering effectual the said Navigation; and that the said Navigation should be so perfected within Five Years after the passing of the same Act; and that the said Commissioners, being of Opinion that the said Act, as it now Hands, cannot be carried into execution, or the said Navigation otherwise effected than by private Undertaking, and having duly considered the said Proposal, did fully approve thereof.

London whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and' new ueets. Commons, of the City of , in Common Council

assembled, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the feme, as k appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act made in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for widening certain Streets, Lanes, and Passages, within the City of London and Liberties thereof, and for opening certain new Streets and Ways within the feme, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, was read: Then,

Mr. William Davidson, Clerk to the Comptroller of the Chamber of London, being examined, said. That great Progress hath been made in carrying the said Act into execution, but Doubts have arisen, whether the Schedules annexed to the same are well and sufficiently referred to, by reason whereof the Proceedings carried on under the said Act, may hereafter be drawn into Question, and the City liable to vexatious Suits, unlefe the same be explained and amended.

Mr. Recorder of London informed your Committee, That upon Application to the Court of Aldermen, in pursuance of this Act, to have Estates valued, which the City have found necessary to purchase for the Purposes of the Act. when the Jury have been impannelled and sworn, and the Court ready to proceed, the Parties have not agreed concerning the Titles of the respective Owners, or Proprietors, or Persons claiming to be such, in which Cafes the Court hath been greatly embarrassed how to proceed, not conceiving themselves or such J ury 2a'

to be a proper Jurisdiction to try Titles — and lie further informed your Committee, that there is no Provision in the Act, for the Determination of Questions arising upon Titles; that the Court of Aldermen are obliged to take upon themselves to determine such Questions in a particular Cafe, under a few general Words, which provide, that the Purchase Money for Estates shall be paid out of the Bank as the Court of Aldermen shall direct — That he does not think the Court of Aldermen a Jurisdiction proper to have Powers of this Sort given to it; and that other Provisions are necessary, in order to give Parties interested in any of the Premises, to be purchased under the Act, an easy and effectual Method of ascertaining their respective Interests, and coming at the Value thereof.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain, amend, and render more effectual, the Powers of an Act, made in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, intituled, An Act for widening certain Streets, Lanes, and Passages, within the City of London, and Liberties thereof, and for opening certain new Streets and Ways within the same, and for ot her Purposes therein mentioned: And that Sir Robert Ladbroke, Mr. Paterson, Mr. Alderman Bedford, Sir

Richard Glyn, and Mr. Alderman Harley, do prepare, and bring in, the feme.

A Petition of several Noblemen, Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants, Parishioners of the Town and Parish of Richmond, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Poor belonging to the said Town and Parish are numerous, idle, dissolute, and unemployed, and the Streets, Lanes, and Passages thereof, are, in general, ill paved, and are not properly cleansed and lighted, and the public Highways are greatly out of Repair; and there is no Nightly Watch; and representing to the House, that, if the Poor were properly employed and regulated, and the Streets, Lanes, and Passages, well paved, cleansed, lighted, and watched, and the Public Highways repaired, it would be a great Benefit to the Inhabitants, and all Persons possessed of Estates within the said Town and Parish: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Mr. Josiah Wedgzcood, being examined, said. That there are several large Manufactories in the Neighbourhood of the intended Canal, particularly a great Pottery near Nexccastle under Lyne, and that the raw Materials and manufactured Goods, carried to and from that Manufactory annually, amount, to io or 12,000 Ton, and that if the intended Canal is made, it will be a great Advantage to the said Manufactory by reducing the Price of Carriage; that the Iron Manufactory of Birmingham and Wolverhampton, and the Country adjacent, will be greatly benefited, and that great Quantities of Coal that lie near where the intended Canal is to go, are now carried 10 or 15 Miles by Land; and the Witness said, that there will be in general a Saving of Three Fourths of the Expence of Carriage.

Mr. Thomas Bentley, being examined, said. That the Carriage of Goods from Birmingham to Liverpool is at present. £. 4 per Ton, Land Carriage, but if the intended Navigation is made, he apprehends all Goods will be conveyed by Water at about 30.?. per Ton; that the Town of Manchesterpays about 24,000 a Year for Carriage of Goods to London by Land, and nearly as much back; that the present Price is about £. 7 per Ton, but if this Navigation is made, they will fend their Goods halfWay by Water at about 30V. per Ton, and from thence to Ixnby Land, for about £. 3 per Ton, which will be a great Saving in the Article t of Carriage; and the Witness said, that he apprehends

the completing this Navigation will be attended with great Advantages to the several Towns and Places through and near which it will pass, and be of great Utility to the Public in general.

Mr. John Sparrow informed your Committee, That £. 63,000 has been already subscribed towards carrying on this navigable Cut; and that he apprehends the whole Sum necessary will be ealily obtained.

mond, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are informed that Application is making to Parliament for a Bill to regulate the Poor and repair the i iighw’ays of the said Parish, and to pave and light the Streets of the said Town-, and other Purposes; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, that the Laws in being are very sufficient for regulating the Poor of the said Parish, and for repairing the Highways there; and that the Poor are now, and have been, regularly and decently cloth-

6 Geo. III. 7* Februari 521

ed, fed, and otherwise taken Care of; and that the Highways have been, and may be, Kept in Repair at a very easy Expence to the Inhabitants of the said Parish; and that the Pavements of the said" Town are now in much better Repair than they have been for many Years; and the Town, being no great Thorough-fare, may be kept sufficiently paved without the Interposition of any new Law; and that the Inhabitants of the said Town chiefly conlift of Persons who let Lodgings, deal in Provisions, Household Necessaries, and other Matters, which produce only a bare Maintenance for themselves and Families; and that they are in general already burthened with as many Taxes as they well can bear; and that the Petitioners are fully convinced, that, if the said Application should succeed, and an Act pass for the several Purposes above-mentioned, the Inhabitants of the said Town will be charged with a very large and additional Tax, in every respect unnecessary: And therefore praying. That the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Application; and that no Bill may pass for any of the above-mentioned Purposes.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Dealers in Broad Woollen Cloth, manufactured in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act passed in the last Session repealing several Laws relating to the Manufacture of Woollen Cloth, in the County of York , and also so much of the several other Laws as prescribes particular Standards, of Width and Length, of such Woollen Cloth, and for substituting other Regulations of the Cloth Trade, within the West Riding of the said County, for preventing Fraudsincertifying the Contents of the Cloth, and for preserving the Credit of the said Manufacture at the Foreign Markets; and that the Trade, within the said West Riding, is of a large and

VqIm 30.

exfenfive Nature; and that a great Number of Broad Woollen Cloths have been, for many Years last past, vended for the Supply of Home Consumption, as well as for the Foreign Markets; and that the Petitioners find that the Regulations,-substituted by the said late Act, are inadequate for preventing Frauds, in certifying the true Contents of the Cloth, and consequently of preserving the Credit of the said Manufactures in Foreign Markets; and that the Petitioners are exposed to very great Hardships, by the said Act, in conducting a Trade of the highest Importance to the Welfare*of this Kingdom in general; and from the Number of Cloths necessary to be bought for the Supply of Foreign Markets, it is, by the Rules established by the said l aws, rendered impossible for the Petitioners (be their Intentions ever so upright,) to guard themselves, and their Property, against the Penalties inflicted by the said Act: and that the Petitioners are thereby subjected to many grievous Penalties, and even to corporal Punishment, for the Acts of others, and which it is not in their Power to prevent: And therefore praying. That the Petitioners may be relieved in the Premises, and that Leave may be given to bring in such a Bill, for the better Regulation of a Manufacture of so great Importance to this Kingdom, in such Manner as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to She Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

That several of the Proprietors have refused to pay the Tax laid upon their Grounds for the Purposes of the Act, and there is no Way to compel them to pay it, as the Act refers to a Level Tax, as the Mode of making the Assessment, which Level Tax does not at present exist; and the Trustees have no Way of raising Money but by Mortgage, which is ineffectual, as the Lands are not yet drained; that if the whole Tax could be levied it would not be sufficient for the Purposes of the said Act; and that it will not be possible to drain the said Lands efi'eftually, unless the said Act be explained and amended.

Britishi A Petition of the Trustees of the British

Museum. being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth. That, in the 2d Year of His present Mar

jesty, the Petitioners represented to Parliament, that the Sum allowed for the Establishment and Support of the said Museum, was reduced to a Capital of £.3 0,000 reduced Hank Annuities, the Dividend of which amounting to £.900 was, notwithstanding their utmost Attention to theirforming the irEstablilliment with Frugality, greatly insufficient for that Purpose; upon which Representation they obtained a Grant of a further Sum of £.2000; and upon a like Application in the Fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, the Petitioners obtained a Grant of £.2000 for the same Purpose, which Sum, together with the Produce of the said £.30,000, are so for spent, that what remains is not more than sufficient to defray the Expences of the last Year: And therefore praying the House, to grant the Petitioners suchfurther Support, towards enabling them tocarry on the execution of the Trust reposed in them by Parliament, for the general Benefit of Learning and useful Knowledge, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of Stephen Fuller, Esquire, Agent of the Island of Jamaica, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in the Year 1760, there broke out Two Rebellions in the said Island, which threatened not only the Destruction of the Inhabitants, but the Loss of that valuable Colony to Great Britain; and that, after the said Rebellions, the Assembly of the said llland thought proper, in order to defray the Expences that increased on account thereof, to lay a Tax by way of Stamps, which Tax was laid in the Year 1760, and continued till December 1763, when that Law was fullered to expire, on account, as the Petitioner is informed, and believes, of its being unequal and burthensome, as it certainlywasinahigh degree; and that the Petitioner most humbly conceiving that the Act for imposing certain Stamp Duties in the British Colonies and Plantations in America will be attended with the same Inconveniences,. if not greater, (on account that the Forfeitures and Penalties incurred may be sued for and recovered in any Court of Record, or in any Court of Admiralty or Vice Admiralty in the Island, at the election of the Informer or Prosecutor) prays such Relief in the Premises, as to the House thall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Cooke took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Cooke reported from the Committee, That tljey had examined several other Witnesses, and had made a further Progrefo in the Matter to them referred; and that he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself.into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the several Papers, which were presented to the House, by Mr. Secretary Conway, upon the 14th, 22d, 27th, 28th, and 31st Days of January last, and the 5th and 1 oth Days of this Instant February, and by Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, upon the 3d and 1 oth Days of this Instant , by His Majesty’s Command.

Ordered, That the several Persons, who were ordered to attend the said Committee this Day, except Barlow Trecothick, Esquire, Mr. Hanbuand Mr. Mildred, do attend the said Committee Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Sir William Meredith reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Merchants and Masters of Ships and Vessels of the Port of Liver/wol, whose Names are subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read, and is as followed); viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Hutchinson, beingexamined, said, That he hath

been many Years Captain of a Ship, and is now Dock Master of the Port of Liverpool, and has frequently surveyed the Banks and Entrance into that Port with Mr.. Mackenzie, who was employed by the Government as Surveyor of the Coasts of this Kingdom, and that the Banks and Tide Ways are so intricate and ipterwoven, and there being many moveable Banks and Shoals, the Navigation into the Harbour is very dangerous ;that there have been above 100 Lives, and about 15 Ships totally loft within a few Years pnft, and many others greatly damaged, which hath been owing to the Un-Ikilfulness of Pilots; that he has known a Ship lie off the Harbour Eight Days for want of a Pilot, and was obliged to go to the Me of Man for one; that there is no Law or Charter for ascertaining the Prices for conducting Ships into or out of the said Port; and that the making Provisioti for the proper Regulation of Pilots, and ascertaining their Rates or Prices, would tend greatly to promote and encourage Trade and Navigation, and be of public Utility.

Captain William Dun, being examined, confirmed the above Evidence, as to the great Danger of the Entrance into the said Port; and added, that he himself hath had Persons.ealling themselves Pilots on board his

Vessel Two t>r Three Days, and, when the Weather hath blown hard, and Difficulties arose, they have been totally ignorant 1k>w todoriduft the Vessel ib; and if the Witness liad not been acquainted with the Entrance into the Port better tliah they, he believes his Ship and Cargo must have been loft; that be hath been prevented coming into the (hid Harbotir in badWeather, and hath been obliged to go into another for want of a skilful Pilot, the Entrance into the same being so intricate and dangerous.

Mr. George Campbell, Merchant, being examined, said, That a Vessel bound from North America to Li-verjmol, and consigned to him, was in November last looked upon to be loft, till he received a Letter from the Captain from Cadiz in Spain, advising him, that he was 1b much afraid of the Danger of the Entrance into the Port of Liverpool, and the Uncertainty of getting a skilful Pilot, they being under no Regulation, that he (the Captain) thought it. best to go to Spain, and that he intended to fell his Cargo there.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners or Matters of Ships belonging to the Port of Whitby, in the County of York, in behalf of themselves and many others: And also,

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners or Matters of Ships belonging to Scarborough, in the County of York, in behalf of themselves and many others j

Were presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners and others, are very largely concerned in Shipping, employed chiefly in the CoalTrade, at , Shields, and Sun-

derland, which Business, the Petitioners presume, has, by long Experience, been found of the greater! Advantage to this Nation, by raising and continuing very great Numbers of Seamen (who tipon all Exigencies and Emergencies have been incorporated into the Royal Navy, and otherwise employed to the Safety and Honour of this Kingdom and its Colonies) and by otherwise employ -ingmanyThonfands of theinduftriousPoor; and that the Petitioners apprehend it veryeffential to the Manufacturers and Poor of this Country, to be supplied with Fuel on easy Terms; and that all Proceedings tending to a Monopoly mutt of Course be very prejudicial; and that the Petitioners beg Leave to represent to the House, that, of > late Years, the Persons employed as Fitters in the Coal Trade, at the Ports of Newcastle and Sunderland aforesaid, have become Owners of Ships to a very great extent; and in order to engross and keep the Trade in their own Hands, have made it a Practice to refuse a Loading of Coals, except it be an inferior Sort, to the Petitioners, unless taken upon Freight at a consider* able Under Value, and at other Times obliging them to wait with their Ships Eight or Ten Weeks for a Loading, and at the fanrie Time loading such Ships as they are themselves most interested in immediately on their Arrival, by which Means such Ships frequently make Two or Three Voyages to London, before the Petitioners can get One Loading to fail with, where* by great Numbers of the Petitioners Ships, which used to make Eight or Ten Voyages in the Summer Season, cannot now make above Five or Six in the whole Year, to the great Lois of the Petitioners in their Fortunes, and to the very great Prejudice of the Consumers of Coals at London, and other Places, because the Petitioners are obliged to keep up the Price of their Coals, in order to make themselves some Amends for their extraordinary Expences and Lois of Time; by which Method of monopolizing, the Fitters, whose Ships make so many more Voyages in a Year than the Petitioners, of Course, have immense Profits upon their Coals, and are getting Fortunes upon the Wreck of the Petitioners,* and at the Expence of the Public, and will in a short Time become Matters of the whole Coal Trade, and have it in their Power to prescribe such Rules, and set such Prices, as they shall think proper, for furtheraggrandising the irown Fortunes; and that, upon Account of this great Check the Petitioners have met with in their Trade, they are greatly discouraged from, and find themselves incapable of taking Apprentices, which, the Petitioners with Submission represent, mutt, if not timely prevented, have very dreadful and fatal Effects upon the Trade and Navigation of these zz

Kingdoms, by destroying that great Nurlerv Toi* Seamen; and that, by an Act made in the Sixth and Seventh Year of the Reigns of King IVHug in, Provision was made for regulating the Weight of every Chaldron of Coals; but there being no Powerto punish Persons not complying with the Directions of the said Act:, the same has proved ineffectual, to the further great Prejudice of the Consumers of Coals; that the Petitioners apprehend, that, if the Persons employed as Fitters at Newcastle, Sunderland, and the adjacent Ports, were obliged, as formerly, to keep public Lists in their Offices of such Ships as apply for a Loading, and likewise were obliged to load all Ships as they are entered in their Course; and also if proper Power was givpn for ascertaining the Weight of every Chaldron of Coalsat the several Ports aforesaid, it would be a great Means of preventing the Evils and Disadvantages above complained of, and be of great public Utility: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration; and to grant such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

of Ground, called the I/noer Burying Ground, which is the Property of the said Parish, and, for Time immemorial, hath been made Use of as a Burying Ground for the said Parish, and which, being ill an airy Situation, is very proper to build a Workhouse upon, or ppon Part thereof, for the Use of the Poor of the said Parish, and cannot be attended with any Inconvenience to the Parishioners, by reason they have other Burying Ground sufficient within the said Parish; and that there are several other Pieces of Ground ad joining and contiguous to, but not within, the said Parish, very proper and convenient to build a Workhouse upon for their Poor, but the Trustees are not empowered by the said Act to purchase the fame; and that the Petitioners apprehend some further Alterations may be necessary to be made in the said Act, for the more effectually putting the said Act in execution: And therefore praying. Folkestone A Petition of the Mayor, .1 urats, and Commoners, of

Church, the Town of Folkestone, in the County and of several of the principal Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish of Folkestone, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Parish Church of Folkestone aforesaid is situate at the upper End of the said Town, at a small Distance from the Cliff; and that, by the continual flowing of the Tide, and raging of the Sea again A the said Cliff, the Bank whereof is a loose sandy Soil, the same is considerably washed away, whereby the said Parish Church is in Danger of falling, unless timely prevented by erecting one or more substantial Jettee, or Jettees, at the Foot of the said Cliff, under the said Church; and that the lower Part of the said Town, and the Beach whereon the Fishermen are accustomed to resort to, have been, from Time to Time, preserved from, and defended against, the overflowing and raging of the Sea, by Two large Jettees, or Heads, one at the East, and the other at the West End of the said Town, which Jettees, or Heads, have been, from Time to Time, kept in Repair by the Fishermen, and other Inhabitants of the said Town, by a voluntary Subscription; and that, by Length of Time, and many high and raging Tides, the said Jettees, or Heads, are become very ruinous; and should they go entirely to Decay, not only the said Beach, but all the lower Part of the said Town, must inevitably be overflowed and carried away by the Sea; and that the Fishermen of the said Town are become very poor, and neither they, nor the other Inhabitants of the said Town, who are burthened with numerous Poor, are able to raise so large a Sum of Money as will be needful to be expended in erecting a good and substantial Jettee, or Jettees, for the Security and Support of the said Parish Church, and to repair, and keep in Repair, the said Jettees, or Heads, without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for erecting a Jettee, or Jettees, for supporting the said Church, and for repairing, and keeping in Repair, the said Jettees, or Heads, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

(after repeated Complaints from the Corporations of the Trinity House in the North of England, and from the Merchants and Navigators) in or about the Month of F'ebruary 1765, presented their Petition to His Majesty,

Praying, that His Majesty would be pleased to signify His Royal Pleasure, that the said Letters Patent should be made void; and that His Majesty was pleased to refer the said Petition to His then Attorney and Solicitor General, who reported they were of Opinion that the rrtaterial Fa6ts alleged in the said Petition were well founded, and were a sufficient Ground to warrant the proceeding to revoke the said Letters Patent; but in-as much as the said Spume Lights were a valuable Inheritance, and had been long in the Possession of Mr. Ai-gell and his Family, and as the Petitioner (who had been excluded from any Share of the Management and Direction of the Light Houses) appeared to have been, and had expressed himself before them to be, deli rous that the heft and moll effectual Measures should be taken for fulfilling the Purposes of the said Letters Patent, and to contribute his Proportion of the Expence; and as the Corporation of the Trinity House at Deptford Strond were willing to undertake the Conduct and Direction of rebuilding the Light Houses, and placing them in a proper Situation, they were of Opinion it might be advisable, if His Majesty should so please, to suspend, for a short Time, the Steps necessary to be taken for vacating the said Patents, in order that the Patentees might have an Opportunity, if they thought fit, of authorizing the Corporation of the Trinity House of Deptford Strond to take such Measures as they should think proper, at the Expence of the Patentees, for taking down the present Light Houses, and erecting and building others in such Places, and in such Manner, and for so keeping and preferring the Lights therein, as should, in their Judgment, moll effectually conduce to the Safety of the Navigation of those Seas; and if the Patentees should refuse or neglect, forthwith to give such Authority and Security for defraying the Expence of the said Erection, to the Satisfaction of the Corporation, or should thereafter retard or attempt to frustrate the fame, or to obllruct or render ineffectual the Execution thereof, it seemed advisable, if His Majesty should so please, that the speediell Means the Law would allow should be used for vacating the said Grants; the New Soil thrown up at the Spume Point, under a conditional Agreement to be made with the said Mr. Constable; that the Right to the Spot where the Lights should be fixed should be determined after they were set up; that, in consequence of the said Direction, a Proposal, or Agreement, was prepared, and approved of by the Counsel for the said Mr. Angell, but he has hitherto neglected, and upon an Application made to him by the Petitioner’s Agents for that Purpose, refused to sign or deliver the fame, or any other Proposals, to the said Corporation; and that the Petitioner is ready and willing to take down and remove the present Light Houses, and to erett and build others instead thereof, in such Place or Places, near to the present Point, and

in such Manner and Form, as shall be thought most proper and convenient, under the Inspection and Di-reftiou of the said Corporation, and to conform to the Proposition made by His Majesty's Attorney and Soli-citor General as aforesaid, upon his having the Liberties, Duties, and Profits, granted by the said Letters Patent, vested in him, so as to enable him to borrow Money for that Purpose on the Credit thereof; and that the Three Fourth Parts of the said Liberties, Duties, and Profits, belonging to the said John Angell and his Heirs, may be a Redeemable Intereli in him, upon his or their paying to the Petitioner, or the Person or Persons from whom such Money shall be borrowed, his the said John Angell's Proportions of such Money, and the Intereli thereof, and upon the Petitioner being enabled to charge the remaining Fourth Part of the Money, so to be borrowed, on the said Fourth Part of the said Lands, Light Houses, Duties, and Profits, to which he is liirn-l'elf entitled for his Life j the Petitioner keeping down the Intereli thereof during his Life; but, by reason of the Estate and Interest which he the said John Angell hath in Three Fourth Parts of the said Lands, Light Houses, Duties, and Profits, and by reason that his

Condition of Health, Manner of Life, and State of Mind, are such that the Petitioner has no Expectation of being able to effect the Purposes aforesaid by Agreement with the said John Angell, and also by reason that the said Petitioner is only Tenant for Life in the said Fourth Part of the said Premises, he cannot be enabled so to do without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying, That, upon Proof of the Allegations aforesaid, Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable him to take down and remove the present Light Houses, near the Spume Point, and to erect others inllead thereof, in a Place nearer to the said Spume Point, and more convenient and useful to the Northern Navigation, and to enable him to borrow Money for that and other Purposes to be therein mentioned, upon the Credit of the Duties payable for Ships and Vessels passing the Spume Lights, and to apply the same in erecting such new Light Houses, and for other Purposes therein to be mentioned; or to effect the Ends and Purposes aforesaid, by such other Means as to the House shall seem meet.

Were severally presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That the Petitioners being in-, formed, that an Application is intended to be made to the House, for a Bill to make a Navigable Cut, or Canal, from the River Severn, at Tern Bridge, in the County of Salop, to Wilden Ferry (on the River Trent) in the County of Derby, and from the said Cut, at or near Bridge-ford, in Slaffordshire, to the River Weaver, in the County of Chester; and that the Petitioners conceive, that the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Trading Towns of Birmingham, Wolverhampton, Walsall, Stourbridge, Kidderminster, Bewdley, and Dudley, and Places adjacent, in the several Counties of Warwick, Stafford, and Worcester, cannot receive the lead Benefit from the said intended Navigation, as every Part thereof will be at a greater Distance from them respectively, than the River Severn is, nor can the same be in any Shape serviceable to the Cities of Glouces-

ter, and Worcester, or the Trading Towns of Upton and Bewdley, and other Trading Towns on the Severn, and the less so, as there are several Shallows therein betwixt Bewdley, and Tern Bridge aforesaid, which render it impossible for the Vessels and Boats thereon to car:y a greater Weight than a Broad-wheeled Team; and that the Freight thereof is near adequate to Land Carriage; and that the said Navigable Cut is intended to pass through a Country remote from any Manufactories, and near to which are very few Mines; and that, consequently,. the same cannot be, as the Petitioners apprehend, of any Service to Trade in general, or Utility to the Public: And therefore praying, That, if such intended Bill should be brought into the House, the same may not pass into a Law; and that, as the Petitioners are advised, it may be material and necessary for them to have the Assistance of Counsel in Opposition to the said Bill, that they may be at Liberty to be heard by their Counsel.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Confederation of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Land Owners, Tradesmen, and Manufacturers, residing in the County of Chester, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, is referred; and these several Petitioners are to be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their said Petitions, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an InllruClion to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said former Petition, against the Petitions now presented.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That a certain Piece of Land* now called Cherry Cobb Sand, supposed, by the Petitioners, to have arisen out of the Bed Of the River j in York-

shire, and to have first made its Appearance about Fifty or Sixty Years since, ha’s inereased by Degrees, and is now become a very valuable Spot of Land, containing One thousand Six hundred Acres, or thereabouts; and that the Petitioners being seised in Fee of an Estate, at Saltagh Grange, opposite to the said Sand, in of about the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-nine, petitioned the then Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury for a Grant of Five hundred Acres, Part of the said Sand, lying nearest to the Petitioner’s Estate, for the Benefit of the said Charity, and Charles Poole Esquire, petitioned about the same Time, for a Grant of the whole Sand, and William Constable Esquire, who was in Possession of the said Sand, and claimed it as Lord of the Seigniory, Dominion, and Honour of derness, petitioning also cither to be quieted in the Pof-session thereof, or to have a Grant of lo much of the said Sand as arose between high and low Water Mark; all the Three several Petitions were referred to His Majesty’s then Attorney General for his Opinion thereupon, who, on the Fifteenth Day of February, One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty, reported, that he was of Opinion, that his late Majesty was intitled to the said Sand, and that the Right of the Crown ought forthwith to be ascertained; and that, in Pursuance of such Report, their Lordships were pleased, by their Warrant, todiredt Five hundred Acres, Part of the said Sand, called Cherry Cobb, lying contiguous to the Petitioners said Estate, to be granted to them, for a Term of Thirty-one Years, without Fine, for the Benefit of the said Charity, but subject to the Rent of Sixty six Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence per Annum; and to a Covenant to try the Crown’s Right, at the Expence of the Petitioners, with the Aid of the Exchequer; and the Remainder was ordered to be granted to the said Mr. Poole, subject to a Rent of One hundred and Forty-six Pounds per Annum, on the like Conditions* which Grant he afterwards declined; and that* afterwards, and before a Grant of the said Five hundred Acres was made to the Petitioners, they, with the Leave of their Lordships, caused an Information to be fled, in the Name of His Majesty’s Attorney General, in the Court of Exchequer, against the said William for the recovering the Possession of the same j to which Information, the said Defendant having appeared, and pleaded Not Guilty j the Information came on to be tried, by a Special Jury, at the Summer Assizes holden at York, in One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-three; the Jury found a Verdict for the Defendant William Constable, and that the Petitioners, beingdiflatisfied with such Verdict, presented another Memorial to the then Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, praying their Lordships to order a new Information to be brought, in the Name of the Attorney General, for the Recovery of the Possession of the whole Sand, to be tried at the Bar of the Court of Exchequer, at the Expence of the Crown, upon which the then Lords of the Treasury were pleased, by their Order of the Tenth Day of December, One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-three, to signify their Disapprobation of trying the Right at the Expence of the Crown -, but if the Proprietors were inclined to prosecute their Claim, their Lordships would order a new Information of Intrusion to be brought, and tried at the Expence of the Petitioners; and it the De-cifion should be in favour of the Crown, that they would grant the whole Sand to the Petitioners, for the Benefit of the said Charity, subject to the same Quit-rents and Conditions, and for the same Term, as were directed to be inserted in the intended Grants to the

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That several Attempts have, for many Years part, been made, by different Persons, to bring Water to the West End of the Cities of London and Westminster, from the River Colne above Uxbridge, the general Utility of which to the said Cities is universally known and admitted, although the Design has never been effected, which the Petitioners apprehend is to be attributed to the several Proposals, having been made for taking the said Water out of the River Colne, above the Town of Uxbridge, whereby several valuable Mills would have been manifestly injured; and that the Petitioners, from accurate Surveys made, find that a proper Supply of Water may be had, which they pro-pole to bring from the said River Colne, at or near a Place called Hobarls Mill, about Three Miles below

Uxbridge, by a Cut navigable for Boats, Barges, and othei* Vessels, to a Place near Williams Farm in

the Parish of St. Mary Le Bon, by which Method very few Mills will receive any kind of Detriment, and the Petitioners are willing to make proper Satisfaction to the Owners and Occupiers thereof; and that the Petitioners, in consequence of this Plan, have a Proposal depending for an Agreement with the Governor and Company of

Che’feaWater Works, for uniting the Petitioners Undertaking with the said Company, and making them one United Company with a Joint Stock, and for carrying the same into Execution by virtue of an Act of Parliament for that Purpose; and that the Advantages resulting to the Cities of London and Westminster, from the Execution of this Plan, are great and obvious, not only by a Supply of Water, but from the said Navigation: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for supplying the Cities of London and Westminster with Water from the River Colne, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall teem proper, and for carrying into Execution such Agreement as the Petitioners shall make with the said Governor and Company of Water

Works.

laid. That there is a Road from into Leicester-

Side of Lord Douegall’iPark, to the North Gate ofi the said Park, and from thence in Leveral Branches through the said Park, very near his Lordship’s House, over the River Lame, by Three several Fords in the said River; and that the said Branches from the said Fords, unite again on the East Side of the said River, near a certain Mill called Elf or d Mill.

That the said Fords are oftentimes impassable on account of the Floods, and the Conflux of the Rivers Trent and Meefe, near the Mouth of the River Tame, except at One of the said Fords near Elford Hall, where Passengers are conveyed over in small Ferry Boats, and in high Floods are obliged to walk from the Boats over the Meadows through the Water.

That the Road leading from Litchfield into Leicester-shire, through Whittington, and by the South and East Sides of the said Park on the Outside thereof, and over the River Tame at the Southermost of the said-.Fords at Elford Mill, is in general in good Repair, except from Hademove Gate, to the said Ford, which Lord DonegalIpropo.es to repair and maintain at his own Expence.

That there is not at present any Bridge over thfc River Tame, South of Elford Mill, nearer than Hopwas, which is Four Miles from the said Mill, nor any Bridge North of the said Mill, nearer than Salter’s Bridge, which is above Three Miles from the said.Mill; and that the said Hopwas, and Salter's Bridges, are frequently inaccessible in Floods for Foot Passengers-rand, in high Floods, it is dangerous to pal’s with Horses^o* Carriages.

That if a Bridge was erected for the free Passage of Cattle, Carriages, and Travellers at.ill Times, over the River Tame, at Elford Mill, it would establish an easy, sese, and certain Communication between the said City of Litchfield, the Borough of Waif all, and other great Trading Towns and Places on the West Side of the said River, and the Villages of Harlafton,

ton, Clifton, and Parts adjacent, in the County of Stafford, Edingale, in the County of Derby, and with The County of Leicester, on the East Side of the said River, whereby the Inhabitants on the East and West Sides of the River, may respectively more conveniently be supplied with Corn, Coals, and Lime.

And that Lord Donegall is willing and desirous to erect and maintain at his own Expence, a substantial and convenient Public. Bridge for the free Passage of Cattle, Carriages, and Travellers at ail Times, over the said River Tame, at Elford Mill, in case he shall be authorized to flop up and discontinue the Use of all' the Roads through and over his Park, and the Fords and Passages leading into the fame.

Mr. Cooke reported from the Committee, to whom the Whitechapel Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, Overseers of the foot.

Poor, and Parishioners, of the Parish of St. , Whitechapel, within the Tower Division, and County of Middlesex, the Liberty of His Majesty’s Tower of London, and Liberty of the City of London, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwardsdelivereditinat the Clerk’s Table:

Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Third Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for maintaining, regulating, and employing the Poor in the said Parish, was read; whereby Power is given to purchase Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, within the said Parish, and to alter, repair, and fumish any Buildings within the same, for receiving, maintaining, and employing the Poor of the said Parish, or to build or hire any House or Houses within the said Parish, for the Purposes aforesaid; and to raise the Sum of £. 4,000, to be charged on the Rates authorized to be levied by the said Act.

Mr. Thomas Price, Treasurer to the Trustees appointed by the said Act, being examined, said, That the said Trustees had endeavoured, several Times, to purchase Lands for erecting a Workhouse, but without Effect; for the Proprietors, knowing that they were confined to the Parish, always asked them an exorbitant Price: Which Evidence was confirmed by Mr. Robert Brownfon and Mr. John Moore, Two of the said Trustees; and all the said Witnesses agreed, that there is a Piece of Ground, which was formerly used as a Burying Ground, on the North Side of Whitechapel Road, near the London Work-house, which would be extremely proper for the Scite of a Workhouse for the Poor of the said Parish; and that the said Parish have Three Acres of Ground adjoining thereto, which is now lett upon Lease, Twenty-six Years of which are yet unexpired.

Mr. Edward Hawkins, being examined, said, That he had surveyed the said Burying Ground, which is about Three Quarters of an Acre; that this will be a very commodious Place for a Workhouse; and that there are not any Tomb Stones on that Part where the House is proposed to be built.

Mr. William Hamilton, being examined, said. That it was intended to remove the Bodies from that Part of the Burying Ground, where the House was to be built, and to inter them decently in another Part of the Ground; and to bury no more there for the future: That the other Burying Grounds belonging to the Parish are sufficient, in his Opinion, with proper Management; but, if not, the Parishioners have contracted for another.

Mr. William Kirby, one of the Churchwardens of the said Parish, being examined, said, That the Expence of maintaining, regulating, and employing the Poor of the said Parish, is much greater at present than it would be if a Workhouse was built.

Mr. Thomas Deming, being examined, said, That there are many Pieces of Ground near or adjoining to the faict Parish, which would be very convenient for building a Workhouse, particularly a Place called The Mulberry Gardens, which he thought as convenient a Situation as possible.

Mr. John Billington, being examined, said, That the Trustees have already borrowed £.1,100 on the Credit of the said Act, upon Annuities for Lives.

That feme Alterations are necessary to be made in the said Act, particularly to impower the Trustees to raise a larger Sum of Money, and to allow them to give larger Interest than Nine/>fr Cent. Life Annuities; and that several additional Powers are wanting to enforce the Execution of the said Act.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to tender more effectual an Act, made in the Third Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for maintaining, regulating.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the King’s Majesty, by and with the Advice and Consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, had, hath, and of Eight ought to have, full Power and Authority to make Laws and Statutes, of sufficient Force and Validity to bind the Colonies and People of America, Subjects of the Crown of Great , in all Cases

whatsoever.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Tumults and lnfurreftions of the most dangerous Nature have been raised, and carried on, in several of the North American Colonies, in open Defiance of the Powers and Dignity of His Majesty’s Government, and in manifest Violation of the Laws and Legislative Authority of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Tumults and lnfurreftions have been greatly countenanced and inflamed by Votes and liefo-lutions, passed in several of the Assemblies of the said Provinces, highly injurious to the Honour of His Majesty’s Government, and tending to destroy the Legal and Constitutional Dependency of the said Colonies on the Imperial Crown and Parliament of Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Persons, who, on account of the Desire which they have manifested to comply with, or to assist in carrying into execution, any Acts of the Legislature of Great Britain, relating to the British Colonies in North America, have suffered any Injury or Damage, ought to have full and ample Compensation made to them for the fame, by the respective Colonies in which such Injuries or Damages were sustained.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, to resolve and declare, that all His Majesty’s Subjects, residing in the said Colonies, who have manifested their Desire to comply with, or to assist in carrying into execution, any Acts of the Legislature of Great Britain, relating to the British Colonies in North America, have acted as dutiful and loyal Subjects, and are therefore entitled to, and will assuredly have, the Protection of the House of Commons of Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Persons, who, by reason of the Tumults and Outrages in North America, have not been able to procure Stamped Paper, since the passing of the Act for laying certain Duties of Stamps in the Colonies, ought to be indemnified from all Penalties and Forfeitures, which they may have incurred, by Writing, ingrafting, or printing, on Paper, Vellum, or Parchment, not duly stamped, as required by the said Act, under proper Restrictions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill to repeal an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting and applying certain Stamp Duties, and other Duties, in the

British Colonies and Plantations in America, towards " further defraying the Expences of defending, protecting, and securing the fame; and for amending such Parts of the several Acts of Parliament, relating " to the Trade and Revenues of the said Colonies and " Plantations, as direct the Manner of determining and " recovering the Penalties and Forfeitures therein mentioned."

To prove the Allegations of the said first-mentioned Petition, Mr. PercivatHart, being examined, said. That he lives near the Workhouse at Richmond-, that it is a very corrupt House; that the Poor are fed with brown Bread; that the Parish have paid for a Pound and an Half of Bread for One Person a Day; that they may be furnished with a sufficient Quantity of white Bread at a leis Expence; that no well regulated Workhouse within Five Miles of London, consumes more than Five Pound and an Half of Bread, for One Person, a Week.

That the Witness was Churchwarden in the Year 1761, when he found a Debt of £. 140 on the Parish; that in order to pay the lame, the Rates were raised from 18 d.to is. in the Pound; by which Means the Debt was discharged, the Poor maintained, and a Balance of £.129. 1 ij. 2 \d.was paid over to Mr. King, the next Overseer; that they endeavoured to set the Poor to work, but could not accomplish it; that they took off the Salary of the Mailer of the Workhouse, and gave him the Labour of the Poor for his Wages.

That the Poor have not been maintained for leis than £. 800 per Annum for Six Years pall; that the Expence is double to what it was formerly; and the Witness thinks they may be maintained in a better and more regular Manner, and at less Expence, if proper Powers were given for that Purpose; that there has been a total Neglect of the Workhouse for several Years.

That the Pavements and Highways of the said Town are in general in a very ruinous Condition, and not cleansed or lighted; that it is necessary to make a large Drain from the Eall to the West End of the Town, in order to carry off the Water and Filth into the 'Thames -, that it appears by a Survey taken, that the making such Drain will cost £. 500.

That the Streets are not lighted, not having Power to compel Persons to hang out proper Lights; that if Power was given to Trustees to regulate the Streets and Highways, and appoint a Nightly Watch, it would be of great Benefit to the Town; and that it would tend much to the Safety of the Inhabitants, if a regular Watch was established to patrole the Streets, in case of Fires.

Mr. Edward Collins, being examined, laid. That he was Overseer of the Poor in the Year 1761; that he collected £.960. 11 s. 1 \d. and maintained the Poor for £.645.

7 d.and paid over a Balance of £. 315. ij. 10 to the next Overseers, and all the Debts were discharged.

That the Witness thinks the Poor are not in want of Food, but want regulating; that a poor Woman of 80 Years of Age complained to him for Want; Ihe is not maintained in the Workhouse, but is allowed One Shilling per Week; that there is a Man maintained in the Workhouse, who is able and does go out to work, and puts his Earnings into his own Pocket.

That he does not think, the Poor are so well maintained and regulated, nor so cheap, as they might be, if proper Powers were given for that Purpose by Act of Parliament.

That the Streets in the said *Town are in general very ill paved; that he apprehends a capital Drain is wanted, as well for Cleanliness as Health; that he thinks these Regulations may be effected without laying any great Burthen on the Inhabitants, but will rather be an Advantage to them by casing them of their

Statute Labour, as it is proposed to exempt all Persons from paying to the Rates who do not rent a House of Six Pounds a Year.

Henry Hobart, Esquire, being examined, laid. That his House is so near the Workhouse, that he is able to fee and hear what passes there; that lie cannot speak as to the Manner of feeding the Poor, but they are not kept in any Order or Regulation whatsoever; that the House appears to be very dirty, and the People ill clothed; that he apprehends if the Poor were to wear Badges, many Persons who now receive Money would refuse to do it; and that he thinks they may be better maintained and regulated, if proper Powers were given for that Purpose.

That the Streets of the said Town are in many Parts very ruinous; that the Statute Labour, and the Nine Shilling Rate, cannot possibly put them into sufficient Repair, nor can it be done by any other Means than by Act of Parliament.

Colonel Pechel confirmed Mr. Hobart's Evidence.

To prove the Allegations of the Second mentioned Petition, Mr. Thomas Bordican, being examined, laid. That he was Overseer in the Year 1762; that he often visited the Workhouse, and has seen many of the Poor; that he never heard any. Complaints from them; that they were employed by Mr. Clark, who was to have the Profits of their Labour for looking after them; that the Number of Poor at present maintained in the Workhouse is Eighty-two.

Mr. John Lewis, being examined, said, That he is an Inhabitant of Richmond; that he lives near the Workhouse, and frequently calls in to fee whether the Poor are properly taken Care of; that he never heard any Complaints.

That the Workhouse was not so clean as it ought to be, the latter Part of the late Mailer’s Time; but fine* his Death, it has been kept as clean as any Workhouse in the Kingdom; that many of the Poor are very old and infirm; those that are able are employed in making Mop Yarn; and he does not think there is a Necessity for any new Regulations.

That the Streets and Highways are in very good Condition, and there is not an immediate Necessity for any Reparation of them; and he thinks if the Laws relating to the Poor and the Highways were properly enforced, they are sufficient to regulate them without the Addition of any new Taxes; and that he believes there are Three to One of the Inhabitants of,

against the present Application.

Mr. Ambrose Parish, the Mailer of the Workhouse, being examined, said. That there are Eighty-two Persons under his Care; that they are furnished with good Victuals and Drink, and such as are able are set to work; and that their Earnings have amounted to £. S in about Four Months; that many of them are employed in attending upon those that are unable to work by Age or Infirmity; that there is a Surgeon and an Apothecary to attend those that are lick; that they are kept very clean, constantly attend divine Service, and are neither idle, dissolute, or unemployed; and he does not think any new Regulation would be any Advantage to the Inhabitants, as the Witness apprehends they cannot be more properly taken Care of, or at any leis Expence.

Mr. Charles Scott, being examined, said, That the Streets and Highways were never in better Repair in his Memory than at present; that the Footways are but indifferent, but he thinks the Statute Labour and a Rate of Sixpence in the Pound would put them into sufficient Repair; that he does not think there is any Necessity for more Lights than there are at present; that he never heard of any Robberies or Burglaries; that Lamps were set up by Subscription, but they were not thought necessary, and have therefore been discontinued.

The respective Book-keepers to the,

‘ " Chester, Norwich, Mancheft and Birmingham Common

Stage Waggons, being severally examined, laid, in general, That their Waggons usually carried from 50 Hundred Weight to Four Tons, and fqmetimes Four Tons and an Half.

That in those Places where the Price of Carriage has been settled by the Quarter Sessions, they usually take the full Price from Gentlemen, arid somewhat leis from Tradesmen, as Tradesmen’s Goods are, in general, much heavier in Proportion to the Space they bccupy; and all the Witnesses Laid, that when Goods are bulky and light, they are usually carried by. Contract, at a higher Price than is allowed, or taken, for more weighty Commodities; and that, in this respect, they make -no Difference -- between Gentlemen and Tradesmen; and that as to Money, Plate, Writings, and -other- yaluable Effects, if entered as such, they are looked upon to be insured by- the Mailers of the Waggons, and are paid for accordingly.

Thai an Act of the 3d Year of King William' and ' Queen Mary,.Cap. 12. and another, made in the 21ft

Year of King George 2d, Cap. 28. were reach

By the former of which, Justices of the Peace are required, at their Quarter Sessions after Easter, yearly, to assess the- Prices of Land Carriage of Goods to be brought into, any Place within their Jurisdictions, by any Common Carrier, and such Rates -to certify to the Mayors, and other -Chief Officers of the Market Towns, to be hung up in some public Place; -and no Common Carrier shall take above such Rates, upon _ pain of forfeiting Five Pounds, to be levied by Distress

- and Sale of his Goods, by Warrant from any Two

V'-’-'- ' Justices where such Carrier shall relide: And by the latter of the said Acts, it - is enacted, That if any Waggoner shall demand or take any greater Price for "bringing of Goods to the City of London, or any Place within the Bills of Mortality, than is allowed by the -Justices -of the-Peace, for the County or Place from whence such Goods are brought, for carrying of Goods from London to the said County or Place, every such Waggoner shall forfeit the Sum of Five Pounds, to be levied in the Manner by the last mentioned Act directed, or by Distress and Sale of his Goods, by Warrant from Two Justices of the Peace for the Counties of -

sex or Surrey, or the City of London, or the City and Liberty of Westminster , and the respective Clerks of the Peace are required, immediately after Easter Session yearly, to certify to the Lord Mayor of the City of London, and to the Clerks of the Peace of and Surrey, and City and Liberty of ,the

Rates made for the Carriage of Goods, in pursuance of the said Act, in their respective Counties and Places; which Certificate, or. an attested Copy thereof, is to be deemed sufficient Evidence of the Rates and Prices set for the carrying Goods to any County or Place.

Then your Committee, in order to ascertain how far the said Acts had been complied with in relation

to fixing such Rates, and transmitting Certificates thereof in the Manner thereby directed, examined

Mr. James Jefferson, Deputy Clerk of the Peace for the County of Middlesex, and the Chief Clerk in the Office of the Town Clerk of the City of London; by

whose Examination, and by the Certificates by them produced, it appeared, that there are Eighteen Counties in England,-from which.no Certificate has ever

been returned in pursuance of the said last rhentioned Ad.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee Came to the following Resolutions

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the several Laws for settling the Rates of Carriage of Goods are not complied with.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Prosecutions of Offenders.against the Acts of the Third Year of King William and Queen Mary, and of the 21 ft Year of King Georgeyhc Second, for settling the Rates of the Carriage of Goods, are attended with Difficulties; as the Penalties are to be recovered in the Place where such Offenders reside, or in the Cities of London or Westminster, or in the Counties of Middlesex or

Surrey, and not elsewhere.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain, amend, and reduce into One Ad, so much, of the said. Acts, as relates to the settling the Rates of the Carriage of Goods.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. David Griffin, being examined, said, that Olave's Street and Bermoudfey Street lead from London Bridge, to the Kentish Road; and that Saint Olave's Street and Freeschool Street lead directly from London Bridge, to His Majesty’s Victualling Office and Dock Yard at Deptford, in the County of Kent that the said Streets are great Thoroughfares, and at present very i;l paved, and not sufficiently cleansed, lighted, and watched; and that there are many Obstructions and Annoyances in the said Street?.

That if the Provisions of the intended Bill for paving. cleansing, and lighting the High Street ;*nd Kent Street, in the Borough of Southwark, were extended to Saint Olave's Street, Freeschool Street, and Bennoiulfey Street, the same would be of great Advantage to tire Inhabitants of the said Streets, and to the Public in general.

That if a, small Toll was laid upon all Cattle and Carriages passing on Sundays through the Turnpikes on the Roads which communicate with the said Streets, and the Inhabitants thereof were enabled to make Rates on themselves, the said Streets might be properly paved, watched, lighted, and cleansed.
