Mr. Edmonfone reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, appointed by an Act, pafiTed in the Twenty-sixth Year of his late Majesty, for repairing several Roads leading to the City of Glasgow, thereunto subscribing; and also the Peti-tition of the Merchants and Traders in the City of Glasgow, and its Neighbourhood, subscribing; and also the Petition of Merchams and Traders of the Town of Dumbarton, and its Neighbourhood, subscribing; and also the Petition of the Merchants and Traders in the Town oi Renfrew, and its Neighbourhood, subscrib-

ing; and also the Petition of the Merchants and Traders in the Town of Paisley, and its Neighbourhood, subscribing; were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, the said Act was read, whereby it appears, That the Trustees therein named were impowered to repair, among others, the Road leading from the City of Glasgow, to Luggie Water, and from thence to the Town of Cumbernauld, and Redburn Bridge; and also the High Road lead-

Voi.. 30.

I ig from Inchbelly Bridge, through the Town of Kirkintilloch, to the City of Glasgow: And,

Mr. Samuel Garbet, being examined, said, That a great deal of Work has been done upon the said Road leading from Glasgow to Redburn Bridge, but that it is found impracticable to carry on the further Repairs of the said Road, so as to answer the good Purposes intended by the said Act, on account of the^many steep Hills, which renders it impracticable for Carriages, even if the Road was in good Repair; that if Power was given to carry the Road on the North Side of Garngadhill, South Side of Germifiorenhilt, by Provan Mill, North Side of Hogganfidd Hill, and from thence, in the old Direction, to the East End of Gamkirks Inclostires; from thence to BeertIsland Bridge; and from thence to or near BadenHeath Cafle-, from thence to Wefier Air dice \ from thence to Mainhead; and from thence to or near Redburn Bridge; it would open an easy Communication between the Two Seas, whereby the Carriage of Goods would be rendered less expensive, and would be of great Advantage to the Commercial Interests of Great Britain in general, and tso that Part of the Country in particular, to the Amount of several thousand Pounds a Year.

Then the said Witness produced a Letter from several Gentlemen of Glasgow, approving of the Application to Parliament, for the intended Alteration, and determining the old Road to be impracticable.

And he further laid. That if the Term and Powers of the said Act were enlarged with respect to both the before-mentioned Districts of Roads, and Power given to turn the Road as aforesaid, the Creditors under the former Act would be better secured than at present.

Mr. Charles Gascoigne, being examined, confirmed the aforegoing Evidence; and added, That there are several Hills upon the old Road leading from to Redburn

Bridge, which rife one Foot in Six for One hundred Yards together; and that Carriages from Eighteen to Twenty hundred Weight, drawn by Two Horsesupon a common Read, could not be drawn up those Hills with the same Number of Horles with more than Seven hundred and an half Weight.

That there is not a Hill upon the intended Road that riles more than one Foot in Twenty, and that Two Horses might draw Eighteen or Twenty hundred Weight upon any Part of it.

That the Price of Carriage is at present One Shilling a Hundred, but, upon the intended Road, would be carried for. Nine Pence; and that the Witness would give Security to carry for Nine Pence a hundred Weight all the Y’ear round; and that, upon the whole, he apprehends there would be a Saving in the Price of Carriage of upwards of Three thousand Pounds a Year, according to the Quantity of Goods now carried; and would be a Means of a much greater Quantity coming into the Country, if they could go by that Road; that, in the new Line of Road, a Bridge of One Arch only will, be necessary over Luggie Water, which will not cost above Three hundred Pounds; whereas to make a fulfi-cient Bridge over the same Water in the present Lire of Road, would cost one thousand Six hundred Pounds; of which an Estimate has been made by Order of the Court of Session, and given in upon Oath.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, to enlarge the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Twenty-sixth Year of King George the Second, for repairing several Roads leading into the City of Glasgow, so far as the same relates to the Districts of Roads, from Inchbelly Bridge to Glasgow, and from Glasgow to Luggie Water, Cumbernauld, and Redburn Bridge; and for altering the Course of the last mentioned District of Roadj And that Mr. Edmonfone, Mr. Butler, Lord Frederick Campbell, the Lord Advocate of Scotland, and Mr. Wed-derburn, do prepare, and bring in, the feme.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, Mr. Robert Dewsbury, being examined, said, That he is acquainted with the Coal Trade, at Neivcaflle and -land; that it is my extensive; that many Inconveniences arile to the.Trade from the Methods now used by the Coal Fitters at those Ports, by frequently refilling Loadings to Masters of Ships who apply for the fame, and from other Proceedings of such Fitters; and the Witness apprehends, that many of the Inconveniences which the Masters of Ships ate liable to would be prevented, if the Persons employed as Fitters in the Coal Trade at the said Ports were obliged to keep public Lifts in their Offices of all Ships applying, for Loadings;- and alto to load all such Ships as shall be entered in their due Course; and that Masters of Ships should be obliged to load with the Fitters in whose Office they shall enter and fix.

Mr. William Chapman, being examined, said. That he has been present when Coal Fitters at Sunderland refuted to load Ships that offered, saying, they must give the Preference to their Friends; and that the Ships they gave the Preference to were then at London-, and that he has known the Master of a small Ship from Plymouth apply to several Fitters at Sunderland for a Loading, which being refused him, he was obliged to go to Newcastle.

and that the Justices for the County of Lanerk, on the Sixth of November 1761, had reverted the Order of the Trustees, and ordained the Turnpike Road to be carried through that County in the perfect Direction, to Luggie Water but the Justices of the County of Dumbarton, on the Second of March 1762, affirmed the Sentence, or Order, of the Trustees appealed from; A Petition of several Nobleman, Gentlemen, and others, residing at Richmond and Kew, in the County of Surrey, and of several Freeholders and others, possessed of Estates there, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Highway, from the late Horse Ferry at Kew, to Richmond, was over Kew Green, and through Kew Lane; that the late Queen

Caroline, about the Year 1731, caused the Hoad from the said Horse Ferry, to the End of a Lane, on the West Side of the Royal Garden, to be made a convenient Carriage Way, and after such Carriage Way was made, it was occasionally used by Passengers from the said Ferry to Richmond; that a Bridge hath been lately built near the lower Ferry at Kew, and a new Road made over the Green to Kew-Lane, which is now the common Highway from Kew to Richmond, and consequently the Carriage Way made by her late Majesty is useless; that Kew-Lane is much out of Repair, and in some Parts narrow j and that the Petitioners have reason to believe the King’s Most Excellent Majesty will be pleased, at His own Expence, to cause the said Lane to be amended, and made commodious for Passengers and Carriages, and the Road from the said Bridge to Richmond to be kept in good Repair for the future, in case the Carriage Way, from the late Horse Ferry, to the End of the Lane on the West Side of the Royal Gardens, and also the Carriage and Foot-way, from the End of the said Lane to Richmond Green, shall be respectively (hut up, and discontinued; thjtf a Bill is now depending in the House, for the Relief and Employment of the Poor, and for repairing the Highways, paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching the Streets, and other Places, in the Town and Parish of Richmond, in the County of Surrey; and that as the amending, and keeping in Repair, the Road from Kew to,

A Petition of several Gentlemen and others, Inhabitants of the Town of Richmond., in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That a Bill is depending in the House for the Relief and Employment of the Poor, and for repairing the Highways, paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching, the Streets and other Places in the Town and Parish of Richmond, in the County of Surrey; that it would greatly conduce to the Benefit and Convenience of the Petitioners, and all Persons residing in or referring to the said Town, if the Trustees to be named in the said Bill were authorized and impowered to take away all Posts, and to remove all Obstructions, Incroachments, and Annoyances# in the said Streets and other Places, and to prevent the like for the future; and also, if the Owners of Houses, and other Buildings, in the principal and most frequented Parts of the Town, were obliged to cause the V\ ater to be conveyed by proper Pipes, from the Roofs of their Houses, and other Buildings, down the Sides thereof, into the Streets, or the Grounds or Lands belonging to the Owners thereof: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the said Bill for the Purposes aforesaid; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the last preceding Petition is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Message from the Lords, by. Mr. Montagu and Mr. Cuddon:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for punishing Mutiny and Desertion, and for the better Payment of the Army and their Quarters, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing the Common Fields, Common Pastures, Common Meadows Common Grounds, and Waste Grounds, of and in the Manor and Parish of Then-ford, otherwise Feuford, in the County of Northampton, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting Part of the Fee Simple Estate of George late Lord Viscount Midleton, of the Kingdom of Ireland, in Trustees to be sold for paying the Debts, Legacies, and Incumbrances, mentioned in, and appointed to be paid by, his Will; and for executing and effectuating several Contrafts entered into by him for felling and leafing divers Farms and Lands in; and for making

the Exemplification of his Will Evidence in Law and Equity; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

SIR Robert Ladbroke Reported from the Committee, to AUhallowr whom the Petition of several, of the Trustees appoint; 011Wall ed to put in execution an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for rebuilding the Parish Church of Allhallows on the Wall, in the City of London, and for rebuilding the House belonging to the Rector of the said Parish, and for purchasing several Pieces of Ground and Tenements thereon, to renefer the Passages to and from the said Church and House more commodious, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was. referred.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the feme was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the fai<L Act was read, whereby the Trustees are impowered tq borrow a Sum of Money, not exceeding .4,000.

Mr. William Deyongh, Clerk to the said Trustees, produced an Account, whereby it appeared, that the said Trustees had borrowed the said Sum of £. 4,000, and had paid. or contrafted to pay, the Sum of £.4,062. 5J. for rebuilding the said Church and Rector’s House only; apd that the other Works necessary fox making commodious Ways, and carrying the other Purposes of the said Act into execution, are estimated at £.415. 19*

And, being examined, he said, That great Progress ha* been made in repairing the said Church, which is already nearly completed; but that it will not be possible to carrythe said Act into execution, without the furtbej Assistance of Parliament; the present Rate being insufficient for that Purpose.

Mr. George Dance, Surveyor, being examined, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Deyongh.

Owners, and Coal Fitter?, of the said River, Port, and Haven, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by several Acts of Parliament, the Petiti-tioners, and all other Coal Owners of the River Wear, are liable to pay Three Half-pence for every Chalder of Coals and Cinders brought to the Harbour of Sunderland, and the Coal Fitters and Factors One Halfpenny for every such Chalder, for the Preservation and Improvement of the Port and Harbour of and making

the River Wear navigable; and that the Petitioners observe, from the Votes, that Leave has been given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Duty of One Farthing per Chalder on Coals, granted by former Acts of Parliament, for improving and repairing the Piers and Harbour of Whitby, in the County of , and for the better regulating the Shipping the re; and representing, that the further Continuance of the said Duty of One Farthing per Chalder upon all Coals shipped at the Port of Sunderland, will be a heavy Charge upon the same Port, and tend to the Discouragement of Trade there; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if the said Bill (liould pass into a Law, it will greatly affect the Trade and Property of the Petitioners, and many others: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the said Bill; and that the House will give them such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

It appears by an Account from the Custom House referred to your Committee, that the Quantity of Foreign manufactured Leather Gloves and Mitts, which have been seized in the lad Seven Years, have greatly increased; it appearing by the said Account, that the Quantity seized in One thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-eight, was Two hundred and Seventy-three Dozen and Eight Pair; and in the Year 1764, One thousand Six hundred and Sixty-eight Dozen and Seven Pair;

that in the last Year, there was only Five hundred and Sixty-two Dozen and Eight Pair -, but your Committee apprehends the reason of the Difference in the last Year to be owing to the Application made to Parliament by the Trade in the last Session, which deterred the French from venturing so many as they otherwise would have done.

That by another Account from the Custom House,' referred to your Committee, it appears that the Quantity of Foreign manufactured Leather Gloves and Mittens imported into England for the last Seven Years, and which have paid Duty, amounts only to One hundred and Twenty-three Dozen and One Pair, the Duty of which is £.39. 5s. 3 \d.

Then Mr. George Jennings, a Glove Manufacturer, informed your Committee, that, of late Years, great Quantities of Gloves have been clandestinely brought into this Kingdom, by which Means the Trade is greatly decreased; that he has not Employ for a Fourth Part of the Hands as he had formerly; that the Revenue is likewise affected thereby, in proportion to the Number of Gloves smuggled in; and that if the Importation of Foreign Manufactured Gloves and Mitts was prohibited, the Skins, of which such Gloves ate made, would be imported into this Kingdom, in order -to be manufactured here.

Mr. John Pitt, a Glove Manufacturer, confirmed the aforegoing Evidence.

Mr. James Knowles, a Leather Dresser, being examined, said, That formerly he has imported large Quantities of Skins, but that now he cannot get them, owing not only to the French manufacturing their own Kid and Lamb Skins, but to their buying up others at Foreign Markets; and that the Witness was prevented by that Means of having Forty thousand Slans from one House in Italy last Year, which the French bought up for their own Use,

Mr. Robert Perry, a Leather Dresser, confirmed the last Evidence, with respect to the Decline of the Trade, and gave the same Reasons; and added, That he does not employ a Third Part of the Hands he did formerly. 1

Mr. Richard Griffith, a Glove Seller, said, That great Quantities of Gloves are clandestinely brought into this Kingdom, and whenever they are seized, are sold at the Custom House with certain Stamps; and that, under cover of such Gloves so fold and damped at the Custom House, great Quantities of Foreign manufactured Leather Gloves that have been fmUggled into this Kingdom, and escaped Seizure, are daily vended and fold; to the great Distress and Blin of our own Manufacturers.

To prove the Allegations of the fourth mentioned Petition, Mr. Samuel Short, being examined, said. That he has lived near Walsall Sixty Years, and has kept a Waggon Ten Years; that lie never apprehended any Danger in the said Streets, and has drawn Three Ton up High Street at. all Times of the Year; that the nar-roweft Part of Rushall Street is Six Yards wide or near it; and has seen Two Broad Wheel Waggons pass each other within a Month part; that the Turning from High Street into Rtifiall Street is not very steep, and Two Broad Wheel Waggons may pass there; and that he never saw any Obstruction: That there is a Street in Birmingham much steeper, and not so broad.

That he don’t know whether making the proposed Road would hurt the Town; but if Waggons should go the new Road, it will he a great Inconvenience to Tradesmen to carry their Goods to them, as the}’ are now taken up at their Doors.

are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and ’

other Inhabitants, within the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That under the Powers of an Act passed in the Tenth Year of Queen Anne, for building Fifty, new Churches in and about Ixnulon and Westmiijtcr, and the Suburbs thereof, the said Parish of Saint George the Martyr was taken out of that Part of Saint Andrews, Ho, which lies in the County of Middlesex, called the Liberty of Saint Andrew, Holboum, above the Bars, and made a distinct

Parish, to all Intents and Purposes, except as touching Church Rates, the Relief of the Poor, and Rates for the Highways; that, in pursuance of a Special Provision in the said Act, a perpetual Division of the Church Rates between the said Two Parish es, was duly made, by Instrument in Writing for that Purpose, as the said Act directs; and that the Choice of Overseers of the Poor, Surveyors of the Highways, and Scavengers, and the Management of those Affairs, remain jointly in the Inhabitants of the said Liberty, including the said Parish of Saint George; but the Inhabitants of the said Liberty, exclusive of the said Parish of George, are more numerous than the Inhabitants of the said Parish, andconl’equently have the ablblute Power in the Election of Officers, and Management of the Affairs, which jointly concern the said Liberty, and Parish of Saint George the Martyr; and that the Assessment of these Rates are so absolutely in the Power of the Inhabitants of Saint Andrews, , that those of Saint George the Martyr can in no wife avoid, or controul them, although ever so unreasonable, whereby the Petitioners have long been, and continue to be, excessively over-rated, beyond their Proportion of the said Rates, to the great Grievance of the Petitioners; and that it would he greatly to the Ease, Ad-, vantage, and Convenience of the Petitioners, and all the Parishioners of the said Parish of Saint George the Martyr, was that Parish wholly separated, and made a distinct Parish from the said Parish of Saint Andrew, llol-bourn, as well in respect of the said Rates for Relief of the Poor, and for the Highways, as the same now is in all other Respects; and that the Petitioners observing, by the Votes of the House, that Application has been made by the Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint drew, Holboum, above the Bars, and others, for a Bill touching the Nightly Watch, and for cleansing and enlightening the Streets, and for providing a more suitable and competent Maintenance and Support for the Poor, by consolidating the Rates of the same into One joint Fund; Arid therefore praying, that Provision may be made in the said Bill, for making the said Parish of Saint George the Martyr a separate and distinct Parish from that of Saint Andrew, Holboum, as well in respect to the Rates for the Poor, Highways, and Scavengers, as all other Respects whatsoever, in such Manner

'J'hat the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Agent for the Petitioners produced to your Committee, Copy of Letters Patent of the 25 th of October, 27 Car. 2. granting to JudinianAngel, his Heirs and Assigns, certain Duties on Shipping passing by a Light House erected by the said JuJ/inAngel, at the Spurn Point, near the Mouth of the Humber, 1'ubject to the Payment of a yearly Rent of Five Pounds; ami providing, that if at any ’l ime it should appear to His Majesty, His Heirs, or Succefi’ors, that the said Grant was inconvenient for the Public; that then, he or they, by Signification or Declaration, under their Signet nr Privy Seal, of such Prejudice or Inconvenience, the said Tetters Patent were to be void and determine.

And the Copy of other Letters Patent of the 14th Day of June, in the 30th Year of the Reign of his said l&te Majesty Ring Charles the Second, for granting an additional Duty te the said JuJUnian Angel, his Heirs Vol. 30.

and Assigns, for the Purposes aforesaid, subject to a Humber Rent of Five Pounds per Annuih.Light House*

Then there was produced to yonr Committee, a Spurn point. Lease and Release, dated the 10th and 1 ith of 1692; whereby it appeared, That Edzcard the Petitioner’s Great Grandfather, purchased Cue Fourth Part of the Land of the said Jujiin Angel,

whereon the said Light Houses were erected, and of the Duties arising therefrom.

Then the original Will of Edward Thompson, Esquire, the Petitioner’s Uncle, was produced, and read; whereby it appeared, that he devised his Interest in the said Land and Light Houses to the Petitioner $ and Mr. Leuyns Baldero said. That he had received the Rents and Profits of the Premises for the Use of the Petitioner: Then,

Mr. William Hammond produced to your Committee,

Two Surveys of the Entrance of the Humber, one made in the Year 1674, and the other by Captain Mitchell, aS it is at present; by which Surveys it appeared, that Part of the Ground near the Spurn Point had been wralhed away, and other Ground thrown up, so that the Point of the Spurn now lies at a considerable Distance from the said Light House: And, being examined, he said, That the Situation of the present Lights is very inconvenient , for Navigation, and frequently occasions the Loss of Shipping, which is become much more frequent of late Years; that the Witness saw Three Wrecks of Ships in October 1764, which Were owing to the Situation of the Lights; and that he believes 40 or 50 Ships have been loftfihce the Year 1741, from the same Reason: That Shipwrecks have increased considerably of late Years $ and that sometimes you cannot get into the lower Light House for Two or T hree Hours, as the Wind and Tide happens; and that the Sea, in high Winds and Tides, sometimes comes up to the higher Light House; and that the late Keeper of the Li^ht House said, he durst not stay in the Tower in a high Gale of Wind; that the Danger is not- confined to Vessels employed in the Humber, but to Coasting Vessels, Which in bad Weather dare not come in, on account of the bad Situation of the Lights, which, if properly placed, they might easily and safely do; and that the Witness himself, going up the Ilumber in Company with another Ship, in a dark blowing Night, was confounded, and could not tell whether he was on the Bull Sand or on the Point, because he could Hot discover at whatDistance the Lights were; and that the other Ship was wrecked the same Night; and that this Danger and Loss would have been prevented, if the Lights had been properly placed.

Captain Robert Mitchell, late Commander of the King’s

Ctrftoin House Sloops on the Ilumber Station, confirmed the Evidence given by the last Witness; and added, that the present Distance from the higher Light House to the lower one, is so short, that they are of very little, if any. Service to Vessels entering the Ilumber: That he has known several Vessels loft upon the Pitch of the Point, and the Crews of several of them drowned; and such of the Crews as were saved, said, that the Loss of their Vessels was owing to the ill Situation of the Lights; that he has known 14 or 16 Ships loft within thele 13 Years- and that the Point is increased about a Quarter of a Mile filled the Witness knew it; and that the Lights are at such a Distance, that Ships frequently run on the Point, when they think they are to the Southward.

That there are safe Roads in the Humber when the Wind blows a,t East, North Ealt, and South East, which aredaugerons Windson the Coast; and that it would be a great Advantage, nbt only to the Coasting Trade, but to the Baltic Ships, if the coming in were safe; for a Ship that draws 14 Feet Water has no other Place but the Ilumber to put into; and they arc obliged toftayout at Sea from the Defeat of the Lights: That the Mailers of Colliers have told him this has frequently been the Cafe; and that the Witness himself who knows the Place ag well as any one, has been obliged to do so; but that " £ G ’ if

Humber if the tights were placed on the Points, it would be Light Houset safe coming in; that Two Ships were loft last Year, the Spurn Joint. Crew of one of which all perished; and the Malier of the other made Affidavit, that his Loss was owing to the Situation of the Spurn Lights: Then,

A Member present informed your Committee, That he is well acquainted with the Navigation; that there is no Harbour from the of Forth to the Humber, for that Ships dare not take Tinmouth Bar if the Wind is at North, N. N. tail, or East; that Ships would often take Shelter in the Humberto avoid going over the Deeps; but that the Lights in their present Situation are a mere I , and no Master or Pilot can go in with Safety; that this has been the Complaint of the Trade several Years; and that himself had often gone into the Humber at a very great Ritk.

Mr. Charles Wildbore, chief Clerk to the Trinity House, laid, That he had frequently attended at Mr. Angel's before the Petition had been presented to His Majesty, but could never get Access to him; and that he did not remember that Mr. Angel's Agent ever applied to the Trinity House for Directions, where the lower Light should be set up; and that several Complaints have been made from the several Trinity at Hull and A Tewcajtlefor Removal of the Lights.

Then a Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants of the Corporation of the Trinity House of Deptford Strand, to His Majesty, was read; whereby it appeared, that the said Master, Wardens, and Assistants, did, on or about the Month of February 1765, present a Petition to H is Majesty to make the said Letters Patent void.

'Then the Reference of the said Petition to the Attorney and Solicitor General, was read, and like wife their Report thereupon; whereby it appeared, that they were of Opinion, that the material Facts alleged in the Petition were well founded, and were a sufficient Ground to warrant the Proceeding to revoke the Letters Paten!; but, for the Reasons given in the said Report, thought it advisable to suspend, for a Time, the vacating the said Letters Patent, that the Patentees might have an Opportunity of authorizing the Trinity House, at the Expence of the Patentees, to take down the present Light Houses and erect others; and if the Patentees should refuse to consent, that it seemed advisable that the speediest Means the Law would allow, should be used to vacate the said Letters Patent.

Then the Agent for the Petitioner produced to your Committee, aProposal of the Petitioner to the Trinity House, for contributing his Proportion of the Expence of taking down the present, and.erecting new Light Houses under the Direction of the said Corporation, and keeping and preferring the Lights, as the said Corporation should think proper: And,

Mr. Wildbore said. That he had frequently attended at Air. Angel's since the said Report was made, but could never be admitted to fee him: That he had indeed written several Letters to the Trinity House, but they were all argumentative and evasive.

Then a Second Petition presented to His Majesty, to the same Purpose of the former, with the original Reference to the Attorney and Solicitor General, were read.

to the Country in general, by reducing the Price of Carriage Three Parts in Four at leati.

Mr. James Perry, being examined, said, That the making such Canal will be attended with great Advantages to the several Iron Manufactories, and be of -great Benefit to the several Coal and Lime Works, by reducing the Price of Carriage; — that the Price of Carriage at present is Eight Shillings per Ton for Ten ’ Miles, and the Price upon the intended Canal will be about One Shilling and Nine Pence.

That a great Majority of the Owners of Lands; through which the Canal is to go, have already consented; and that the making such Canal will be of great Utility to the Country, and the Public in general.

Mr. John Baker, being examined, confirmed Mr. Perry’s Evidence, and added, That, by Means of this VoL. 30.

Canal, a Communication will be opened between the Ports of Bristol, Hull, and Liverpool, and to the Town of Manchester; — and both the Witnesses said, That the said Canal will be of great Advantage to the Iron Works upon the River Slowr, as they will get their Materials at a cheaper Rate, and that the Water will not be decreased, but, on the contrary, they will have an Addition of Water to their Works.

A Petition of the Magistrates, Merchants, Heritors, and Inhabitants, of the Town of Kirkintilloch, in the County of Dumbarton, thereunto subscribed, was also prefen ted to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the high Road leading from Inchbelly Bridge, to the City of Glasgow, has been, for Time immemorial, the Post Road betwixt the Cities of Edinburgh and Glasgozc and is the only convenient Road for marching of His Majesty’s Troops betwixt those two Cities; that the moil Part of the said Turnpike Road is already made, and in good Repair, excepting in the Neighbourhood of the City of Glasgow, where it is broke with the Carriages loaded with Dung and Stones, which pass the Bar free of Toll; and that, in case the Bill, as petitioned for, pass into a Law, not only the Road from Inchbelly Bridge, to Glasgozc, which has been made at great Expence, will be of little or no Use to the Public, but alfe the greatest Part of the Road, where the same is made, which leads from the Town of Cumbernauld, through the County of Dumbarton, to LuggieWater, and from thence through the County of Lanark, and joins the Post Road in the Neighbourhood of the City of Glasgow, will also be loft, and of no Use to the Public: And therefore praying, That the House may allow them to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill; and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Nlr.Plumptre reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the principal Hosiers, and Manufacturers of Framework-knitting Goods, residing in the Town of Nottingham, on behalf of themselves, and all others concerned in the said Trade, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Vol. 30.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. If rad Ellington, a Hosier in London, being examined, said, That great Frauds are committed in marking of Stockings and Pieces, and other Framework-knit Goods; and that Two-Thread Goods are frequently marked as Three Threads, and Three Threads as Four Threads; and he produced a Pair of Stockings, which he bought as he came to attend the Committee, marked as Four-Thread Stockings, which, upon being exa-. rained, appeared to your Committee to be only Three Threads; and the Witness said, it was a common Practice for some Manufacturers to mark their Goods in this fraudulent Manner, by which Practice they undersell the fair Trader.

Mr. Charles Tyrrell, also a Hosier in London, being examined, confirmed Mr. Ellington’s Evidence; and added. That his Customers had frequently complained that he did not serve them so cheap as some other Persons could do, and hadlhewn him the Goods they had bought as Three Threads, and some as Four Threads, both which were only Two Threads; and that he had cut the Goods before their Faces, and shewn them the Fraud.

That there are very great Frauds practised in marking of Pieces of Framework-knit Goods; and that by marking them falsely the Makers fell them at a much higher Price than they would fell for if they were truly marked.

And the Witness said. That great Complaints have been made from abroad of the Practice of false marking of Goods, which Practice discredits the Manufacture of this Country.

That an Order was offered to a Manufacturer for a large Parcel of Goods to be falsely marked, which he refused to comply with; but the Offer was accepted by another Person, and he had an additional Price for marking his Goods with false Marks.

And the Witness said, that some of the most considerable Manufacturers in Town make use of this Method ®f false marking their Goods.

Mr. Thomas Waller, a Hosier in London, confirmed Mr. Tyrrell's Evidence as to the Frauds committed in marking Framework-knit Goods.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the fraudulent Marking of Framework-knitted Manufactures: And that Mr. Colonel

Howe, Mr. Hewett, and Mr. Willoughby, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, in or near the Parish of Kingston vpoji Thames, in the County of Surrey, and the Neighbourhood thereof, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is depending in the House, for enlarging the Term and Powers of several Acts, for repairing several Roads, from the Stones End, in the Borough of Southwark, to several Places in the Comities of Surrey and Suffer, and for enlightening the said Roads, and establishing a regular and nightly Watch thereupon, to a certain Distance from the said Borough of Southwark, and for repairing the Road from Smitham Bottom, to the End of Wooley Lane, and from Wandsworth, through Garratt, to Tooting; and that the Roads from the Robin Hood to Kingston, are so deep and sandy in many Places, and the Hill so deep, that it is not only very inconvenient for Travellers, but a great Injury to the Turnpike, as many Carriages avoid that Road on that Account; and that the Petit ioners apprehend Putney Heath and Gallozvs Hill, to be the most dangerous Part of the Road from London to Kingston, in respect to robbing; yet, by the Bill now under Consideration, that Part of the Road is not to be watched or lighted; and that, by watching and lighting only Six Miles of that Road, it will be a means of driving the Robbers to Putney Heath and Gallows Hill, whereby the Inhabilants of Kingston and the Neighbourhood of that Town will be in continual Danger in travelling to and from London; and that the Petitioners therefore hope, the House will prevent so much of the said Bill, now depending, taking E(Ted, as relates to watching and lighting any Part of the said Road, unless the same is extended as far as Kingston.

A Petition of the Coal Fitters, and Owners or Masters of Ships, belonging to the Port of Sunderland, near the Sea, in the County of Durham, also of the principal Merchants and Inhabitants of the said Port, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill is ordered to be brought in, to regulate the Loading of Ships with Coals, in the Ports of Newcastle and Sunderland; and alleging, that there is no Oeca-fion for the Provisions of the Bill with respect to Sunderland, Coal Ships having at all Times been regularly loaded there in Turn; and that any Law, which may be made for altering the present Method of carrying on the Coal Trade of Sunderland, will be attended with many Inconveniences, and cannot, as the Petitioners apprehend, be fully complied with by them: And therefore praying. That, in case any new Law should be made to alter the present Method of carrying on the Coal Trade, the same may not extend to Sunderland; but that the Coal Trade there may be carried on in the same Manner as it now is; and, in case such a Bill should be brought in, that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the said Bill, so far as it relates to the Port of Sunderland, or have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill to regulate the Loading of Ships with Coals, in the Ports of Newcastle and Sunderland, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their laid Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that tliev do admit Counsel to be heard, at tIn-same Time, iu Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, in support of the said Bill, and that the same may pass -into a Law.

It appeared to your Committee, by the Evidence of Mr. John Sabatier,a Silk Weaver, in Spitlal Fields',

That the Importation of French and Wrought

Silks had for many Years been a great Discouragenient to the British Silk Manufacture: and that greaterQuan-tities of loch Foreign Silks hav e been lately imported than heretofore.

That great Numbers of Silk Weavers are now out of Employment; and that the Witness liimself has now several Looms unemployed: — That tali Summer, upon a Promise of the Mercers not to import any Foreign Silks, he had set several Looms to work, which he had since been forced to lay down.

That the Quantity of Goods which he used to manufacture for the Spring Trade, which were plain Silks, is much deereased, and the Manufacture, which employs many thousand Hands, will fall to decay without some Relief from Parliament.

That lad May he employed 70 Men, and the Year before about 80; and now lie employs only 48: That during the late War the Silk Trade was very brilk, and fmee the Peace it has declined very much; which he attributes to the Importation of Foreign Silks: — That the late Mourning may have affected the Silk Manufacture, though, about a Week before the Death oft lie Duke of Cumber land, the Witnessturnedoffabout ThirtyMen;

And by an Account from the Custom House, referred to your Committee, it appeared, that the Importation of Italian Silks in the last Year, amounted to lb. 18,709 f, and of French, lb. 1,559 i-

Then to shew, that a total Prohibition of Foreign Wrought Silks would encourage the Manufacture more than a high Duty, and would be more agreeable to the Mercers in general; the Agent called,

Mr. John Harris, a Mercer, who said, that he apprehends an absolute Prohibition of the Importation of Foreign Wrought Silks to be more eligible for the Trade, than an additional Duty: That if a Prohibition was to take Place, he thinks it would encourage the Manufacturers to increase their Trade, but while the Importation is allowed, the Masters are afraid to manufacture a Quantity, being uncertain what Orders may be sent abroad: That this would certainly improve the Manufacture, be a Saving to the Nation of the Money now annually sent abroad, and be advantageous to the Mercers in general, for that the great Houses only import, and all Persons flock to them, and totally neglect the small Houses.

That he thinks, in same of a Prohibition, it would be more easy to distinguish smuggled Goods, as we should then have more Pattern Drawers of our own, whose Work we should easily know from the Foreigners.-

That he thinks a Prohibition never could produce a Monopoly, but quite the reverse, as the Number of Weavers is so great; and being asked the Questiorf, he said. That he never heard of any Attempt to advance the Price of Silk amongst the Weavers during the Time the Bill was depending in Parliament last Year.

That a Prohibition is a much more effectual Method to prevent Smuggling than a high Duty; for if the Importation is allowed, an Ell of Silk is brought from abroad and stamped, and then whole Pieces of the same Pattern may be run in and fold, as if the Duty had been paid; for the Ell is rolled in with a Piece, and then the whole Piece appears to have a Stamp to it.

That an absolute Prohibition would be more agreeable to the Witness, and he believes to the Mercers in general, than a high Duty; for by that Means they should set out with fresh Patterns, and get Possession of the Trade before the French could serve their Cuf-tomers; and that we have better Patterns than he ever saw come from abroad, and they would still be improved by Encouragement.

That Orders have been sent to Italy for Lutestrings to be made of the same Breadth of our own, in order to make them pass for in which they have so

That His Majesty also pays Salaries to some head Workmen, and also advances great Sums of Money to the Weavers, wit hout Interest, to enable them to carry on their Manufactures.

And being asked, how he came to the Knowledge of the several FaClshe had mentioned relating to the Silk Manufacture at Berlin ? he said. He was told so by Mr. GolzkonJbj and several other Gentlemen then employed in the Manufacture, and that he believed it to be true.

That the Importation of Foreign Silks at Berlin is prohibited, and that before the Prohibition took place, there, the Witness used to import Silks to Berlin but since that Time he has not sent One Piece there.

Then Mr. Abraham Ogier, a Master Weaver, said. That he used to fend great Quantities of Silk to Berlin, but that since the Prohibition took Place he had had no Orders; and upon hisafking the Reasons, he had beep told by the Persons he used to serve, that the Importation cff Silks were prohibited, and they could give no more Orders.

APPENDIX, N®. III.

EDICT concerning the Importation and Stamping the Light Woollen Goods or Stuffs, and other Foreign

Manufactures allowed to be imported.

Done at Florence, Anno 1745.

EDICT.

\IjT WHEREAS we the Royal Council of Finances, in pursuance of the Edict of the 27th January, g \ Christi 1738, relating to the Light Woollen Goods and other Foreign Manufactures allowed to be imported, have examined the Plan of Regulation delivered by the Deputies of the Art of Wool of this City of Florence, and likewise have examined the Representations made by the Fanner General, in behalf of the Custom House: Therefore to remove all Difficulties arising daily fresh the Importation of the aforesaid allowed Goods, as well by reason of the Inspection of said Goods, as by reason of the Taxes and Duties which they are liable to pay; and for to prevent the Royal Treasury being defrauded, and the Merchants and other Persons being aggrieved, we do publicly proclaim and notify as follows;

ift. That in the general Prohibition of Foreign Cloths, ordered by the aforesaid Edict, there are to be understood as prohibited, likewise all Sorts of Goods which are also manufactured in these happy States, agreeable to the Lift thereof!pecified at the End of this Edict, declaring. That all Foreign Goods, not mentioned in said Lift ('till new Order to the contrary) shall be allowed to be imported, as likewise the fiiperfine and fine Says, and Bosley Says of what Sort soever, the Camel itan natural Says, the Bergamo grey Says, because, though the aforesaid Sorts of Goods, in some Measure, are likewise manufactured in these States, as yet they turn inferior so thp r

ones in regard to Quality, and not sufficient in Quantity to answer our Home Confupxption.

Vol. 30.

e

728 14* Aprilis. A. 1766.

snk 2d. The Goods allowed to be imported by virtue of this present Declaration, may be freely imported, bought, Manufacture. ang worn through all these imppy Dominions, till the Importation offome Sort of them shall be prohibited by a special Order; as it may so happen that, in Process of Time, and by the Industry of the Manufacturers, a good and sufficient Manufactory of some Sort of said Goods might be settled in these Dominions.

3d. In order to prevent the Importation of prohibited Woollen Goods, under the Name and Sanction of light Woollen Goods and other Foreign'Manufactures allowed to be imported, it is necessary that a proper Inspection be made, and thereby to ascertain that said Goods are such as are allowed to be imported; and for this Effect they must be entered at any One of the following Custom. Houses; viz. Siena, , Monte

San Severino, Caliglipn, Fiorentina, Anghiary. It is hereby to be understood, that the Parties concerned shall be obliged to get a Certificate of said Goods at the First Custom House of the State.

4th. As soon as the aforesaid'Woollen Goods shall be entered at any One of the afore-recited Custom Houses, and there ascertained as allowed to be imported, they may be cleared out on paying the Duty at the Rate of 5 Sols per Pound Weight, for any Place whatsoever of these Dominions, no Matter whether said Goods have been imported from any Place whatsoever.

5th. After the aforesaid Duty being paid, every Piece of the afore-recited Goods shall be stamped at the Two head Ends of each Piece with a particular Stamp, such as shall be pointed out and directed by the Custom House of Florence to the other Custom Houses, so that One of the Stamps or Seals may remain always tied to the Piece, though in part disposed of.

6th. At the Time of being stamped or sealed, any Piece that shall be cleared out for the City of Florence, a Duty ought to be paid for each Piece at the Rate of Livres 2. 10. and for any other Piece 1.5.

7th. All the Woollen Goods allowed to be imported, if they had been previously imported and not stamped, shall be entered at any One of the aforementioned Custom Houses within the Term of Two Months, to commence from the Day of the Publication of this present Regulation at each respeti ive Place, in order that they may be there stamped; and this ought to take Place, not only in regard to the whole Pieces, but likewise for all Cuts and Remnants, as any One of them shall be stamped separately, and though One should in this same pay for the said Stamp or Seal the aforesaid Duty as it was practised in the Year 1694, when the Seal was first established in order to favour still further the Public Trade, the aforesaid Royal Council does order and command, that said Seal shall be affixt gratis, and without the Officers deputed thereto daring to take any Fees.

8th. But as the aforesaid Goods allowed to be imported, are necessarily liable to the Payment of the Duty; therefore those Persons that shall not be able to produce Vouchers of having paid the fame, shall be obliged, at the Time offtamping the Goods, to pay the Duty of 5 Sols per Pound Weight, let the Goods be imported from, or be cleared out for, any Place whatsoever; and in this same the General Farmer shall not infill on bein g pid the Difference and Deficiency, should any one have paid a lesser Duty than that now decreed.

9th. After the aforesaid Term of Two VI onths shall be elapsed, if any light Woollen Goods, or any other Foreign Manufactures allowed to be imported, shall be found in any Place of these happy Dominions, even if it should be a privileged Place (of which a special and distinct Mention should have been made) excepting yet the <City of Leghorn and the County of Lanaggiana; we say, if any whole Pieces should be found without, the Two Stamps or Seals, and any Remnant, let it be ever so small, without One Seal, they shall be deemed smuggled Goods, and as such to be forfeited, together with the Vessel and Carriage loaded and conveyed by, besides a pecuniary Fine, at the Discretion of the Judges, and agreeable to the Circumstances of the same and Quality of the Persons; the Fine to be applied to the Use prescribed by ihe Law.

10th. In each of the aforementioned Custom Houses, besides the usual Book of Seals, a Register. shall be kept, whereinihall be set down the Name, Surname, and Place of Habitation of the Owners of the light Woollen Goods, and other Foreign Manufactures allowed to be imported, the Quality, the Quantity, the Colour, and all other Specifications of each Piece and Remnant that shall have been stamped, in order that it may serve as a Check, in case that any Difference should arise concerning the Stamps or SeaJs, or the Payment of the aforesaid Duty.

nth. And to the end that the Privileges of the Fair of Pisa may not be infringed by the present Regulation, ’ nor the System altered, which is practised in that Custom House, in regard to the Merchandize that there enjoy the Benefit of the new Duty of Carriage, and in order that, under the Pretence of the aforesaid Privileges, no Frauds might be committed in Prejudice of the Tax and Duty, it is hereby enacted, that all Sorts of Woollen Goods allowed to be imported, shall be stamped with a particular Stamp or Seal, expressing the Words, Fair of Pisa, to be stamped gratis by the Custom House Officers; and even on the Supposition that the aforesaid Woollen Goods should be cleared out at the Time of the Fair for any other Place of these happy Dominions, ought, and shall pay the aforesaid Duty and Tax, and to the same shall be affixt the usual Seal, as if they had not been imported at the Time of the Fair.

12th. In regard to the aforesaid Woollen Goods, which at Pisa enjoy the Benefit of the new Duty of Carriage, they likew'ife, whenever they shall be cleared out at the Custom House, for to be conveyed to the Merchants Houses, shall be stamped, without paying any Charges, with a particular Seal, the WTords new Stallaggio, or new Duty of Carriage; — and in same the Merchants should be w'illing afterwards to clear out the said Goods, either for Pisa or any other Place of these Dominions, they shall be obliged to bring them anew to the Custom House, and there to pay the aforesaid Duty and Tax, and to have the usual Stamp affixed to the said Goods, in lieu of the former Stamp, which shall be taken off.

13th. Those Persons that shall be willing to get from Leghorn, either by Land or Water, the aforesaid Woollen Goods allowed to be imported, for to import them into whatsoever Place of these happy Dominions, ought indif-penfably to get a Certificate for the Custom House of Pisa (and no otherwise) and there they shall be obliged to enter them, and all those Stagemen, Boatfmen, and Carriers that shall be found travelling writh the Cockets of the Custom House of Leghorn, made against the Disposition of the present Order, shall be liable to those Penalties in Article the 9th of the present Regulation.

14th.Ifit should so happen that Woollen Goods allowed to be imported into the State of Siena, and there entered without the previous Payment of the aforesaid Duty and Tax, and damping of Goods, all the Clearings and Exportation of the aforesaid Woollen Goods, for any Place of the Slate of Siena (if it shall be requested) ought to be done at the Custom House of Siena; and in same the Owners of said Woollen Goods should be willing to clear them out, either for the said City, or for any other Place, as well of the said State of Siena, as that of , -they

shall pay at the aforesaid Custom House the said Duty and Tax, and get the prescribed Seal affixt to the Goods.

15th. All those Woollen Goods and the like, that shall be conveyed into these happy Dominions, for to be

N\ IV.

Translated from the Italian.

His Imperial Majesty being willing to provide for the Advantage and Benefit of the Silk Manufactures of his Great Duch/of Tuscany, by prohibiting the Exportation of Raw Silks out of these happy States: — Therefore, renewing, the Laws and Proclamations heretofore published for that Effect, doth order and command, That no Person of any Quality, Degree, or Denomination whatsoever, shall export out of this Great Duchy, Silk of any Sort whatsoever, as well raw as manufactured in Organzine or Tram, as well single as double, under the Penalty . t of forfeiting the Silk, or the just Value thereof, and as much more as the Value thereof, to be applied, Half to the Informer, either private or public, a Quarter Part to the Treasury, and the Remainder to the Magistrate or Judge who shall condemn the fame.

The present Order shall be inviolably observed in all the Limits of the Great Duchy, including the State of Siena, the City and Mountain of Pifioia, and generally every other Place whatsoever, although privileged, and of which individual and special Mention ought to have been made.

Done at Florence, the 22nd August 1749.

Mr. Benjamin Peach, being examined, said, That several Sums of Money had been advanced on the Credit of the 'Foils of the First District of the said Roads; and that upwards of £.2,000 is now owing on the Credit thereof; and that the Tolls of the said District are now let to Farm at the Annual Rent of £.221.

1 hat he had attended several Meetings of the Trustees for the Second District of the said Roads, particularly One in last June was Twelve Months; that it had been proposed, at the said Meetings, to erect Turnpikes, and carry the said Act into execution; but that this Proposal had been always over-ruled, and the Aftflill remains unexecuted in the said Second District, under Pretence that it is not possible to raise a sufficient Sum of Money, notwithstanding the Witness himself had oftered to lend £. 2,000 for that Purpose.

That when it has been proposed to erect Turnpikes, at any of the Meetings of the Trustees, the Proposal has always been carried in the Negative; and notwithstanding the Trustees have constantly met in June annually, for Six or Seven Years past, they have always adjourned for a Year, without doing any Business.

That the Roads in the Second District are in a very ruinous Condition; and lie never knew them worl'e than at present.

In support of the Second mentioned Petition, the same Witness said, That repairing the Roads in the Second District will be a great Advantage to the neighbouring Parts, and to the Public in general.

That the said Roads cannot be effectually repaired, and the present Debt discharged, in case the Two Districts should be consolidated, unless the Term and Po wers granted by the said Act, are further continued and enlarged.

And that the Witness applied to Samuel Salmon, the Clerk to the Trustees for the Second District, to attend the Committee, with his Books, 011 Monday last; but that he wrote him an Answer, that he was engaged, and could not attend.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That from and after the said 10th Day of October 1766, there shall be paid for every Window, or Light, in every Dwelling House, inhabited or to be inhabited, within the Kingdom of Great Britain, which shall contain Seven Windows, or Lights, and no more, the yearly Sum of Two Pence for each Window, or Light, in such House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That from and after the said 10th Day of October 1766, there shall be paid for every Window, or Light, in every such Dwelling House, which shall contain Eight Win-flows, or Lights, and no more, the yearly Sum of Sixpence for each Window, or Light, in such House.

ting forth, That the Trade to Africa, and the West Indies, is One of the moll considerable Branches of Commerce, carried on from this Kingdom; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, nothing could be more conducive to the farther Improvement of this advantageous Trade, and to the Support of an extensive Branch of Manufacture, which is at this Time in Danger of declining, from the want of Raw' Materials at a moderate Price, than the Opening of One or more Free Ports in British America, at such Place or Places, and under such Regulations, as may seem moll expedient.

A Petition of William Wright, of White Fryars, Lon- Escifej don, Distiller, whose Name is thereunto subscribed, was Duty* presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner now, and for Four Years pad, has car- *>ints' ried on the Trade of a Distiller and Rectifier of Spirits for Exportation; and that, by an Act of the Second Year of His present Majesty, for encouraging the Exportation of British made Spirits, it is provided, that, if any Distiller for Exportation, after he has deposited any Spirits, made for Exportation, in the Warehousos for the keeping his Spirits, shall be defrrous of using any such Spirit^ for Home Consumption, and shall signify such Desire to the Commissioners of Excise, it shall be lawful for them to direct the Spirits, so desired, to be taken out of such Warehouse, and delivered to such Distiller, on his Payment of the Duty; and that* notwithstanding the Petitioner hath, several Times, applied to the Commissioners of Excise for Liberty to take out a Quantity of such Spirits, they have objected to his said Request, under Pretence that Melasses Spirits were not included in such Provision, and that the Revenue would suffer thereby, although such Pretence was entirely without Foundation, and which the Petitioner explained to them, and which several of them, as also their Officers who were referred to, were then convinced of; and the Commissioners then informed the Petitioner that they w ould take the Attorney General’s Opinion on such Provision, and that the Petitioner

6 (Jeo. III. 240 Aprilis. ' 759

tioner should then have an Answer; in consequence of; which, the Petitioner made frequent Application to the

Sptiits. Solicitor for the Excise, for the Result of such Opinion, but he could never obtain Satisfaction whether the same was had, although he had great Reason to believe that it was very soon obtained, and was in his Favour; upon which he frequently renewed such Application to the Commissioners, but could never obtain any Answer, and thereupon took the Opinion of Two very eminent Counsel himself on such Point, who were both clearly of Opinion, that the said Provision extended to Melasses as well as Malt Spirits, and that he was entitled to such Benefit; upon which an Application was made, on his Behalf, to the present Chancellor of the Exchequer, that the Commissioners might be called upon for their Reason for such Refusal, which was done accordingly; and they, the Commissioners, in conference thereof, sent the Petitioner word, by their principal Officer, that he might renew his Application to the Commissioners; but they having, for fio long Time, refused to comply therewith, by which, to his great Detriment, he had loft the Sale of such Spirits, and having then no Occasion for them in the said Way, he gave the said Officer such Answer; but in some little lime afterwards, having a further Call, he again applied to the Commissioners, when he was directed to bring Proof that the said Spirits had been secured, from their first Distillation, according to Law, in an Exportation Ware-house; upon which he, having then very lately, by the Commissioners Di rest ions, and at the Expence of Two hundred Pounds, erected Warehouses under the foie Eye and Directions of such principal Officer, and in which the said Spirits were then secured, called upon the said Officer to make his Report thereof, who then, in the Petit ioner’s Presence, adored the Commissioners, that such Warehouses were the belt and most secure of any in Town, and that the Surveyor and Officer had each of them their Locks thereon; but that the Commissioners, as a further Pretence for not-complying with such Request, then asked, if the Petitioner had his own Lock, which the Law had provided merely for the Trader’s own Security, thereon, to which the said Officer answered, that as the Petitioner had a Lock upon his Distilling House, wherein were the said Warehouses, that he had thought that sufficient for his own Security, and therefore had not put such his own Lock on the said Warehouses; upo.n which they refused to grant his said Request; and One of them further told him, in a very rough Way, that he had incurred a Penalty of Five hundred Pounds on such Account, and the next Day sent him Notice to put on such Lock, which he accordingly did; and that, a few Days ago, he having made another Quantity of such Spirits, in every Re-spedt according to Law, under the Infoe&ion of the several Excise Officers who survey his House, and secured such Spirits in such Warehouses, under the Three Locks, as literally directed by the Act, and having Occasion for a Ton of such Spirits, he again applied for the fame, but such Request was notwithstanding, in like Manner as before, refused; and on asking them the Reason for such Refusal, they denied giving him any; and that inasmuch as, by the ordinary Course of Law, he is without Remedy to recover an adequate Satisfaction for the great Injury he has sustained from such repeated A<?ls of Oppression, and which, he is appre-hensive, will be continued, and which will be a Means of entirely putting a Stop to his Trade, he has been advised to lay such his Hardships before the House; whom be therefore entreats to grant him such Relief as they shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Sugar Refiners of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are unable-to contend with the French, in supplying Foreign Markets with refined Sugar, by reason of the High Prices of British Muscovado Sugars, in proportion to the Prices of French; and that the High Duties hn-posed on all Foreign Sugars, except Danish, imported into Great Britain, amount to a Prohibition; and that

the Petitioners are of Opinion, that, if the High Duties on Foreign Muscovado Sugars were reduced, it would tend to enable them to export Br Refined Sugars; And therefore praying, That the High Duties now payable on Foreign Muscovado Sugars, imported into Great Britain, may be. so reduced, as to enable Great Britain to share with France, in supplying Foreign Markets with refined Sugars.

A Petition of the Manufacturers, Dealers, and Con-fumers of Sugars, in the City of Bristol, was also pre-fented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Price of Muscovado Sugars is of late Years greatly increased, beyond the Price they usually bore in Time of Peace, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners and Loss of the Nation, in the Export of Refined Sugars: And therefore praying, That the Manufacture and Consumption of Foreign Muscovado Sugars, imported into this Kingdom from America, in British built Ships.navigated according to Law, may be allowed it»

Great Britain, under such Duties and Regulations, as to the House shall appear sufficient to prevent Frauds, and leave the British Planter in Possession of every reasonable Preference at the Home Market.'

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. George Box, Clerk to the said Commissioners, being examined, said, That it would tend to facilitate the Execution of the said Acts, if the same were consolidated, and the Powers thereof reduced into One Act of Parliament; and that some Alterations and Amendments are necessary to be made in the said Acts.

Mr. Box was likewise examined, in regard to the second-mentioned Petition, who said. That the Money raised for the Purposes of the said Acts is nearly expended, and that it is necessary to have some further Fund than the Commissioners have at present, to carry on the Works with the greater Expedition.

Sir Joseph Maxobey reported from the Committee, Com Trad*, appointed to consider of the State of the Corn Trade of this

6 Gto. III.

2 5° dprilis. 763

this Kingdom, , and the several Laws relating thereto, That the Committee had considered the same accordingly; and had directed him to make a Report of the Proceedings of the Committee to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Mr. John Warrington, a considerable Farmer at

Morden, in the County of Surrey, said, That Persons who are called Jobbers conliantly attend the Com Market at London, and buy up great Quantities of

Oats, which they lay up in their Granaries in Order to bring to Market again.

That these Persons, by their Agents, buy great Quantities of Oats of the Farmers about HarvestTime, when the Farmers are in want of Money, which they lay up in Granaries in the Country, and bring to Town foaringly, as they think they are wanted, by which Practice they keep up the Price.

That when the Port of London has been opened, great Quantities of Oats have been brought from abroad, but being brought sparingly to Market, the Price has still been kept up; and the Witness said. He thought this Practice might be remedied, if the Port of London was to be opened for the Importation of Oats Four Times in the Year.

Then the Witness mentioned the Names of several Persons who had bought up Corn at the Market in London, and laid up in Granaries in the Manner he had mentioned.

And being desired to explain the Difference between Corn Factors and Corn Jobbers, he said. That by a Corn Jobber he meant aPerson who buys Corn in one Market and carries it to another Market within a little Time, or buys it in the Country before it comes to Market; and that by a Factor he meant a Gentleman

who kept a Stand at Market, And received Corn from Cota 'f itnifi* the different Counties, and fold it for the Owners by Commission, and did not deal in Corn upoti his own Account.

And being asked, Whether the Corn so sent up by the Farmers to their Fa6tors was not laid up by theiC Factors in Granaries ? he Laid, He believed they might lay it up in their Granaries when it was cheap, and fend it into the Market when it was dear; which Practice, in his Opinion, kept up the Price of Corn at the Market.

That he was of Opinion, if the Port of London wds to be opened Four Times in the Year, it would be of Advantage to the Farmers, as they would find a better Market for their Com than at present, and would tend to prevent the Practice of buying Corn upon Specu* lation; and the Farmer would then bring his Corn to Market, where it would be bought by the People who are the real Consumers, and not by the Jobbers.

That when the Time is near for opening the Ports, the Jobbers bring groat Quantities to Market in order to lower the Price; and that when the Time for opening the Ports has elapsed, the Witness has constantly db-served the Price-of Corn to rife; and that he thinks this Grievance would be remedied, if Power was given to open the Port of London Four Times in the Yean

Then Mr. John Jacob, a Lighterman, was examined, who said. That he was employed in carrying Corn to the London Market; and that the Factors have at this Time got great Quantities of Com by them, and that some of them have or 5000 Quarters of Foreign Oats in One Place.

Then your Committee proceeded to take into Consideration- the Returns of the Prices of Corn at the Markets, at Oxford, Cambridge, and Winchester, for several Years pall, which were referred to them by the House, and are hereunto annexed, N° 1, 2, and 3.

AS Clerks of the Market for the Town of Cambridge, we have endeavoured, as far as we were able, to fltew our Pelves obedient to the Order of the honourable House of Commons, which we received the eighth Infiaut: But we cannot find that any Public Register of the Prices of Malt has heretofore been kept; or any other Accounts of the Prices of Wheat, but those delivered in to the Chief Magistrate, from Time to Time, for setting the Assize of Bread. These Accounts since the Year 1758, are of such a Nature as to answer the Purpose required} those preceding are only Accounts of the Middle Prices of Wheat delivered upon any considerable Alteration of the Prices in the Market. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Sum of Eighty thousand Pounds, remaining in the Receipt of the Exchequer, which was granted to His Majestyjin the last Session of Parliament, upon Account, for defraying the Charge of the Pay and Clothing of the Militia for One Year, beginning the 25th Day of 1765, be issued and applied towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty in this Session of Parliament.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enlarging the Term and Powers of Two Acts, made in the Eighth and Twenty-seventh Years of his late Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from Rochdale, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, to the Towns of Halifax and Ealand, in the County of York, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for div iding and inclosing the Open and Common Fields, Half Year Lands, Commons, and Waste Grounds, in the Parishes of Carlton Forehoe, and Kimberley, in the County of Norfolk, without any Amendment: And also, The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing several Open and Common Fields, Common Meadows, Commons, and Waste Grounds, within the Lordship or Liberty of Bametby upon the fVoulds, in the County of Lincoln, without any Amendment.

RefoLvecl, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties of Six Pence and One Shilling per Gallon, on Brandy Spirits, and Aqua Vitae, imported, not being the Produce of the Bri Colonies and Planta--tions, be applied to the same Lies, as the Duties laid on Brandy Spirits, and Aqua Vitae, by the said Act of the Thirty-third Year of Kin gGeorgthe Second, were made

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That for encouraging the Exportation of Hempen Cordage man ufaCUired, in Great Britain, from Hemp imported from Foreign Parts, and also from Hemp of the Growth of Great Britain, there be allowed, upon the Exportation thereof, a Bounty of Two Shillings and Four Pence Three Farthings for every Hundred Weight of such Cordage so exported; the said Bounty to be paid upon Exportation out of the Net Duties, which have been, or shall be, paid upon the Importation of all foreign I Iemp into this Kingdom.

Rrfolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the encouraging the Exportation of Hempen Cordage manufactured in Great Britain, the Drawback of Two Shillings and Ten Pence Halfpenny, now payable on all foreign Hemp exported from to Fo-

reign Parts, do cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Refulved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Part of the Duties, laid by a Resolution of this House, of the Tenth Day of this inilant May, upon Sugars imported into this Kingdom, from any British Colony, or Plantation on the Continent of America, as shall arise over and above the Duties now payable upon Sugars so imported, be paid into the Receipt of the Exchequer, and reserved for the Disposition of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duty of Three Shillings, laid by a Resolution of this House, of the said Day, upon every Piece of Cambrick and French Lawns, exported from this Kingdom to the British Colonies and Plantations in America, be also paid into the said Receipt, and reserved for the Disposition of Parliament.

Act of Parliament, for repairing any particular Highway, and to report the Matters as they shall appear to ' them, together with their Observations and Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House, That the Committee had inquired accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table;

Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

It appearing to your Committee, from the Evidence of Mr. Dalby, Clerk to the Trustees for repairing the Road from Tetbury towards Cirencester, in the County of

Gloucester, that the Act of Parliament now in Force, for repairing the said Road, was not properly executed; that the foils were greatly evaded; and that great Part of the said Road was Hill in a bad Condition, came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Carriages are permitted to travel upon the said Road, drawn by more Horses than are allowed by Act of Parliament; and that the Toll Renters take an extraordinary Price for such Horses.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Road in many Parts is not of sufficient Width, and that the Number of Quarries, upon the Sides thereof, makes it dangerous for Travellers.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That there is no Surveyor appointed for the said Road, but the Road let out to Day Labourers, and Men that give no Security for performing their Contracts.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.
